abstract: This paper deals with a neural network model in which each neuron performs a threshold logic function. An important property of the model is that it always converges to a stable state when operating in a serial mode [2,5]. This property is the basis of the potential applications of the model such as associative memory devices and combinatorial optimization [3,6]. One of the motivations for use of the model for solving hard combinatorial problems is the fact that it can be implemented by optical devices and thus operate at a higher speed than conventional electronics. The main theme in this work is to investigate the power of the model for solving NP-hard problems [4,8], and to understand the relation between speed of operation and the size of a neural network. In particular, it will be shown that for any NP-hard problem the existence of a polynomial size network that solves it implies that NP=co-NP. Also, for Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), even a polynomial size network that gets an €-approximate solution does not exist unless P=NP. The above results are of great practical interest, because right now it is possible to build neural networks which will operate fast but are limited in the number of neurons.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether fast neural hardware can solve hard combinatorial problems with reasonably sized networks. Its model uses neurons that perform threshold logic functions and always reaches a stable state when operated serially. That convergence property motivates applications in associative memory and optimization, while possible optical implementations motivate interest in operating speed.

The main results place complexity-theoretic conditions on network size. For any NP-hard problem, the existence of a polynomial-size network that solves it would imply NP equals co-NP. For the traveling salesman problem, the paper states that even a polynomial-size network producing an epsilon-approximate solution cannot exist unless P equals NP.

These are conditional limits on what the model can achieve with polynomially growing resources. They distinguish rapid operation of individual devices from the number of neurons needed to solve a problem. This distinction matters for the hardware motivation: a network can operate quickly while remaining constrained in size, and guaranteed convergence alone does not remove the computational difficulty of the optimization task.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional complexity limits showing that fast threshold networks still face strong size barriers when solving NP-hard problems.

title: On the Power of Neural Networks for Solving Hard Problems

abstract: We study networks of spiking neurons in which spikes are fired as a Poisson process. The state of a cell is determined by the instan(cid:173) taneous firing rate, and in the limit of high firing rates our model reduces to that studied by Hopfield. We find that the inclusion of spiking results in several new features, such as a noise-induced asymmetry between "on" and "off" states of the cells and probabil(cid:173) ity currents which destroy the usual description of network dynam(cid:173) ics in terms of energy surfaces. Taking account of spikes also al(cid:173) lows us to calibrate network parameters such as "synaptic weights" against experiments on real synapses. Realistic forms of the post synaptic response alters the network dynamics, which suggests a novel dynamical learning mechanism.

paragraphs: The paper studies networks in which neurons emit spikes according to a Poisson process. Each cell's state is described by its instantaneous firing rate. At high firing rates, the model approaches the Hopfield model, establishing a connection between the spiking formulation and a familiar description based on continuously represented neural activity.

Explicit spikes introduce effects that change the network's dynamics. Spike-related noise produces an asymmetry between cells' on and off states. The model also develops probability currents, which invalidate the usual account of network behavior in terms of an energy surface. Spiking therefore changes the structure of the dynamics rather than merely adding fluctuations to an otherwise equivalent model.

The formulation also connects network parameters, including synaptic weights, to experimental measurements of real synapses. Incorporating realistic postsynaptic responses further alters the dynamics and suggests a possible dynamical learning mechanism. The paper thus ties the mathematical consequences of spikes to the physical response properties of synapses and their potential role in learning.
summary.tldr: Explicit spiking creates asymmetries and probability currents that undermine the usual energy-surface description of neural network dynamics.

title: Non-Boltzmann Dynamics in Networks of Spiking Neurons

abstract: Central to the performance improvement of a committee relative to individual networks is the error correlation between networks in the committee. We investigated methods of achieving error indepen(cid:173) dence between the networks by training the networks with different resampling sets from the original training set. The methods were tested on the sinwave artificial task and the real-world problems of hepatoma (liver cancer) and breast cancer diagnoses.
originalAbstract: Central to the performance improvement of a committee relative to individual networks is the error correlation between networks in the committee. We investigated methods of achieving error indepen(cid:173) dence between the networks by training the networks with different resampling sets from the original training set. The methods were tested on the sinwave artificial task and the real-world problems of hepatoma (liver cancer) and breast cancer diagnoses.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to make a committee of neural networks more useful than its individual members. Its central concern is the relationship between their errors. If members tend to make mistakes on the same cases, combining them has less opportunity to improve performance. The authors therefore focus on encouraging independence among those errors.

Their approach trains the networks on different resampled versions of the original training set. Changing which examples each member learns from offers a way to influence the similarities between the resulting networks. The question is whether differences introduced through training data can produce the error diversity that a successful committee needs.

The methods are tested on an artificial sinwave task and on hepatoma and breast cancer diagnosis problems. This places the investigation in both an artificial setting and practical diagnostic applications. The abstract describes the methods and testing scope without stating a measured improvement. The contribution is the investigation of resampling as a way to control committee error relationships, a property that individual network accuracy alone does not capture.
summary.tldr: The paper studies whether training networks on different resampled datasets can reduce shared errors in diagnostic committees.

title: Improving Committee Diagnosis with Resampling Techniques

abstract: Many classification problems have the property that the only costly part of obtaining examples is the class label. This paper suggests a simple method for using distribution information contained in unlabeled examples to augment labeled examples in a supervised training framework. Empirical tests show that the technique de(cid:173) scribed in this paper can significantly improve the accuracy of a supervised learner when the learner is well below its asymptotic accuracy level.
originalAbstract: Many classification problems have the property that the only costly part of obtaining examples is the class label. This paper suggests a simple method for using distribution information contained in unlabeled examples to augment labeled examples in a supervised training framework. Empirical tests show that the technique de(cid:173) scribed in this paper can significantly improve the accuracy of a supervised learner when the learner is well below its asymptotic accuracy level.

paragraphs: In many classification tasks, collecting inputs is inexpensive while obtaining their labels is costly. A supervised learner may therefore have access to far more raw examples than labeled ones. This paper proposes using the distributional information in those unlabeled inputs to strengthen supervised training.

The method augments the information supplied by labeled examples with structure learned from the unlabeled sample distribution. Its purpose is to make better use of the examples already available, rather than treating every unannotated observation as unusable. The learning setup remains directed toward a classification task defined by the labeled data.

Empirical tests show significant accuracy improvements when the supervised learner is well below its asymptotic accuracy level. That condition highlights where additional distributional information can be especially valuable: the labeled sample alone has not yet exhausted the model’s achievable performance. The contribution is an early demonstration that useful supervision can be supplemented by abundant unlabeled data.
summary.tldr: Using unlabeled input-distribution information improves supervised classification when labeled-data performance remains below its asymptotic level.

title: Using Unlabeled Data for Supervised Learning

abstract: We present a Monte-Carlo simulation algorithm for real-time policy improvement of an adaptive controller. In the Monte-Carlo sim(cid:173) ulation, the long-term expected reward of each possible action is statistically measured, using the initial policy to make decisions in each step of the simulation. The action maximizing the measured expected reward is then taken, resulting in an improved policy. Our algorithm is easily parallelizable and has been implemented on the IBM SP! and SP2 parallel-RISC supercomputers. We have obtained promising initial results in applying this algo(cid:173) rithm to the domain of backgammon. Results are reported for a wide variety of initial policies, ranging from a random policy to TD-Gammon, an extremely strong multi-layer neural network. In each case, the Monte-Carlo algorithm gives a substantial reduction, by as much as a factor of 5 or more, in the error rate of the base players. The algorithm is also potentially useful in many other adaptive control applications in which it is possible to simulate the environment.

paragraphs: This paper improves a controller’s decisions by simulating what could happen after each available action. A starting policy supplies the decisions made later in each simulated trajectory. By repeating these simulations, the algorithm estimates the long-term expected reward associated with each candidate action and selects the one with the highest estimate.

The procedure uses an existing policy as the basis for real-time improvement. Its simulations are readily parallelized, and the authors implement it on IBM SP1 and SP2 parallel computers. The approach is potentially applicable to other control problems where the environment can be simulated, because its action comparisons depend on those simulated futures.

Initial backgammon results cover starting policies ranging from random play to the strong neural-network player TD-Gammon. Every tested starting policy benefits, with reported error-rate reductions reaching a factor of five or more. The findings show that simulation-based lookahead can improve both weak and strong decision rules by evaluating their longer-term consequences at the moment an action is needed.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo lookahead substantially improves backgammon policies by comparing simulated long-term rewards before each decision.

title: On-line Policy Improvement using Monte-Carlo Search

abstract: We study generalization capability of the mixture of experts learn(cid:173) ing from examples generated by another network with the same architecture. When the number of examples is smaller than a crit(cid:173) ical value, the network shows a symmetric phase where the role of the experts is not specialized. Upon crossing the critical point, the system undergoes a continuous phase transition to a symme(cid:173) try breaking phase where the gating network partitions the input space effectively and each expert is assigned to an appropriate sub(cid:173) space. We also find that the mixture of experts with multiple level of hierarchy shows multiple phase transitions.

When the number of examples is smaller than a crit(cid:173) ical value, the network shows a symmetric phase where the role of the experts is not specialized. Upon crossing the critical point, the system undergoes a continuous phase transition to a symme(cid:173) try breaking phase where the gating network partitions the input space effectively and each expert is assigned to an appropriate sub(cid:173) space. We also find that the mixture of experts with multiple level of hierarchy shows multiple phase transitions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a mixture of experts develops useful specialization as the number of training examples increases. The analysis assumes that examples come from another network with the same architecture. Within this matched setting, it examines when the learner’s experts begin taking on distinct roles and how that relates to generalization.

Below a critical number of examples, the system remains in a symmetric phase: its experts have not specialized. Once the sample size crosses that point, a continuous phase transition occurs. The gating network begins dividing the input space effectively, and each expert becomes associated with an appropriate part of that space.

For mixtures with multiple hierarchical levels, the authors find multiple phase transitions. This means the emergence of organization can involve more than one transition as data accumulate. The contribution provides a statistical-mechanics account of specialization: simply including several experts does not ensure distinct responsibilities, and sufficient training evidence is needed for the division of labor to emerge in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: A mixture of experts begins specializing after a critical sample size, with multiple transitions appearing in hierarchical models.

title: Statistical Mechanics of the Mixture of Experts

abstract: We describe the design, fabrication and test results of an analog CMOS VLSI neural network prototype chip intended for phase-based machine vision algorithms. The chip implements an image filtering operation similar to Gabor-filtering. Because a Gabor filter's output is complex valued, it can be used to define a phase at every pixel in an image. This phase can be used in robust algorithms for disparity estimation and bin(cid:173) ocular stereo vergence control in stereo vision and for image motion analysis. The chip reported here takes an input image and generates two outputs at every pixel corresponding to the real and imaginary parts of the output.
originalAbstract: We describe the design, fabrication and test results of an analog CMOS VLSI neural network prototype chip intended for phase-based machine vision algorithms. The chip implements an image filtering operation similar to Gabor-filtering. Because a Gabor filter's output is complex valued, it can be used to define a phase at every pixel in an image. This phase can be used in robust algorithms for disparity estimation and bin(cid:173) ocular stereo vergence control in stereo vision and for image motion analysis. The chip reported here takes an input image and generates two outputs at every pixel corresponding to the real and imaginary parts of the output.

paragraphs: This paper develops a physical neural network chip for an image-processing step used in phase-based vision. The authors describe its design, fabrication, and testing in analog CMOS circuitry. Its central operation resembles Gabor filtering, which transforms an image into a representation that carries local phase information.

The important feature is that the filter output has two parts: real and imaginary. Together, these define a phase value at each pixel. The chip produces both parts directly from an input image, making the information needed for phase-based processing available through its hardware outputs.

The abstract connects this representation to estimating differences between stereo images, controlling the alignment of binocular views, and analyzing image motion. These are motivations for the filtering hardware rather than separate reported application results. The contribution is a fabricated and tested prototype that implements the relevant image transformation, providing a concrete hardware building block for vision algorithms that use phase.
summary.tldr: A fabricated analog neural-network chip produces the two image-filter outputs needed to compute local phase for machine vision.

title: An Analog VLSI Neural Network for Phase-based Machine Vision

abstract: This paper applies the Mixture of Gaussians probabilistic model, com(cid:173) bined with Expectation Maximization optimization to the task of sum(cid:173) marizing three dimensional range data for a mobile robot. This provides a flexible way of dealing with uncertainties in sensor information, and al(cid:173) lows the introduction of prior knowledge into low-level perception mod(cid:173) ules. Problems with the basic approach were solved in several ways: the mixture of Gaussians was reparameterized to reflect the types of objects expected in the scene, and priors on model parameters were included in the optimization process. Both approaches force the optimization to find 'interesting' objects, given the sensor and object characteristics. A higher level classifier was used to interpret the results provided by the model, and to reject spurious solutions.

paragraphs: The paper applies Gaussian mixture modeling to three-dimensional range data used by a mobile robot. Expectation maximization fits the model, producing a probabilistic summary of the sensor observations. The approach is intended to handle uncertainty in sensing and allow prior knowledge to influence low-level perception in the robot-docking setting.

The authors address problems with the basic method in two ways. They change the mixture's parameterization to reflect the kinds of objects expected in a scene, and incorporate priors on model parameters into optimization. These choices steer the fitted model toward objects of interest given the sensor characteristics and the expected object structure.

A higher-level classifier then interprets the model's output and rejects spurious solutions. The resulting approach combines probabilistic data summarization, object-informed fitting, and subsequent classification. Its significance is that obtaining a useful scene interpretation involves more than fitting a generic mixture: knowledge about the expected objects guides optimization, and a separate interpretation stage filters out misleading results.
summary.tldr: Gaussian mixtures summarize robot range data, with object-specific parameterization, priors, and a higher-level classifier guiding useful interpretations.

title: Robot Docking Using Mixtures of Gaussians

abstract: We present ongoing work on a project for automatic recognition of spon- taneous facial actions. Spontaneous facial expressions differ substan- tially from posed expressions, similar to how continuous, spontaneous speech differs from isolated words produced on command. Previous methods for automatic facial expression recognition assumed images were collected in controlled environments in which the subjects delib- erately faced the camera. Since people often nod or turn their heads, automatic recognition of spontaneous facial behavior requires methods for handling out-of-image-plane head rotations. Here we explore an ap- proach based on 3-D warping of images into canonical views. We eval- uated the performance of the approach as a front-end for a spontaneous expression recognition system using support vector machines and hidden Markov models. This system employed general purpose learning mech- anisms that can be applied to recognition of any facial movement. The system was tested for recognition of a set of facial actions deﬁned by the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). We showed that 3D tracking and warping followed by machine learning techniques directly applied to the warped images, is a viable and promising technology for automatic facial expression recognition. One exciting aspect of the approach pre- sented here is that information about movement dynamics emerged out of ﬁlters which were derived from the statistics of images.

paragraphs: Recognizing spontaneous facial behavior requires handling more than deliberately posed expressions. People turn and nod their heads, changing how facial movements appear to a camera. This project explores how to recognize those movements when the face rotates out of the image plane, moving beyond collection conditions that require subjects to face the camera.

The proposed front end uses three-dimensional tracking and image warping to transform facial images into standardized views. Support vector machines and hidden Markov models then operate on the warped images. This arrangement makes viewpoint handling part of the recognition process, so the learning methods can work with images brought into a more consistent orientation.

The prototype was tested on a set of movements defined by the Facial Action Coding System. The authors describe the combined tracking, warping, and learning approach as viable and promising for spontaneous expression recognition. They also report that filters derived from image statistics captured information about movement dynamics. These findings support the approach as ongoing prototype work, rather than establishing complete recognition of spontaneous facial behavior.
summary.tldr: A prototype combines 3D face tracking and image warping with learned classifiers to recognize spontaneous facial actions despite head rotation.

title: A Prototype for Automatic Recognition of Spontaneous Facial Actions

abstract: The equivalent kernel [1] is a way of understanding how Gaussian process regression works for large sample sizes based on a continuum limit. In this paper we show (1) how to approximate the equivalent kernel of the widely-used squared exponential (or Gaussian) kernel and related kernels, and (2) how analysis using the equivalent kernel helps to understand the learning curves for Gaussian processes.
originalAbstract: The equivalent kernel [1] is a way of understanding how Gaussian process regression works for large sample sizes based on a continuum limit. In this paper we show (1) how to approximate the equivalent kernel of the widely-used squared exponential (or Gaussian) kernel and related kernels, and (2) how analysis using the equivalent kernel helps to understand the learning curves for Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: This paper uses the equivalent kernel to explain Gaussian-process regression when the sample size is large. The equivalent-kernel viewpoint relies on a continuum limit, replacing the finite collection of observations with a mathematical description suited to large-sample analysis. Its purpose is to make the regression method's behavior easier to understand in that regime.

The first contribution is a way to approximate the equivalent kernel associated with the widely used squared-exponential, or Gaussian, kernel and related kernels. This gives the analysis a concrete target rather than leaving it as a general viewpoint. The approximation concerns the equivalent kernel used to understand regression, with the large-sample continuum setting remaining part of its interpretation.

The second contribution uses that analysis to explain Gaussian-process learning curves: how learning behavior changes with the amount of data. Together, the two results connect a kernel approximation with questions about improvement as samples accumulate. The paper's emphasis is explanatory, providing a mathematical route from the kernel choice to understanding large-sample regression behavior.
summary.tldr: Equivalent-kernel approximations help explain large-sample Gaussian-process regression and its learning curves.

title: Using the Equivalent Kernel to Understand Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: This paper proposes a method for computing fast approximations to support vector decision functions in the field of object detection. In the present approach we are building on an existing algorithm where the set of support vectors is replaced by a smaller, so-called reduced set of synthesized input space points. In contrast to the existing method that finds the reduced set via unconstrained optimization, we impose a structural constraint on the synthetic points such that the resulting approximations can be evaluated via separable filters. For applications that require scanning large images, this decreases the computational complexity by a significant amount. Experimental results show that in face detection, rank deficient approximations are 4 to 6 times faster than unconstrained reduced set systems.

In the present approach we are building on an existing algorithm where the set of support vectors is replaced by a smaller, so-called reduced set of synthesized input space points. In contrast to the existing method that finds the reduced set via unconstrained optimization, we impose a structural constraint on the synthetic points such that the resulting approximations can be evaluated via separable filters. For applications that require scanning large images, this decreases the computational complexity by a significant amount. paragraphs: The paper aims to make support vector decision functions faster to evaluate for object detection. Detection can require scanning large images, so the cost of repeatedly applying the decision function matters. The starting point is an existing approximation that replaces the original support vectors with a smaller collection of synthesized points in the input space.

The authors change how those replacement points are constructed. Instead of allowing unconstrained optimization, they impose a structural restriction that makes the resulting approximation evaluable using separable filters. Thus, the method reduces computational effort through the form of the replacement points as well as through the smaller size of the set.

In face-detection experiments, the rank-deficient approximations run four to six times faster than unconstrained reduced-set systems. This result directly supports the computational value of the structural constraint in the tested application. The broader contribution is an approximation strategy that takes the eventual cost of scanning images into account when constructing a faster decision function.
summary.tldr: Structurally constrained support-vector approximations enable separable filtering and achieve four-to-sixfold speedups over unconstrained reduced-set systems in face detection.

title: Face Detection --- Efficient and Rank Deficient

abstract: Images represent an important and abundant source of data. Understanding their statistical structure has important applications such as image compression and restoration. In this paper we propose a particular kind of probabilistic model, dubbed the "products of edge-perts model" to describe the structure of wavelet transformed images. We develop a practical denoising algorithm based on a single edge-pert and show state-ofthe-art denoising performance on benchmark images.
originalAbstract: Images represent an important and abundant source of data. Understanding their statistical structure has important applications such as image compression and restoration. In this paper we propose a particular kind of probabilistic model, dubbed the "products of edge-perts model" to describe the structure of wavelet transformed images. We develop a practical denoising algorithm based on a single edge-pert and show state-ofthe-art denoising performance on benchmark images.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a probabilistic model for the statistical structure of images after a wavelet transform. The motivation is that understanding image statistics can support applications such as compression and restoration. The representation being modeled is therefore the transformed image, and the contribution concerns how its structure is described probabilistically.

The authors call their model a product of edge-perts. Alongside the modeling proposal, they develop a practical denoising algorithm based on a single edge-pert. This distinction matters: the broader probabilistic model and the demonstrated restoration procedure are related, but the denoising result is specifically attributed to a single component.

On benchmark images, the algorithm achieves what the authors report as state-of-the-art denoising performance. This supplies an application-based demonstration of the usefulness of their image model. Although compression is part of the motivation for studying image statistics, the stated experimental finding concerns denoising. The paper thus links a proposed statistical representation to a concrete image-restoration method and reported benchmark results.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model of wavelet-transformed images leads to a single-edge-pert denoiser with reported state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

title: Products of ``Edge-perts

abstract: We propose a model that leverages the millions of clicks received by web search engines, to predict document relevance. This allows the comparison of ranking functions when clicks are available but complete relevance judgments are not. After an initial training phase using a set of relevance judgments paired with click data, we show that our model can predict the relevance score of documents that have not been judged. These predictions can be used to evaluate the performance of a search engine, using our novel formalization of the confidence of the standard evaluation metric discounted cumulative gain (DCG), so comparisons can be made across time and datasets. This contrasts with previous methods which can provide only pair-wise relevance judgements between results shown for the same query. When no relevance judgments are available, we can identify the better of two ranked lists up to 82% of the time, and with only two relevance judgments for each query, we can identify the better ranking up to 94% of the time. While our experiments are on sponsored search results, which is the financial backbone of web search, our method is general enough to be applicable to algorithmic web search results as well. Furthermore, we give an algorithm to guide the selection of additional documents to judge to improve confidence.

paragraphs: Search engines collect abundant clicks, but complete human judgments of document relevance are harder to obtain. This paper learns a relationship between clicks and relevance using paired training data, then predicts relevance scores for documents that have not been judged. Those predictions make it possible to compare ranking functions despite incomplete judgments.

The authors also formalize confidence in discounted cumulative gain, a ranking evaluation measure. This supports comparisons across time and datasets, extending beyond relative judgments between results displayed for the same query. An additional algorithm selects documents for further human judgment with the aim of improving confidence in the evaluation.

In experiments on sponsored search, the method identifies the better of two ranked lists up to 82% of the time without relevance judgments, and up to 94% with two judgments per query. These are reported maximum results in the evaluated setting. The authors describe the method as general enough for ordinary web search as well, while the experiments themselves concern sponsored results.
summary.tldr: A model linking clicks to relevance supports ranking evaluation with incomplete judgments and quantifies confidence in the resulting scores.

title: Evaluating Search Engines by Modeling the Relationship Between Relevance and Clicks

abstract: We present a simple variant of the k-d tree which automatically adapts to intrinsic low dimensional structure in data.
originalAbstract: We present a simple variant of the k-d tree which automatically adapts to intrinsic low dimensional structure in data.
title: Learning the structure of manifolds using random projections

abstract: Many motor skills in humanoid robotics can be learned using parametrized motor primitives as done in imitation learning. However, most interesting motor learning problems are high-dimensional reinforcement learning problems often beyond the reach of current methods. In this paper, we extend previous work on policy learning from the immediate reward case to episodic reinforcement learning. We show that this results into a general, common framework also connected to policy gradient methods and yielding a novel algorithm for policy learning by assuming a form of exploration that is particularly well-suited for dynamic motor primitives. The resulting algorithm is an EM-inspired algorithm applicable in complex motor learning tasks. We compare this algorithm to alternative parametrized policy search methods and show that it outperforms previous methods. We apply it in the context of motor learning and show that it can learn a complex Ball-in-a-Cup task using a real Barrett WAM robot arm.

However, most interesting motor learning problems are high-dimensional reinforcement learning problems often beyond the reach of current methods. In this paper, we extend previous work on policy learning from the immediate reward case to episodic reinforcement learning. We show that this results into a general, common framework also connected to policy gradient methods and yielding a novel algorithm for policy learning by assuming a form of exploration that is particularly well-suited for dynamic motor primitives. The resulting algorithm is an EM-inspired algorithm applicable in complex motor learning tasks. We compare this algorithm to alternative parametrized policy search methods and show that it outperforms previous methods. We apply it in the context of motor learning and show that it can learn a complex Ball-in-a-Cup task using a real Barrett WAM robot arm.

paragraphs: Parameterized motor primitives provide a way to represent robot skills using adjustable movement patterns. Although such representations are useful in imitation learning, improving complex movements through reinforcement learning remains difficult in high dimensions. The paper develops policy learning for these motor representations over complete episodes.

The authors extend earlier work on immediate rewards to episodic reinforcement learning, producing a common framework connected to policy gradient methods. Within it, they assume an exploration form particularly suited to dynamic motor primitives. This leads to a new policy-learning algorithm inspired by expectation-maximization.

The approach matters because it links how a movement is represented with how the learner explores changes to that movement. The authors compare the algorithm with alternative parameterized policy search methods and report better performance than previous methods in their comparisons. They also demonstrate learning a complex Ball-in-a-Cup skill on a real Barrett WAM robot arm. This application provides a concrete motor-learning demonstration alongside the broader algorithmic framework.
summary.tldr: An EM-inspired episodic policy-search algorithm uses exploration suited to motor primitives and learns Ball-in-a-Cup on a real robot.

title: Policy Search for Motor Primitives in Robotics

abstract: We propose new methodologies to detect anomalies in discrete-time processes taking values in a set. The method is based on the inference of functionals whose evaluations on successive states visited by the process have low autocorrelations. Deviations from this behavior are used to flag anomalies. The candidate functionals are estimated in a subset of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with the set where the process takes values. We provide experimental results which show that these techniques compare favorably with other algorithms.
originalAbstract: We propose new methodologies to detect anomalies in discrete-time processes taking values in a set. The method is based on the inference of functionals whose evaluations on successive states visited by the process have low autocorrelations. Deviations from this behavior are used to flag anomalies. The candidate functionals are estimated in a subset of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with the set where the process takes values. We provide experimental results which show that these techniques compare favorably with other algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper detects anomalies in processes observed at discrete time steps. It learns functions that turn each visited state into a numerical evaluation, then examines how those evaluations relate across time. The target behavior is low autocorrelation, meaning that successive evaluations have little of the temporal correlation being measured.

Anomalies are flagged when the evaluations depart from that learned behavior. This makes the temporal relationship among transformed states the detection signal. The method therefore depends on learning a useful transformation of the state sequence, rather than assessing each state only through its individual appearance.

The candidate functions are estimated within a subset of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with the process's state set. This gives the learning problem a structured family of possible transformations. Experiments show that the proposed techniques compare favorably with other algorithms. The contribution is a detection strategy organized around departures from low temporal autocorrelation, together with a kernel-based method for learning the functions that expose those departures in the observed process.
summary.tldr: Learned functions expose anomalies through deviations from low autocorrelation in transformed process states.

title: White Functionals for Anomaly Detection in Dynamical Systems

abstract: Given a matrix M of low-rank, we consider the problem of reconstructing it from noisy observations of a small, random subset of its entries. The problem arises in a variety of applications, from collaborative filtering (the ‘Netflix problem’) to structure-from-motion and positioning. We study a low complexity algorithm introduced in [1], based on a combination of spectral techniques and manifold optimization, that we call here OPTSPACE. We prove performance guarantees that are order-optimal in a number of circumstances.

We study a low complexity algorithm introduced in [1], based on a combination of spectral techniques and manifold optimization, that we call here OPTSPACE. We prove performance guarantees that are order-optimal in a number of circumstances.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reconstruct a low-rank matrix when only a small, randomly selected portion of its entries is observed and those observations contain noise. Low rank supplies the structure that makes reconstruction possible: the matrix has fewer independent directions of variation than a general matrix of the same size.

The authors analyze OPTSPACE, a previously introduced algorithm that combines spectral techniques with manifold optimization. Spectral techniques work with the matrix's underlying linear structure, while manifold optimization provides a way to optimize over structured candidates. The paper describes the algorithm as having low computational complexity, making the relationship between efficient computation and reconstruction quality central to the study.

Its main contribution is a set of proven performance guarantees that are order-optimal in a number of circumstances. This is a qualified optimality statement about how performance scales in those circumstances. The problem connects to collaborative filtering, structure from motion, and positioning, where useful information must be recovered from incomplete and imperfect measurements.
summary.tldr: OPTSPACE combines spectral methods and manifold optimization to recover low-rank matrices from noisy partial observations, with order-optimal guarantees in several circumstances.

title: Matrix Completion from Noisy Entries

abstract: We propose a computationally efficient random walk on a convex body which rapidly mixes to a time-varying Gibbs distribution. In the setting of online convex optimization and repeated games, the algorithm yields low regret and presents a novel efficient method for implementing mixture forecasting strategies.
originalAbstract: We propose a computationally efficient random walk on a convex body which rapidly mixes to a time-varying Gibbs distribution. In the setting of online convex optimization and repeated games, the algorithm yields low regret and presents a novel efficient method for implementing mixture forecasting strategies.

paragraphs: The paper develops a random-walk method for online convex optimization and repeated games. In these settings, decisions are made over time, and low regret is a way to assess their cumulative quality. The proposed algorithm connects that sequential decision problem to efficient sampling within a convex body.

Its central property is rapid mixing toward a Gibbs distribution that changes over time. Mixing describes how the random walk approaches the target distribution. The moving target is important here: the method is designed to follow an evolving distribution, rather than only approximate a single fixed one. The abstract states that this process is computationally efficient.

Applied to online optimization and repeated games, the algorithm yields low regret and provides an efficient implementation of mixture forecasting strategies. The contribution brings together the quality of sequential decisions and the computation needed to produce them. A rapidly mixing walk supplies the computational mechanism, while the low-regret result connects that mechanism to the forecasting and game-playing settings identified in the paper.
summary.tldr: An efficient random walk tracks changing Gibbs distributions to implement mixture forecasting with low regret.

title: Random Walk Approach to Regret Minimization

abstract: This paper is concerned with the generalization analysis on learning to rank for information retrieval (IR). In IR, data are hierarchically organized, i.e., consisting of queries and documents per query. Previous generalization analysis for ranking, however, has not fully considered this structure, and cannot explain how the simultaneous change of query number and document number in the training data will affect the performance of algorithms. In this paper, we propose performing generalization analysis under the assumption of two-layer sampling, i.e., the i.i.d. sampling of queries and the conditional i.i.d sampling of documents per query. Such a sampling can better describe the generation mechanism of real data, and the corresponding generalization analysis can better explain the real behaviors of learning to rank algorithms. However, it is challenging to perform such analysis, because the documents associated with different queries are not identically distributed, and the documents associated with the same query become no longer independent if represented by features extracted from the matching between document and query. To tackle the challenge, we decompose the generalization error according to the two layers, and make use of the new concept of two-layer Rademacher average. The generalization bounds we obtained are quite intuitive and are in accordance with previous empirical studies on the performance of ranking algorithms.

The paper argues that earlier generalization analyses did not fully represent this structure. The contribution clarifies how training-data organization enters theoretical accounts of ranking performance.
summary.tldr: A two-layer generalization analysis accounts separately for sampled queries and their documents when explaining ranking performance.

title: Two-Layer Generalization Analysis for Ranking Using Rademacher Average

abstract: Developments in neural recording technology are rapidly enabling the recording of populations of neurons in multiple brain areas simultaneously, as well as the identification of the types of neurons being recorded (e.g., excitatory vs. inhibitory). There is a growing need for statistical methods to study the interaction among multiple, labeled populations of neurons. Rather than attempting to identify direct interactions between neurons (where the number of interactions grows with the number of neurons squared), we propose to extract a smaller number of latent variables from each population and study how the latent variables interact. Specifically, we propose extensions to probabilistic canonical correlation analysis (pCCA) to capture the temporal structure of the latent variables, as well as to distinguish within-population dynamics from across-population interactions (termed Group Latent Auto-Regressive Analysis, gLARA). We then applied these methods to populations of neurons recorded simultaneously in visual areas V1 and V2, and found that gLARA provides a better description of the recordings than pCCA. This work provides a foundation for studying how multiple populations of neurons interact and how this interaction supports brain function.

Directly modeling every neuron-to-neuron connection becomes cumbersome because the number of possible interactions grows quadratically with neuron count. This paper instead summarizes each labeled population with a smaller set of latent variables and studies relationships among those summaries.

The authors extend probabilistic canonical correlation analysis to incorporate temporal structure. Their method, Group Latent Auto-Regressive Analysis, or gLARA, also distinguishes dynamics within a population from interactions across populations. That separation is central: variation internal to one group and variation associated with another group are represented as different components of the analysis.

Applied to simultaneous recordings from visual areas V1 and V2, gLARA describes the recordings better than probabilistic canonical correlation analysis. This empirical result supports including both temporal dynamics and population structure in the model. The approach provides a foundation for studying interactions at the population level through a compact representation, without requiring a direct connection estimate for every pair of recorded neurons.
summary.tldr: gLARA models temporal activity within and between neural populations through latent variables, improving the description of simultaneous V1 and V2 recordings.

title: Extracting Latent Structure From Multiple Interacting Neural Populations

abstract: We present a general framework for constructing prior distributions with structured variables. The prior is defined as the information projection of a base distribution onto distributions supported on the constraint set of interest. In cases where this projection is intractable, we propose a family of parameterized approximations indexed by subsets of the domain. We further analyze the special case of sparse structure. While the optimal prior is intractable in general, we show that approximate inference using convex subsets is tractable, and is equivalent to maximizing a submodular function subject to cardinality constraints. As a result, inference using greedy forward selection provably achieves within a factor of (1-1/e) of the optimal objective value. Our work is motivated by the predictive modeling of high-dimensional functional neuroimaging data. For this task, we employ the Gaussian base distribution induced by local partial correlations and consider the design of priors to capture the domain knowledge of sparse support. Experimental results on simulated data and high dimensional neuroimaging data show the effectiveness of our approach in terms of support recovery and predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to build prior distributions that respect structural constraints. Starting with a base distribution, it defines the prior through an information projection onto distributions supported by the desired constraint set. The construction connects an existing probabilistic model with knowledge about which variable configurations should be allowed.

When the exact projection is computationally intractable, the authors introduce parameterized approximations based on subsets of the domain. For sparse structure, they show that approximate inference using convex subsets is tractable and equivalent to a cardinality-constrained submodular maximization problem. The authors use a Gaussian base distribution induced by local partial correlations and construct priors encoding sparse support. Experiments on simulated and neuroimaging data show effectiveness in support recovery and prediction. The approximation guarantee concerns the specified optimization objective; it provides a principled computational route despite the general intractability of the optimal prior.
summary.tldr: Information-projected priors encode structural constraints, with a tractable sparse approximation that supports a 1−1/e greedy optimization guarantee.

title: On Prior Distributions and Approximate Inference for Structured Variables

abstract: In this paper, we consider the Forward--Backward proximal splitting algorithm to minimize the sum of two proper closed convex functions, one of which having a Lipschitz continuous gradient and the other being partly smooth relatively to an active manifold $\mathcal{M}$. We propose a generic framework in which we show that the Forward--Backward (i) correctly identifies the active manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in a finite number of iterations, and then (ii) enters a local linear convergence regime that we characterize precisely. This gives a grounded and unified explanation to the typical behaviour that has been observed numerically for many problems encompassed in our framework, including the Lasso, the group Lasso, the fused Lasso and the nuclear norm regularization to name a few. These results may have numerous applications including in signal/image processing processing, sparse recovery and machine learning.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we consider the Forward--Backward proximal splitting algorithm to minimize the sum of two proper closed convex functions, one of which having a Lipschitz continuous gradient and the other being partly smooth relatively to an active manifold $\mathcal{M}$. We propose a generic framework in which we show that the Forward--Backward (i) correctly identifies the active manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in a finite number of iterations, and then (ii) enters a local linear convergence regime that we characterize precisely. This gives a grounded and unified explanation to the typical behaviour that has been observed numerically for many problems encompassed in our framework, including the Lasso, the group Lasso, the fused Lasso and the nuclear norm regularization to name a few. These results may have numerous applications including in signal/image processing processing, sparse recovery and machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies Forward–Backward proximal splitting for objectives formed by adding two convex functions. One has a Lipschitz-continuous gradient, meaning its gradient changes in a controlled way. The other is partly smooth relative to an active manifold, a structured region on which its behavior is smoother.

Within the proposed framework, the algorithm has two stages of behavior. It first identifies the correct active manifold after finitely many iterations. It then enters a local linear convergence regime, with geometric progress toward the solution. The authors precisely characterize this second regime, connecting the algorithm's eventual speed to the structure it has identified.

This gives a unified mathematical explanation for behavior previously observed numerically across problems including Lasso, group Lasso, fused Lasso, and nuclear-norm regularization. The contribution is especially useful because these seemingly different regularizers fit a common account of structure identification followed by faster local convergence. The guarantee concerns problems encompassed by the framework and a local convergence phase, rather than asserting a linear rate from the beginning for every convex objective.
summary.tldr: Under the paper's partial-smoothness framework, Forward–Backward splitting identifies active structure finitely and then converges locally at a linear rate.

title: Local Linear Convergence of Forward--Backward under Partial Smoothness

abstract: In many applications of black-box optimization, one can evaluate multiple points simultaneously, e.g. when evaluating the performances of several different neural network architectures in a parallel computing environment. In this paper, we develop a novel batch Bayesian optimization algorithm --- the parallel knowledge gradient method. By construction, this method provides the one-step Bayes optimal batch of points to sample. We provide an efficient strategy for computing this Bayes-optimal batch of points, and we demonstrate that the parallel knowledge gradient method finds global optima significantly faster than previous batch Bayesian optimization algorithms on both synthetic test functions and when tuning hyperparameters of practical machine learning algorithms, especially when function evaluations are noisy.
originalAbstract: In many applications of black-box optimization, one can evaluate multiple points simultaneously, e.g. when evaluating the performances of several different neural network architectures in a parallel computing environment. In this paper, we develop a novel batch Bayesian optimization algorithm --- the parallel knowledge gradient method. By construction, this method provides the one-step Bayes optimal batch of points to sample. We provide an efficient strategy for computing this Bayes-optimal batch of points, and we demonstrate that the parallel knowledge gradient method finds global optima significantly faster than previous batch Bayesian optimization algorithms on both synthetic test functions and when tuning hyperparameters of practical machine learning algorithms, especially when function evaluations are noisy.

paragraphs: The paper addresses black-box optimization when several candidate points can be evaluated simultaneously. One example is testing multiple neural-network architectures using parallel computing resources. The decision is therefore which group of evaluations to run together, making batch selection part of how an optimization method uses the available computational resources.

The proposed parallel knowledge gradient method is a batch Bayesian optimization algorithm. By construction, it chooses a batch that is Bayes optimal for a one-step decision. That qualification matters: the stated optimality concerns the next batch under the Bayesian criterion. The authors also provide an efficient strategy for computing the batch prescribed by that criterion.

Experiments use both synthetic test functions and hyperparameter tuning for practical machine learning algorithms. The method finds global optima significantly faster than previous batch Bayesian optimization methods in those evaluations, with especially strong results when evaluations are noisy. The contribution combines a principled criterion for selecting simultaneous evaluations with a computational strategy and evidence of practical optimization gains.
summary.tldr: Parallel knowledge gradient selects one-step Bayes-optimal evaluation batches and empirically speeds optimization, particularly with noisy evaluations.

title: The Parallel Knowledge Gradient Method for Batch Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Experience constantly shapes neural circuits through a variety of plasticity mechanisms. While the functional roles of some plasticity mechanisms are well-understood, it remains unclear how changes in neural excitability contribute to learning. Here, we develop a normative interpretation of intrinsic plasticity (IP) as a key component of unsupervised learning. We introduce a novel generative mixture model that accounts for the class-specific statistics of stimulus intensities, and we derive a neural circuit that learns the input classes and their intensities. We will analytically show that inference and learning for our generative model can be achieved by a neural circuit with intensity-sensitive neurons equipped with a specific form of IP. Numerical experiments verify our analytical derivations and show robust behavior for artificial and natural stimuli. Our results link IP to non-trivial input statistics, in particular the statistics of stimulus intensities for classes to which a neuron is sensitive. More generally, our work paves the way toward new classification algorithms that are robust to intensity variations.

This paper gives that plasticity a normative interpretation: it identifies a learning problem that a specific form of excitability change can help solve. The focus is learning stimulus classes together with their intensity statistics.

The authors introduce a generative mixture model that accounts for intensity distributions specific to each class. They analytically derive a neural circuit capable of carrying out inference and learning for this model. Its neurons are sensitive to intensity and possess a particular form of intrinsic plasticity, linking the circuit mechanism to the statistical task.

Numerical experiments support the derivations and show robust behavior with artificial and natural stimuli. The findings connect intrinsic plasticity to the intensity statistics of the classes a neuron responds to. More broadly, the authors suggest that this connection could inform classification algorithms robust to intensity variation. That prospective application follows from the model and experiments; it is presented as a direction enabled by the work.
summary.tldr: A generative model explains how a specific form of neuronal intrinsic plasticity can learn class-dependent stimulus intensity statistics.

title: Neurons Equipped with Intrinsic Plasticity Learn Stimulus Intensity Statistics

abstract: Sequentially learning to place items in multi-position displays or lists is a task that can be cast into the multiple-play semi-bandit setting. However, a major concern in this context is when the system cannot decide whether the user feedback for each item is actually exploitable. Indeed, much of the content may have been simply ignored by the user. The present work proposes to exploit available information regarding the display position bias under the so-called Position-based click model (PBM). We first discuss how this model differs from the Cascade model and its variants considered in several recent works on multiple-play bandits. We then provide a novel regret lower bound for this model as well as computationally efficient algorithms that display good empirical and theoretical performance.

paragraphs: A system that repeatedly places items in a list must learn from feedback while deciding what to display next. The difficulty is that an item may receive no useful feedback because the user ignored it. Without accounting for this, the system faces ambiguity about what observed behavior says about the item itself.

The paper studies this problem in a multiple-play semi-bandit setting using the Position-based click model. It proposes exploiting available information about how display position biases user attention. The authors also explain how this model differs from the Cascade model and its variants, making the feedback assumptions central to the learning problem.

The theoretical contribution includes a new regret lower bound for the position-based model, characterizing limits on sequential learning performance. The authors also provide computationally efficient algorithms with favorable theoretical and empirical results. Together, these contributions address both what performance is fundamentally attainable under this click model and how to learn effectively when displayed content may go unnoticed.
summary.tldr: Position-aware bandit algorithms use known display bias to learn from ambiguous click feedback, with new regret bounds and favorable empirical results.

title: Multiple-Play Bandits in the Position-Based Model

abstract: In supervised binary hashing, one wants to learn a function that maps a high-dimensional feature vector to a vector of binary codes, for application to fast image retrieval. This typically results in a difficult optimization problem, nonconvex and nonsmooth, because of the discrete variables involved. Much work has simply relaxed the problem during training, solving a continuous optimization, and truncating the codes a posteriori. This gives reasonable results but is quite suboptimal. Recent work has tried to optimize the objective directly over the binary codes and achieved better results, but the hash function was still learned a posteriori, which remains suboptimal. We propose a general framework for learning hash functions using affinity-based loss functions that uses auxiliary coordinates. This closes the loop and optimizes jointly over the hash functions and the binary codes so that they gradually match each other. The resulting algorithm can be seen as an iterated version of the procedure of optimizing first over the codes and then learning the hash function. Compared to this, our optimization is guaranteed to obtain better hash functions while being not much slower, as demonstrated experimentally in various supervised datasets. In addition, our framework facilitates the design of optimization algorithms for arbitrary types of loss and hash functions.

paragraphs: Supervised binary hashing learns to turn high-dimensional features into binary codes for fast image retrieval. The discrete codes make training nonconvex and nonsmooth. Common approaches simplify the problem by first learning continuous representations or by choosing binary codes before separately learning a function that produces them.

This paper introduces a framework based on auxiliary coordinates that jointly optimizes the codes and the hash function. The two are repeatedly adjusted so that they gradually match. This closes a gap in procedures that optimize codes once and only afterward fit the function: the chosen representations and the function responsible for generating them can influence each other throughout optimization.

Relative to the procedure of first optimizing codes and then learning the function, the authors state a guarantee of better hash functions. Experiments on several supervised datasets demonstrate the improvement with only a modest increase in runtime. The framework also supports designing optimization methods for different losses and hash-function types. Its main contribution is making the relationship between codes and their generating function part of the optimization itself.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary coordinates let binary codes and hash functions improve together, strengthening a common two-stage approach with little reported runtime overhead.

title: Optimizing affinity-based binary hashing using auxiliary coordinates

abstract: Stochastic gradient methods for machine learning and optimization problems are usually analyzed assuming data points are sampled with replacement. In contrast, sampling without replacement is far less understood, yet in practice it is very common, often easier to implement, and usually performs better. In this paper, we provide competitive convergence guarantees for without-replacement sampling under several scenarios, focusing on the natural regime of few passes over the data. Moreover, we describe a useful application of these results in the context of distributed optimization with randomly-partitioned data, yielding a nearly-optimal algorithm for regularized least squares (in terms of both communication complexity and runtime complexity) under broad parameter regimes. Our proof techniques combine ideas from stochastic optimization, adversarial online learning and transductive learning theory, and can potentially be applied to other stochastic optimization and learning problems.

In contrast, sampling without replacement is far less understood, yet in practice it is very common, often easier to implement, and usually performs better. Moreover, we describe a useful application of these results in the context of distributed optimization with randomly-partitioned data, yielding a nearly-optimal algorithm for regularized least squares (in terms of both communication complexity and runtime complexity) under broad parameter regimes. Our proof techniques combine ideas from stochastic optimization, adversarial online learning and transductive learning theory, and can potentially be applied to other stochastic optimization and learning problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods are often analyzed as though each data point is sampled with replacement. Practical training commonly samples without replacement, so examples are not repeatedly selected within the same pass. This paper develops convergence guarantees for that widely used setting, concentrating on runs that make only a few passes over the dataset.

The authors establish competitive guarantees under several scenarios and apply them to distributed optimization with randomly partitioned data. For regularized least squares, the resulting algorithm is nearly optimal in both communication cost and runtime across broad parameter regimes. The random partitioning and stated parameter regimes are part of the setting supporting that application.

The proofs combine ideas from stochastic optimization, adversarial online learning, and transductive learning theory. This combination supplies tools for analyzing sampling behavior that differs from the usual with-replacement assumptions. The authors suggest that the techniques could apply to other optimization and learning problems. That wider applicability is a possibility, while the convergence results and distributed least-squares application are the concrete contributions reported.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence guarantees for without-replacement gradient sampling and derives a nearly optimal distributed least-squares algorithm in broad parameter regimes.

title: Without-Replacement Sampling for Stochastic Gradient Methods

abstract: Better understanding of the potential benefits of information transfer and representation learning is an important step towards the goal of building intelligent systems that are able to persist in the world and learn over time. In this work, we consider a setting where the learner encounters a stream of tasks but is able to retain only limited information from each encountered task, such as a learned predictor. In contrast to most previous works analyzing this scenario, we do not make any distributional assumptions on the task generating process. Instead, we formulate a complexity measure that captures the diversity of the observed tasks. We provide a lifelong learning algorithm with error guarantees for every observed task (rather than on average). We show sample complexity reductions in comparison to solving every task in isolation in terms of our task complexity measure. Further, our algorithmic framework can naturally be viewed as learning a representation from encountered tasks with a neural network.
originalAbstract: Better understanding of the potential benefits of information transfer and representation learning is an important step towards the goal of building intelligent systems that are able to persist in the world and learn over time. In this work, we consider a setting where the learner encounters a stream of tasks but is able to retain only limited information from each encountered task, such as a learned predictor. In contrast to most previous works analyzing this scenario, we do not make any distributional assumptions on the task generating process. Instead, we formulate a complexity measure that captures the diversity of the observed tasks. We provide a lifelong learning algorithm with error guarantees for every observed task (rather than on average). We show sample complexity reductions in comparison to solving every task in isolation in terms of our task complexity measure. Further, our algorithmic framework can naturally be viewed as learning a representation from encountered tasks with a neural network.

paragraphs: A lifelong learner encounters tasks over time and must decide how earlier learning can help with later work. This paper studies a setting where it can retain only limited information from each task, such as the predictor it learned. The challenge is to obtain useful transfer under that restricted memory.

The analysis makes no distributional assumptions about the process generating tasks. Instead, the authors introduce a complexity measure describing the diversity of the tasks actually observed. This shifts the basis for understanding transfer toward the relationships within the encountered sequence. Their algorithm provides error guarantees for each observed task, giving a more individual account of performance than an average across tasks.

The authors show reductions in sample complexity relative to learning every task separately, expressed through their task-complexity measure. These results explain potential savings in training data in terms of observed task diversity. The framework can also be interpreted as learning a representation with a neural network from accumulated tasks. This connects theoretical guarantees for continual information transfer with a representation-learning view of the same process.
summary.tldr: A lifelong-learning algorithm provides per-task error guarantees and task-diversity-dependent sample savings without distributional assumptions on task generation.

title: Lifelong Learning with Weighted Majority Votes

abstract: Cognitive neuroscience is enjoying rapid increase in extensive public brain-imaging datasets. It opens the door to large-scale statistical models. Finding a unified perspective for all available data calls for scalable and automated solutions to an old challenge: how to aggregate heterogeneous information on brain function into a universal cognitive system that relates mental operations/cognitive processes/psychological tasks to brain networks? We cast this challenge in a machine-learning approach to predict conditions from statistical brain maps across different studies. For this, we leverage multi-task learning and multi-scale dimension reduction to learn low-dimensional representations of brain images that carry cognitive information and can be robustly associated with psychological stimuli. Our multi-dataset classification model achieves the best prediction performance on several large reference datasets, compared to models without cognitive-aware low-dimension representations; it brings a substantial performance boost to the analysis of small datasets, and can be introspected to identify universal template cognitive concepts.

This paper approaches that integration as a prediction problem: infer experimental conditions from statistical brain maps across different studies. The goal is to learn representations that carry cognitive information across datasets.

The model combines multi-task learning with dimension reduction at multiple scales. It learns compact representations of brain images that can be robustly associated with psychological stimuli. Sharing the learning problem across studies provides a way to organize their information around related predictive tasks while reducing the dimensionality of the brain maps.

On several large reference datasets, the model achieves the best prediction performance compared with models lacking cognitive-aware low-dimensional representations. It also substantially improves analyses of small datasets. Beyond prediction, the model can be inspected to identify shared template cognitive concepts. The findings connect cross-study representation learning with both stronger classification and a way to examine the cognitive structure learned from the data.
summary.tldr: Learning compact cognitive representations across fMRI studies improves condition prediction and helps identify shared cognitive concepts.

title: Learning Neural Representations of Human Cognition across Many fMRI Studies

abstract: We marry two powerful ideas: deep representation learning for visual recognition and language understanding, and symbolic program execution for reasoning. Our neural-symbolic visual question answering (NS-VQA) system first recovers a structural scene representation from the image and a program trace from the question. It then executes the program on the scene representation to obtain an answer. Incorporating symbolic structure as prior knowledge offers three unique advantages. First, executing programs on a symbolic space is more robust to long program traces; our model can solve complex reasoning tasks better, achieving an accuracy of 99.8% on the CLEVR dataset. Second, the model is more data- and memory-efficient: it performs well after learning on a small number of training data; it can also encode an image into a compact representation, requiring less storage than existing methods for offline question answering. Third, symbolic program execution offers full transparency to the reasoning process; we are thus able to interpret and diagnose each execution step.

This paper separates those responsibilities in a neural-symbolic system. Neural components recover a structured scene description from the image and a program trace from the question; symbolic execution then produces the answer.

Executing a program over that representation also exposes the intermediate reasoning steps, allowing each one to be interpreted and diagnosed. The authors report that this approach handles long program traces more robustly and achieves 99.8% accuracy on the CLEVR dataset.

The system performs well with a small amount of training data, and its compact scene description uses less storage than existing methods for offline question answering. Together, these findings support separating learned recognition from explicit program execution: the former supplies the scene and question representations, while the latter makes the reasoning process inspectable and effective on the evaluated complex tasks.
summary.tldr: NS-VQA combines learned scene and question representations with transparent symbolic execution, achieving 99.8% accuracy on CLEVR.

title: Neural-Symbolic VQA: Disentangling Reasoning from Vision and Language Understanding

abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

paragraphs: A classifier's decision can depend on both features that appear in an input and features that are absent. This paper develops contrastive explanations for black-box classifiers by examining both sides. Its aim is to explain a particular classification through a compact account of what supports it and what must remain missing.

For the present features, the method seeks a minimal set sufficient to justify the predicted class. For absent features, it seeks a minimal account of what necessarily needs to stay absent. These pertinent negatives add information that an explanation focused only on visible evidence can overlook. In an image, the distinction can involve important object pixels and critically absent background pixels.

The authors evaluate the approach on handwritten digits, procurement fraud data, and brain activity strength data. Across these three domains, they report precise explanations that human experts can readily understand and evaluate. The findings support the usefulness of explaining classifications through both presence and absence. The explanations concern the classifier's decision, with the central contribution being the explicit identification of critically missing features.
summary.tldr: The method explains classifications using both minimally sufficient present features and pertinent negatives that must remain absent.

title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives

abstract: The original simplicial method (OSM), a variant of the classic Kelley’s cutting plane method, has been shown to converge to the minimizer of a composite convex and submodular objective, though no rate of convergence for this method was known. Moreover, OSM is required to solve subproblems in each iteration whose size grows linearly in the number of iterations. We propose a limited memory version of Kelley’s method (L-KM) and of OSM that requires limited memory (at most n+ 1 constraints for an n-dimensional problem) independent of the iteration. We prove convergence for L-KM when the convex part of the objective g is strongly convex and show it converges linearly when g is also smooth. Our analysis relies on duality between minimization of the composite convex and submodular objective and minimization of a convex function over the submodular base polytope. We introduce a limited memory version, L-FCFW, of the Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (FCFW) method with approximate correction, to solve the dual problem. We show that L-FCFW and L-KM are dual algorithms that produce the same sequence of iterates; hence both converge linearly (when g is smooth and strongly convex) and with limited memory. We propose L-KM to minimize composite convex and submodular objectives; however, our results on L-FCFW hold for general polytopes and may be of independent interest.

This paper develops limited-memory variants that prevent this continuing growth.
