title: Limited Memory Kelley's Method Converges for Composite Convex and Submodular Objectives

abstract: Bandit algorithms have various application in safety-critical systems, where it is important to respect the system constraints that rely on the bandit's unknown parameters at every round. In this paper, we formulate a linear stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with safety constraints that depend (linearly) on an unknown parameter vector. As such, the learner is unable to identify all safe actions and must act conservatively in ensuring that her actions satisfy the safety constraint at all rounds (at least with high probability). For these bandits, we propose a new UCB-based algorithm called Safe-LUCB, which includes necessary modifications to respect safety constraints. The algorithm has two phases. During the pure exploration phase the learner chooses her actions at random from a restricted set of safe actions with the goal of learning a good approximation of the entire unknown safe set. Once this goal is achieved, the algorithm begins a safe exploration-exploitation phase where the learner gradually expands their estimate of the set of safe actions while controlling the growth of regret. We provide a general regret bound for the algorithm, as well as a problem dependent bound that is connected to the location of the optimal action within the safe set. We then propose a modified heuristic that exploits our problem dependent analysis to improve the regret.

That connection shows how the geometry of the safe choices enters the learning guarantee. The authors also propose a modified heuristic informed by this analysis to improve regret, linking the theoretical characterization to an algorithmic adjustment.
summary.tldr: Safe-LUCB learns unknown linear safety constraints while balancing reward-seeking exploration with high-probability safety at every round.

title: Linear Stochastic Bandits Under Safety Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel implicit semantic data augmentation (ISDA) approach to complement traditional augmentation techniques like flipping, translation or rotation. Our work is motivated by the intriguing property that deep networks are surprisingly good at linearizing features, such that certain directions in the deep feature space correspond to meaningful semantic transformations, e.g., adding sunglasses or changing backgrounds. As a consequence, translating training samples along many semantic directions in the feature space can effectively augment the dataset to improve generalization. To implement this idea effectively and efficiently, we first perform an online estimate of the covariance matrix of deep features for each class, which captures the intra-class semantic variations. Then random vectors are drawn from a zero-mean normal distribution with the estimated covariance to augment the training data in that class. Importantly, instead of augmenting the samples explicitly, we can directly minimize an upper bound of the expected cross-entropy (CE) loss on the augmented training set, leading to a highly efficient algorithm. In fact, we show that the proposed ISDA amounts to minimizing a novel robust CE loss, which adds negligible extra computational cost to a normal training procedure. Although being simple, ISDA consistently improves the generalization performance of popular deep models (ResNets and DenseNets) on a variety of datasets, e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. Code for reproducing our results are available at https://github.com/blackfeather-wang/ISDA-for-Deep-Networks.

The method estimates a feature covariance matrix for each class during training. This captures variation within the class and defines a zero-mean Gaussian distribution for feature perturbations. Instead of explicitly constructing all those augmented samples, ISDA minimizes an upper bound on their expected cross-entropy loss. The resulting objective can be expressed as a robust cross-entropy loss.

This implicit calculation adds negligible computational cost to ordinary training according to the authors. Experiments report consistent generalization improvements for ResNets and DenseNets across datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The central contribution is an efficient way to account for semantic feature variation directly in the training objective, making augmentation possible without separately materializing the perturbed examples.
summary.tldr: ISDA incorporates semantic feature perturbations into a robust training loss, improving generalization with negligible reported overhead.

title: Implicit Semantic Data Augmentation for Deep Networks

abstract: In extreme classification settings, embedding-based neural network models are currently not competitive with sparse linear and tree-based methods in terms of accuracy. Most prior works attribute this poor performance to the low-dimensional bottleneck in embedding-based methods. In this paper, we demonstrate that theoretically there is no limitation to using low-dimensional embedding-based methods, and provide experimental evidence that overfitting is the root cause of the poor performance of embedding-based methods. These findings motivate us to investigate novel data augmentation and regularization techniques to mitigate overfitting. To this end, we propose GLaS, a new regularizer for embedding-based neural network approaches. It is a natural generalization from the graph Laplacian and spread-out regularizers, and empirically it addresses the drawback of each regularizer alone when applied to the extreme classification setup. With the proposed techniques, we attain or improve upon the state-of-the-art on most widely tested public extreme classification datasets with hundreds of thousands of labels.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves choosing among very large collections of labels. The paper investigates why neural classifiers based on embeddings had lagged behind sparse linear and tree-based approaches in accuracy. Earlier explanations often blamed the low dimensionality of the embeddings. The authors challenge that explanation with a theoretical result showing that low-dimensional embeddings do not impose the proposed limitation.

Their experiments instead point to overfitting as the cause of poor performance. This shifts the focus toward how the models learn from their training data. The authors investigate data augmentation and regularization, introducing GLaS, a regularizer that generalizes graph Laplacian and spread-out regularization. Empirically, it addresses drawbacks that arise when either of those regularizers is used alone in extreme classification.

With these techniques, the models match or improve the state of the art on most of the widely tested public datasets considered, including datasets with hundreds of thousands of labels. The findings support a different diagnosis of the performance gap: improving generalization can make embedding-based approaches competitive without treating low-dimensional representations as an inherent barrier.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies overfitting as an empirical obstacle for extreme classification and introduces regularization that makes embedding-based models competitive.

title: Breaking the Glass Ceiling for Embedding-Based Classifiers for Large Output Spaces

abstract: A graphical model is a structured representation of the data generating process. The traditional method to reason over random variables is to perform inference in this graphical model. However, in many cases the generating process is only a poor approximation of the much more complex true data generating process, leading to suboptimal estimation. The subtleties of the generative process are however captured in the data itself and we can ``learn to infer'', that is, learn a direct mapping from observations to explanatory latent variables. In this work we propose a hybrid model that combines graphical inference with a learned inverse model, which we structure as in a graph neural network, while the iterative algorithm as a whole is formulated as a recurrent neural network. By using cross-validation we can automatically balance the amount of work performed by graphical inference versus learned inference. We apply our ideas to the Kalman filter, a Gaussian hidden Markov model for time sequences, and show, among other things, that our model can estimate the trajectory of a noisy chaotic Lorenz Attractor much more accurately than either the learned or graphical inference run in isolation.

paragraphs: A graphical model describes how observations could arise from underlying variables, allowing inference about those hidden variables. Its usefulness depends on how well the assumed process matches reality. When that description is incomplete, inference can remain inaccurate even if it follows the model correctly. The paper explores supplementing this structured reasoning with a mapping learned directly from data.

The proposed hybrid combines graphical inference with a learned inverse model organized as a graph neural network. The overall iterative procedure is formulated as a recurrent neural network. Cross-validation balances how much work is performed by the graphical component and how much by the learned component, allowing their contributions to be selected using data.

The authors apply the approach to the Kalman filter, viewed as a Gaussian hidden Markov model for sequences. In one reported result, the hybrid estimates a noisy chaotic Lorenz trajectory much more accurately than either component alone. This demonstrates that model-based structure and learned inference can complement each other when the assumed generating process misses relevant behavior.
summary.tldr: A hybrid inference network combines graphical reasoning with learned inference and improves noisy Lorenz trajectory estimation over either component alone.

title: Combining Generative and Discriminative Models for Hybrid Inference

abstract: Motivated by cognitive radio networks, we consider the stochastic multiplayer multi-armed bandit problem, where several players pull arms simultaneously and collisions occur if one of them is pulled by several players at the same stage. We present a decentralized algorithm that achieves the same performance as a centralized one, contradicting the existing lower bounds for that problem. This is possible by ``hacking'' the standard model by constructing a communication protocol between players that deliberately enforces collisions, allowing them to share their information at a negligible cost. This motivates the introduction of a more appropriate dynamic setting without sensing, where similar communication protocols are no longer possible. However, we show that the logarithmic growth of the regret is still achievable for this model with a new algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies a multiplayer bandit problem motivated by cognitive radio networks. Several players choose arms simultaneously, and collisions occur when multiple players select the same arm. The central challenge is coordinating learning and choices when decisions are decentralized.

The proposed algorithm deliberately causes some collisions to communicate information between players. Under the standard model, this protocol has negligible cost and enables performance matching a centralized algorithm. The result contradicts existing lower bounds for that problem by exploiting a communication opportunity embedded in the model's collision behavior.

That observation motivates a different dynamic setting without sensing, where comparable collision-based communication protocols are no longer possible. The authors introduce another algorithm and show that regret can still grow logarithmically in this setting. The paper thus contributes both algorithms and a modeling lesson: whether collisions can carry usable information changes what decentralized learners can achieve, so communication possibilities must be reflected in the formulation of the problem.
summary.tldr: Deliberate collisions enable centralized-level multiplayer bandit performance, motivating a no-sensing model that still permits logarithmic regret.

title: SIC-MMAB: Synchronisation Involves Communication in Multiplayer Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Random geometric graphs are a popular choice for a latent points generative model for networks. Their definition is based on a sample of $n$ points $X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_n$ on the Euclidean sphere~$\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ which represents the latent positions of nodes of the network. The connection probabilities between the nodes are determined by an unknown function (referred to as the ``link'' function) evaluated at the distance between the latent points. We introduce a spectral estimator of the pairwise distance between latent points and we prove that its rate of convergence is the same as the nonparametric estimation of a function on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, up to a logarithmic factor. In addition, we provide an efficient spectral algorithm to compute this estimator without any knowledge on the nonparametric link function. As a byproduct, our method can also consistently estimate the dimension $d$ of the latent space.

paragraphs: The paper studies networks generated from hidden points on a Euclidean sphere. Each node corresponds to a latent position, and the probability of an edge depends on the distance between two positions through an unknown link function. The task is to estimate those hidden pairwise distances from the graph.

The authors introduce a spectral estimator and an efficient algorithm for computing it. A central feature is that the algorithm does not require knowledge of the link function. This lets the method target the underlying geometry without first being supplied the rule that converts distances into connection probabilities.

The theoretical convergence rate matches the rate for nonparametric function estimation on the sphere, up to a logarithmic factor. The method can also consistently estimate the latent dimension. These results concern the stated spherical random-geometric-graph model: within that setting, they provide both a computational approach and statistical guarantees for recovering geometric information that is not directly visible in the observed network.
summary.tldr: A spectral method estimates hidden spherical distances and latent dimension from graphs without knowing the connection-probability function.

title: Latent distance estimation for random geometric graphs

abstract: Applying Bayesian optimization in problems wherein the search space is unknown is challenging. To address this problem, we propose a systematic volume expansion strategy for the Bayesian optimization. We devise a strategy to guarantee that in iterative expansions of the search space, our method can find a point whose function value within epsilon of the objective function maximum. Without the need to specify any parameters, our algorithm automatically triggers a minimal expansion required iteratively. We derive analytic expressions for when to trigger the expansion and by how much to expand. We also provide theoretical analysis to show that our method achieves epsilon-accuracy after a finite number of iterations. We demonstrate our method on both benchmark test functions and machine learning hyper-parameter tuning tasks and demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines.

We derive analytic expressions for when to trigger the expansion and by how much to expand. We also provide theoretical analysis to show that our method achieves epsilon-accuracy after a finite number of iterations. We demonstrate our method on both benchmark test functions and machine learning hyper-parameter tuning tasks and demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines.

Choosing a search region becomes part of the optimization problem: the procedure must decide when its current region needs to grow and how large that expansion should be. This paper addresses those decisions through a systematic strategy for expanding search volume.

The authors derive analytic rules for triggering expansion and determining its size. The algorithm repeatedly makes the minimal expansion required by its strategy, without requiring users to specify expansion parameters. These decisions are tied to finding a point whose objective value lies within a chosen tolerance, epsilon, of the maximum.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the method reaches this epsilon-level accuracy after finitely many iterations in the analyzed setting. This makes expansion part of an optimization procedure with a stated accuracy guarantee. Experiments on benchmark functions and machine learning hyperparameter tuning show better performance than the compared baselines. The practical significance is an automatic way to enlarge the domain while continuing to pursue a clear optimization target.
summary.tldr: An automatic search-space expansion strategy gives Bayesian optimization a finite-iteration epsilon-accuracy guarantee in the analyzed setting.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Unknown Search Space

abstract: We present an algorithm for reconstruction of a probabilistic deterministic finite automaton (PDFA) from a given black-box language model, such as a recurrent neural network (RNN). The algorithm is a variant of the exact-learning algorithm L*, adapted to work in a probabilistic setting under noise. The key insight of the adaptation is the use of conditional probabilities when making observations on the model, and the introduction of a variation tolerance when comparing observations. When applied to RNNs, our algorithm returns models with better or equal word error rate (WER) and normalised distributed cumulative gain (NDCG) than achieved by n-gram or weighted finite automata (WFA) approximations of the same networks. The PDFAs capture a richer class of languages than n-grams, and are guaranteed to be stochastic and deterministic -- unlike the WFAs.

The aim is to obtain an automaton that represents the model's language behavior through states, transitions, and probabilities. This turns access to a trained model into a source of observations for learning another representation.

Two changes are central: it observes conditional probabilities, and it allows a tolerance when comparing observations. The tolerance lets the procedure accommodate variation rather than requiring all compared probabilistic observations to match exactly.

title: Learning Deterministic Weighted Automata with Queries and Counterexamples

abstract: We study the complexity of sampling from a distribution over all index subsets of the set {1, ..., n} with the probability of a subset S proportional to the determinant of the submatrix L S of some n x n positive semidefinite matrix L, where L S corresponds to the entries of L indexed by S. Known as a determinantal point process (DPP), this distribution is used in machine learning to induce diversity in subset selection. When sampling from DDPs, we often wish to sample multiple subsets S with small expected size k = E[|S|] << n from a very large matrix L, so it is important to minimize the preprocessing cost of the procedure (performed once) as well as the sampling cost (performed repeatedly). For this purpose we provide DPP-VFX, a new algorithm which, given access only to L, samples exactly from a determinantal point process while satisfying the following two properties: (1) its preprocessing cost is n poly(k), i.e., sublinear in the size of L, and (2) its sampling cost is poly(k), i.e., independent of the size of L. Prior to our results, state-of-the-art exact samplers required O(n^3) preprocessing time and sampling time linear in n or dependent on the spectral properties of L. We furthermore give a reduction which allows using our algorithm for exact sampling from cardinality constrained determinantal point processes with n poly(k) time preprocessing. Our implementation of DPP-VFX is provided at https://github.com/guilgautier/DPPy/.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process assigns probabilities to subsets using determinants of submatrices of a positive semidefinite matrix. These distributions encourage diverse subset selection. This paper targets the setting where the matrix covers n items but a sampled subset has a much smaller expected size k, and many samples are needed.

The proposed DPP-VFX algorithm samples exactly while separating the cost of preparation from the cost of subsequent draws. Its preprocessing takes n times a polynomial in k, and each later sample takes only a polynomial in k. The preprocessing is sublinear in the matrix's n-squared size; it is not claimed to be sublinear in the number of items.

The distinction is important when a large collection yields relatively small subsets repeatedly. Earlier exact samplers required cubic preprocessing in n, followed by sampling costs that were linear in n or depended on the matrix's spectral properties. The authors also provide a reduction for exact sampling with a prescribed subset size, retaining preprocessing of n times a polynomial in k.
summary.tldr: DPP-VFX enables exact diverse-subset sampling with preprocessing sublinear in matrix size and repeated sampling costs independent of the number of items.

title: Exact sampling of determinantal point processes with sublinear time preprocessing

abstract: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) have become a preferred tool for tasks involving complicated distributions. To stabilise the training and reduce the mode collapse of GANs, one of their main variants employs the integral probability metric (IPM) as the loss function. This provides extensive IPM-GANs with theoretical support for basically comparing moments in an embedded domain of the \textit{critic}. We generalise this by comparing the distributions rather than their moments via a powerful tool, i.e., the characteristic function (CF), which uniquely and universally comprising all the information about a distribution. For rigour, we first establish the physical meaning of the phase and amplitude in CF, and show that this provides a feasible way of balancing the accuracy and diversity of generation. We then develop an efficient sampling strategy to calculate the CFs. Within this framework, we further prove an equivalence between the embedded and data domains when a reciprocal exists, where we naturally develop the GAN in an auto-encoder structure, in a way of comparing everything in the embedded space (a semantically meaningful manifold). This efficient structure uses only two modules, together with a simple training strategy, to achieve bi-directionally generating clear images, which is referred to as the reciprocal CF GAN (RCF-GAN). Experimental results demonstrate the superior performances of the proposed RCF-GAN in terms of both generation and reconstruction.

paragraphs: The paper develops a distribution-comparison approach for generative adversarial learning. It starts from GAN variants that use integral probability metrics to improve stability and reduce mode collapse, interpreting these as comparisons of moments in a critic's embedded space. The proposed generalization uses characteristic functions, which uniquely encode a distribution's information.

The authors establish interpretations of characteristic-function phase and amplitude and use these to provide a way of balancing generation accuracy and diversity. They also develop an efficient sampling strategy for calculating characteristic functions. A further theoretical result establishes equivalence between comparisons in the embedded and data domains when a reciprocal exists, making that condition central to the claimed equivalence.

The resulting reciprocal characteristic-function GAN uses an autoencoder structure with two modules and a simple training strategy. Comparisons take place in the embedded space, while the model supports generation and reconstruction. Experiments report superior performance on both tasks. The contribution connects distribution comparison, a conditional domain-equivalence result, and a compact bidirectional generative architecture.
summary.tldr: RCF-GAN compares characteristic functions in an embedded space and reports improved generation and reconstruction using a two-module autoencoder structure.

title: Reciprocal Adversarial Learning via Characteristic Functions

abstract: Compositional generalization is a key challenge in grounding natural language to visual perception. While deep learning models have achieved great success in multimodal tasks like visual question answering, recent studies have shown that they fail to generalize to new inputs that are simply an unseen combination of those seen in the training distribution. In this paper, we propose to tackle this challenge by employing neural factor graphs to induce a tighter coupling between concepts in different modalities (e.g. images and text). Graph representations are inherently compositional in nature and allow us to capture entities, attributes and relations in a scalable manner. Our model first creates a multimodal graph, processes it with a graph neural network to induce a factor correspondence matrix, and then outputs a symbolic program to predict answers to questions. Empirically, our model achieves close to perfect scores on a caption truth prediction problem and state-of-the-art results on the recently introduced CLOSURE dataset, improving on the mean overall accuracy across seven compositional templates by 4.77\% over previous approaches.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires connecting language with what appears in an image. A difficult case arises when familiar concepts appear in combinations absent from training. This paper addresses that form of compositional generalization by representing visual and linguistic information through graphs that explicitly organize entities, attributes, and relationships.

The model uses neural factor graphs to strengthen connections between concepts across modalities. It first constructs a multimodal graph and processes it with a graph neural network to produce a factor correspondence matrix. It then outputs a symbolic program used to predict the answer. This sequence connects structured representations of the inputs with a structured computation for answering the question.

In experiments, the model achieves nearly perfect results on a caption truth-prediction task and reported state-of-the-art performance on CLOSURE. The abstract reports a 4.77% improvement in mean overall accuracy across seven compositional templates over earlier approaches. These results support the usefulness of explicitly linking concepts across image and text representations when evaluating combinations that differ from those encountered in training.
summary.tldr: Multimodal graphs and symbolic programs improve visual question answering on unseen concept combinations, with strong results on compositional benchmarks.

title: Multimodal Graph Networks for Compositional Generalization in Visual Question Answering

abstract: Many recent breakthroughs in deep learning were achieved by training increasingly larger models on massive datasets. However, training such models can be prohibitively expensive. For instance, the cluster used to train GPT-3 costs over $250 million. As a result, most researchers cannot afford to train state of the art models and contribute to their development. Hypothetically, a researcher could crowdsource the training of large neural networks with thousands of regular PCs provided by volunteers. The raw computing power of a hundred thousand $2500 desktops dwarfs that of a $250M server pod, but one cannot utilize that power efficiently with conventional distributed training methods. In this work, we propose Learning@home: a novel neural network training paradigm designed to handle large amounts of poorly connected participants. We analyze the performance, reliability, and architectural constraints of this paradigm and compare it against existing distributed training techniques.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether large neural networks could be trained using computing resources contributed by volunteers. Its motivation is the expense of the infrastructure used for increasingly large models. A sufficiently large collection of ordinary computers could offer substantial raw computing power, but conventional distributed training cannot efficiently use that power under the conditions considered.

The proposed Learning@home paradigm is designed for many participants with poor connectivity. The title frames the approach around decentralized mixtures of experts. The central systems question is how a training design can accommodate the communication conditions of crowdsourced resources, since aggregate computing power alone does not establish that training will be effective.

The authors analyze performance, reliability, and architectural constraints and compare the paradigm with existing distributed training techniques. This makes the work an investigation of what crowdsourced training requires as well as a proposed approach. The abstract presents volunteer-powered training as a possibility to pursue, without claiming that a large volunteer deployment has already achieved it.
summary.tldr: Learning@home explores decentralized training designed to use large numbers of poorly connected volunteer computers.

title: Towards Crowdsourced Training of Large Neural Networks using Decentralized Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Contrastive learning between multiple views of the data has recently achieved state of the art performance in the field of self-supervised representation learning. Despite its success, the influence of different view choices has been less studied. In this paper, we use theoretical and empirical analysis to better understand the importance of view selection, and argue that we should reduce the mutual information (MI) between views while keeping task-relevant information intact. To verify this hypothesis, we devise unsupervised and semi-supervised frameworks that learn effective views by aiming to reduce their MI. We also consider data augmentation as a way to reduce MI, and show that increasing data augmentation indeed leads to decreasing MI and improves downstream classification accuracy. As a by-product, we achieve a new state-of-the-art accuracy on unsupervised pre-training for ImageNet classification (73% top-1 linear readout with a ResNet-50).

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations by comparing different views of the same data, making the choice of views an important part of the learning problem. This paper studies that choice theoretically and empirically. Its central proposal is to reduce the mutual information shared by the views while retaining information relevant to the task.

The requirement to preserve task information is essential to the proposed principle. The authors develop unsupervised and semi-supervised frameworks that learn views by aiming to reduce their mutual information. They also examine data augmentation as another way to achieve this reduction, connecting a common practical technique to their information-based account.

The reported experiments show that stronger augmentation decreases mutual information and improves downstream classification accuracy. As a further result, the work reports state-of-the-art unsupervised ImageNet pretraining accuracy of 73% with a ResNet-50 and linear readout. The findings support the proposed view-selection principle in the studied settings, tying useful representation learning to reducing shared information while preserving what matters for the task.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that effective contrastive views reduce shared information while preserving task-relevant content, supported by theory and experiments.

title: What Makes for Good Views for Contrastive Learning?

abstract: While numerous approaches have been developed to embed graphs into either Euclidean or hyperbolic spaces, they do not fully utilize the information available in graphs, or lack the flexibility to model intrinsic complex graph geometry. To utilize the strength of both Euclidean and hyperbolic geometries, we develop a novel Geometry Interaction Learning (GIL) method for graphs, a well-suited and efficient alternative for learning abundant geometric properties in graph. GIL captures a more informative internal structural features with low dimensions while maintaining conformal invariance of each space. Furthermore, our method endows each node the freedom to determine the importance of each geometry space via a flexible dual feature interaction learning and probability assembling mechanism. Promising experimental results are presented for five benchmark datasets on node classification and link prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Graph embedding methods represent network structure in a geometric space. The paper argues that existing Euclidean or hyperbolic approaches can leave structural information unused or lack the flexibility to capture complex graph geometry. Geometry Interaction Learning, or GIL, combines the two kinds of geometry to make their respective strengths available within one method.

GIL learns structural features in low-dimensional representations while maintaining conformal invariance within each space. Its central flexibility is at the node level: each node can determine the importance of the two geometric spaces. A dual feature interaction mechanism and probability assembly mechanism support this choice, rather than imposing the same geometric emphasis throughout the graph.

The authors report promising results on five benchmark datasets for node classification and link prediction. These tasks examine both predicting properties of nodes and predicting connections between them. The findings support the usefulness of allowing geometric representations to interact, with the contribution centered on flexible use of multiple geometries rather than a claim that one geometry is best for every graph.
summary.tldr: GIL combines Euclidean and hyperbolic graph representations while allowing each node to learn how much to rely on each geometry.

title: Graph Geometry Interaction Learning

abstract: In neural networks with binary activations and or binary weights the training by gradient descent is complicated as the model has piecewise constant response. We consider stochastic binary networks, obtained by adding noises in front of activations. The expected model response becomes a smooth function of parameters, its gradient is well defined but it is challenging to estimate it accurately. We propose a new method for this estimation problem combining sampling and analytic approximation steps. The method has a significantly reduced variance at the price of a small bias which gives a very practical tradeoff in comparison with existing unbiased and biased estimators. We further show that one extra linearization step leads to a deep straight-through estimator previously known only as an ad-hoc heuristic. We experimentally show higher accuracy in gradient estimation and demonstrate a more stable and better performing training in deep convolutional models with both proposed methods.

paragraphs: Networks with binary activations or weights are difficult to train by gradient descent because their responses are piecewise constant. Adding noise before activations produces a stochastic binary network whose expected response varies smoothly with its parameters. That makes a gradient mathematically available, but estimating it accurately remains difficult.

The proposed estimator combines sampling with analytical approximation. It substantially reduces variance at the cost of a small bias, trading exactness in expectation for less fluctuation in the estimated gradient. The authors present this as a practical balance relative to existing biased and unbiased estimators.

They also show that one additional linearization step leads to a deep straight-through estimator, connecting a previously heuristic method to their derivation. Experiments show more accurate gradient estimation and more stable, better-performing training in deep convolutional models for both proposed methods. The contribution therefore includes both a practical estimator and an explanation of how a familiar training heuristic arises from a further approximation.
summary.tldr: A sampling-and-approximation gradient estimator improves binary-network training by substantially reducing variance while introducing a small bias.

title: Path Sample-Analytic Gradient Estimators for Stochastic Binary Networks

abstract: Policy gradient methods have shown success in learning control policies for high-dimensional dynamical systems. Their biggest downside is the amount of exploration they require before yielding high-performing policies. In a lifelong learning setting, in which an agent is faced with multiple consecutive tasks over its lifetime, reusing information from previously seen tasks can substantially accelerate the learning of new tasks. We provide a novel method for lifelong policy gradient learning that trains lifelong function approximators directly via policy gradients, allowing the agent to benefit from accumulated knowledge throughout the entire training process. We show empirically that our algorithm learns faster and converges to better policies than single-task and lifelong learning baselines, and completely avoids catastrophic forgetting on a variety of challenging domains.

We provide a novel method for lifelong policy gradient learning that trains lifelong function approximators directly via policy gradients, allowing the agent to benefit from accumulated knowledge throughout the entire training process. paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn control behavior but can require substantial exploration before producing a strong policy. When an agent encounters a sequence of tasks, starting each learning process without using earlier knowledge wastes an opportunity. This paper develops a lifelong learning method that brings accumulated knowledge into policy-gradient training for new tasks.

The method trains lifelong function approximators directly through policy gradients. Its key feature is that previous knowledge can influence the entire training process, allowing transfer to contribute while the new policy is still being learned. The factored-policy approach is intended to support both efficient acquisition of new behavior and retention of behavior learned earlier.

Across the challenging domains evaluated, the authors report faster learning and convergence to better policies than both single-task and lifelong learning baselines. They also report completely avoiding catastrophic forgetting in those experiments. These are empirical findings within the evaluated domains. Together, they support the possibility of using shared experience to improve new-task learning without sacrificing previously acquired control skills.
summary.tldr: A lifelong policy-gradient method uses accumulated knowledge throughout training, improving learning speed and policy quality without forgetting in the reported experiments.

title: Lifelong Policy Gradient Learning of Factored Policies for Faster Training Without Forgetting

abstract: Research on continual learning has led to a variety of approaches to mitigating catastrophic forgetting in feed-forward classification networks. Until now surprisingly little attention has been focused on continual learning of recurrent models applied to problems like image captioning. In this paper we take a systematic look at continual learning of LSTM-based models for image captioning. We propose an attention-based approach that explicitly accommodates the transient nature of vocabularies in continual image captioning tasks -- i.e. that task vocabularies are not disjoint. We call our method Recurrent Attention to Transient Tasks (RATT), and also show how to adapt continual learning approaches based on weight regularization and knowledge distillation to recurrent continual learning problems. We apply our approaches to incremental image captioning problem on two new continual learning benchmarks we define using the MS-COCO and Flickr30 datasets. Our results demonstrate that RATT is able to sequentially learn five captioning tasks while incurring no forgetting of previously learned ones.

We call our method Recurrent Attention to Transient Tasks (RATT), and also show how to adapt continual learning approaches based on weight regularization and knowledge distillation to recurrent continual learning problems. paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks without losing what it learned earlier. Much of the work motivating this paper focused on feed-forward classification networks. The authors instead study recurrent LSTM models for image captioning, where learning sequential tasks involves generating descriptions with vocabularies that can overlap.

Their method, Recurrent Attention to Transient Tasks, explicitly accommodates that vocabulary overlap through an attention-based approach. Shared words mean task vocabularies cannot simply be treated as separate sets. The paper also adapts weight-regularization and knowledge-distillation methods to recurrent continual learning, creating a broader investigation of approaches for this setting.

The authors define two continual image-captioning benchmarks using MS-COCO and Flickr30. In their reported results, RATT learns five captioning tasks sequentially without forgetting previously learned tasks. That finding establishes the demonstrated behavior on these benchmarks, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary task sequences. The work expands continual-learning evaluation to recurrent language generation grounded in images and highlights overlapping vocabularies as a design concern.
summary.tldr: RATT uses attention to accommodate overlapping captioning vocabularies and learns five tasks without observed forgetting on the proposed benchmarks.

title: RATT: Recurrent Attention to Transient Tasks for Continual Image Captioning

abstract: Weakly Supervised Object Detection (WSOD) has emerged as an effective tool to train object detectors using only the image-level category labels. However, without object-level labels, WSOD detectors are prone to detect bounding boxes on salient objects, clustered objects and discriminative object parts. Moreover, the image-level category labels do not enforce consistent object detection across different transformations of the same images. To address the above issues, we propose a Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation (CASD) training approach for WSOD. To balance feature learning among all object instances, CASD computes the comprehensive attention aggregated from multiple transformations and feature layers of the same images. To enforce consistent spatial supervision on objects, CASD conducts self-distillation on the WSOD networks, such that the comprehensive attention is approximated simultaneously by multiple transformations and feature layers of the same images. CASD produces new state-of-the-art WSOD results on standard benchmarks such as PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 and MS-COCO.

Moreover, the image-level category labels do not enforce consistent object detection across different transformations of the same images. To address the above issues, we propose a Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation (CASD) training approach for WSOD. To balance feature learning among all object instances, CASD computes the comprehensive attention aggregated from multiple transformations and feature layers of the same images. To enforce consistent spatial supervision on objects, CASD conducts self-distillation on the WSOD networks, such that the comprehensive attention is approximated simultaneously by multiple transformations and feature layers of the same images. paragraphs: Weakly supervised object detection trains with labels saying which categories occur in an image, without labels specifying object locations. This leaves considerable ambiguity: a detector may focus on a distinctive part, favor a particularly salient object, or group nearby objects together. Category labels also do not directly require predictions to remain consistent across transformed versions of an image.

Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation addresses these issues by combining attention information from multiple transformations and feature layers of the same image. This aggregated attention is intended to balance feature learning across object instances. It provides a shared spatial target assembled from several views of the network’s own information.

The method then trains multiple transformations and feature layers to approximate that common attention target. This self-distillation step supplies more consistent spatial supervision while retaining image-level labeling. The authors report new state-of-the-art weakly supervised detection results on PASCAL VOC 2007, PASCAL VOC 2012, and MS-COCO, supporting the usefulness of combining attention aggregation with consistency during training.
summary.tldr: CASD aggregates attention across image transformations and network layers to improve object detection trained only with image-level labels.

title: Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation for Weakly-Supervised Object Detection

abstract: Recent advances have shown that implicit bias of gradient descent on over-parameterized models enables the recovery of low-rank matrices from linear measurements, even with no prior knowledge on the intrinsic rank. In contrast, for {\em robust} low-rank matrix recovery from {\em grossly corrupted} measurements, over-parameterization leads to overfitting without prior knowledge on both the intrinsic rank and sparsity of corruption. This paper shows that with a {\em double over-parameterization} for both the low-rank matrix and sparse corruption, gradient descent with {\em discrepant learning rates} provably recovers the underlying matrix even without prior knowledge on neither rank of the matrix nor sparsity of the corruption. We further extend our approach for the robust recovery of natural images by over-parameterizing images with deep convolutional networks. Experiments show that our method handles different test images and varying corruption levels with a single learning pipeline where the network width and termination conditions do not need to be adjusted on a case-by-case basis. Underlying the success is again the implicit bias with discrepant learning rates on different over-parameterized parameters, which may bear on broader applications.

Grossly corrupted measurements complicate this picture: extra capacity can fit corruption when the matrix rank and corruption sparsity are unknown. This paper addresses recovery in that setting.

title: Robust Recovery via Implicit Bias of Discrepant Learning Rates for Double Over-parameterization

abstract: Neural networks often learn to make predictions that overly rely on spurious corre- lation existing in the dataset, which causes the model to be biased. While previous work tackles this issue by using explicit labeling on the spuriously correlated attributes or presuming a particular bias type, we instead utilize a cheaper, yet generic form of human knowledge, which can be widely applicable to various types of bias. We first observe that neural networks learn to rely on the spurious correlation only when it is “easier” to learn than the desired knowledge, and such reliance is most prominent during the early phase of training. Based on the obser- vations, we propose a failure-based debiasing scheme by training a pair of neural networks simultaneously. Our main idea is twofold; (a) we intentionally train the first network to be biased by repeatedly amplifying its “prejudice”, and (b) we debias the training of the second network by focusing on samples that go against the prejudice of the biased network in (a). Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves the training of network against various types of biases in both synthetic and real-world datasets. Surprisingly, our framework even occasionally outperforms the debiasing methods requiring explicit supervision of the spuriously correlated attributes.

Two networks train together. The first is deliberately encouraged to amplify its bias, while the second focuses on examples that contradict the first network’s predictions or prejudice. The method uses a cheaper, more generic form of human knowledge than explicitly labeling every spuriously correlated attribute.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show substantial improvements across several bias types, occasionally exceeding methods that use explicit attribute supervision. The abstract does not specify that generic knowledge or provide numerical gains. The result concerns resistance to evaluated spurious correlations, rather than a guarantee that the resulting classifier satisfies every social or statistical notion of fairness.
summary.tldr: A deliberately biased model identifies examples that help a second model resist spurious correlations.

title: Learning from Failure: De-biasing Classifier from Biased Classifier

abstract: On-device learning promises collaborative training of machine learning models across edge devices without the sharing of user data. In state-of-the-art on-device learning algorithms, devices communicate their model weights over a decentralized communication network. Transmitting model weights requires huge communication overhead and means only devices with identical model architectures can be included. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed distillation algorithm where devices communicate and learn from soft-decision (softmax) outputs, which are inherently architecture-agnostic and scale only with the number of classes. The communicated soft-decisions are each model's outputs on a public, unlabeled reference dataset, which serves as a common vocabulary between devices. We prove that the gradients of the distillation regularized loss functions of all devices converge to zero with probability 1. Hence, all devices distill the entire knowledge of all other devices on the reference data, regardless of their local connections. Our analysis assumes smooth loss functions, which can be non-convex. Simulations support our theoretical findings and show that even a naive implementation of our algorithm significantly reduces the communication overhead while achieving an overall comparable accuracy to the state-of-the-art. By requiring little communication overhead and allowing for cross-architecture training, we remove two main obstacles to scaling on-device learning.

The approach therefore addresses two practical barriers together: transmitting large models and excluding devices with different architectures. The public reference dataset is central because it gives otherwise different models a shared basis for exchanging what they have learned.
summary.tldr: Devices exchange predictions on public reference data to support communication-efficient collaborative learning across different model architectures.

title: Distributed Distillation for On-Device Learning

abstract: The success of deep learning sparked interest in whether the brain learns by using similar techniques for assigning credit to each synaptic weight for its contribution to the network output. However, the majority of current attempts at biologically-plausible learning methods are either non-local in time, require highly specific connectivity motifs, or have no clear link to any known mathematical optimization method. Here, we introduce Deep Feedback Control (DFC), a new learning method that uses a feedback controller to drive a deep neural network to match a desired output target and whose control signal can be used for credit assignment. The resulting learning rule is fully local in space and time and approximates Gauss-Newton optimization for a wide range of feedback connectivity patterns. To further underline its biological plausibility, we relate DFC to a multi-compartment model of cortical pyramidal neurons with a local voltage-dependent synaptic plasticity rule, consistent with recent theories of dendritic processing. By combining dynamical system theory with mathematical optimization theory, we provide a strong theoretical foundation for DFC that we corroborate with detailed results on toy experiments and standard computer-vision benchmarks.

This paper introduces Deep Feedback Control, a learning method motivated by the search for biologically plausible alternatives. A feedback controller drives the network toward a desired output, and the resulting control signal supplies information for updating its connections.

The learning rule is local in both space and time, so updates use information available locally as the system evolves. The authors show that it approximates Gauss-Newton optimization across a wide range of feedback connectivity patterns. This connects the proposed mechanism to an established mathematical optimization method without requiring one narrowly specified feedback arrangement.

The paper also relates the method to a multi-compartment model of cortical pyramidal neurons with voltage-dependent local plasticity. That connection supports its biological plausibility rather than establishing that brains use the algorithm. Dynamical systems and optimization theory provide its theoretical foundation, which the authors corroborate with toy experiments and standard computer-vision benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Deep Feedback Control uses a controller's signals for local learning that approximates Gauss-Newton optimization across varied feedback connections.

title: Credit Assignment in Neural Networks through Deep Feedback Control

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have significantly advanced image synthesis, however, the synthesis quality drops significantly given a limited amount of training data. To improve the data efficiency of GAN training, prior work typically employs data augmentation to mitigate the overfitting of the discriminator yet still learn the discriminator with a bi-classification ($\textit{i.e.}$, real $\textit{vs.}$ fake) task. In this work, we propose a data-efficient Instance Generation ($\textit{InsGen}$) method based on instance discrimination. Concretely, besides differentiating the real domain from the fake domain, the discriminator is required to distinguish every individual image, no matter it comes from the training set or from the generator. In this way, the discriminator can benefit from the infinite synthesized samples for training, alleviating the overfitting problem caused by insufficient training data. A noise perturbation strategy is further introduced to improve its discriminative power. Meanwhile, the learned instance discrimination capability from the discriminator is in turn exploited to encourage the generator for diverse generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of datasets and training settings. Noticeably, on the setting of $2K$ training images from the FFHQ dataset, we outperform the state-of-the-art approach with 23.5\% FID improvement.

InsGen expands that task so the discriminator must also distinguish individual images, whether they come from the dataset or the generator.

The result illustrates how changing what the discriminator learns can improve data efficiency while also encouraging diversity in the images produced.
summary.tldr: InsGen improves GAN training with limited data by teaching the discriminator to distinguish individual real and generated images.

title: Data-Efficient Instance Generation from Instance Discrimination

abstract: Causal inference and discovery from observational data has been extensively studied across multiple fields. However, most prior work has focused on independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. In this paper, we propose a formalization for causal inference between pairs of event variables in multivariate recurrent event streams by extending Rubin's framework for the average treatment effect (ATE) and propensity scores to multivariate point processes. Analogous to a joint probability distribution representing i.i.d. data, a multivariate point process represents data involving asynchronous and irregularly spaced occurrences of various types of events over a common timeline. We theoretically justify our point process causal framework and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of the proposed measure. We conduct an experimental investigation using synthetic and real-world event datasets, where our proposed causal inference framework is shown to exhibit superior performance against a set of baseline pairwise causal association scores.

paragraphs: Many causal inference methods are developed for independent observations, while event-stream data consist of repeated occurrences at irregular times. Different event types share a timeline and need not happen together. This paper develops a framework for asking causal questions between pairs of event variables in that setting, using multivariate point processes to represent the streams.

The approach extends Rubin's treatment-effect framework, including average treatment effects and propensity scores, to these temporal data. A point process takes the representational role that a joint probability distribution plays for independent observations. This allows the proposed causal quantity to be formulated around asynchronous, recurrent events rather than treating the data as ordinary independent records.

The authors theoretically justify the framework and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of their proposed measure. They also evaluate it using synthetic and real-world event datasets. In these experiments, it performs better than the tested pairwise causal association scores, supporting the usefulness of a causal formulation built specifically for event streams.
summary.tldr: The paper extends treatment-effect estimation to irregular recurrent event streams and demonstrates advantages over tested pairwise causal association scores.

title: Causal Inference for Event Pairs in Multivariate Point Processes

abstract: Random Fourier features provide a way to tackle large-scale machine learning problems with kernel methods. Their slow Monte Carlo convergence rate has motivated the research of deterministic Fourier features whose approximation error can decrease exponentially in the number of basis functions. However, due to their tensor product extension to multiple dimensions, these methods suffer heavily from the curse of dimensionality, limiting their applicability to one, two or three-dimensional scenarios. In our approach we overcome said curse of dimensionality by exploiting the tensor product structure of deterministic Fourier features, which enables us to represent the model parameters as a low-rank tensor decomposition. We derive a monotonically converging block coordinate descent algorithm with linear complexity in both the sample size and the dimensionality of the inputs for a regularized squared loss function, allowing to learn a parsimonious model in decomposed form using deterministic Fourier features.We demonstrate by means of numerical experiments how our low-rank tensor approach obtains the same performance of the corresponding nonparametric model, consistently outperforming random Fourier features.

paragraphs: Fourier features make kernel methods more practical for large datasets. Random features are useful but converge slowly, motivating deterministic alternatives whose approximation error can decrease exponentially with the number of basis functions. Extending those alternatives across many input dimensions creates a tensor product whose size becomes a major obstacle.

The paper exploits that tensor structure by representing model parameters through a low-rank tensor decomposition. This compact representation enables learning with deterministic Fourier features without explicitly handling the full parameter tensor. For a regularized squared-loss objective, the authors derive a block coordinate descent algorithm with monotonic convergence and complexity linear in both sample count and input dimension.

Numerical experiments show the proposed representation matching the performance of the corresponding nonparametric model and consistently outperforming random Fourier features. The contribution connects a potentially accurate feature construction with a compact parameterization and a scalable optimization procedure. Its stated computational result applies to the particular regularized loss and decomposed model developed in the paper.
summary.tldr: Low-rank tensor decompositions make deterministic Fourier-feature learning scalable, with strong numerical results against random Fourier features.

title: Large-Scale Learning with Fourier Features and Tensor Decompositions

abstract: Rule sets are highly interpretable logical models in which the predicates for decision are expressed in disjunctive normal form (DNF, OR-of-ANDs), or, equivalently, the overall model comprises an unordered collection of if-then decision rules. In this paper, we consider a submodular optimization based approach for learning rule sets. The learning problem is framed as a subset selection task in which a subset of all possible rules needs to be selected to form an accurate and interpretable rule set. We employ an objective function that exhibits submodularity and thus is amenable to submodular optimization techniques. To overcome the difficulty arose from dealing with the exponential-sized ground set of rules, the subproblem of searching a rule is casted as another subset selection task that asks for a subset of features. We show it is possible to write the induced objective function for the subproblem as a difference of two submodular (DS) functions to make it approximately solvable by DS optimization algorithms. Overall, the proposed approach is simple, scalable, and likely to be benefited from further research on submodular optimization. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: This paper learns predictive models expressed as unordered sets of if-then rules. Each rule combines conditions, and the overall model combines the rules in an OR-of-ANDs form. The authors formulate rule selection using a submodular objective, enabling methods from submodular optimization. To address it, they turn the search for an individual rule into another subset-selection problem, this time selecting features that make up that rule.

The objective for this inner problem can be expressed as the difference of two submodular functions. That structure allows approximate solution using corresponding optimization algorithms, linking rule construction and rule-set selection within one approach. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is a scalable optimization formulation for interpretable models, with the possibility of benefiting from further advances in submodular optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper uses nested subset-selection problems and submodular optimization to learn accurate, interpretable sets of decision rules.

title: Learning Interpretable Decision Rule Sets: A Submodular Optimization Approach

abstract: Randomized smoothing is currently a state-of-the-art method to construct a certifiably robust classifier from neural networks against $\ell_2$-adversarial perturbations. Under the paradigm, the robustness of a classifier is aligned with the prediction confidence, i.e., the higher confidence from a smoothed classifier implies the better robustness. This motivates us to rethink the fundamental trade-off between accuracy and robustness in terms of calibrating confidences of a smoothed classifier. In this paper, we propose a simple training scheme, coined SmoothMix, to control the robustness of smoothed classifiers via self-mixup: it trains on convex combinations of samples along the direction of adversarial perturbation for each input. The proposed procedure effectively identifies over-confident, near off-class samples as a cause of limited robustness in case of smoothed classifiers, and offers an intuitive way to adaptively set a new decision boundary between these samples for better robustness. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly improve the certified $\ell_2$-robustness of smoothed classifiers compared to existing state-of-the-art robust training methods.

This paper uses that connection to reconsider the accuracy–robustness trade-off through the calibration of a smoothed classifier’s confidence.

The procedure targets overconfident samples near regions associated with another class, which the authors identify as a source of limited robustness in smoothed classifiers. Mixing along these directions provides a way to adapt the decision boundary between such samples.

Experiments show significant improvements in certified ℓ2 robustness over the compared state-of-the-art robust training methods. The stated benefit concerns certified robustness of smoothed classifiers, connecting the training change to a formal robustness setting. The work’s central insight is that shaping confidence around difficult nearby samples can help improve the robustness achievable through smoothing.
summary.tldr: SmoothMix trains on mixtures along adversarial directions to calibrate smoothed classifiers and improve certified ℓ2 robustness.

title: SmoothMix: Training Confidence-calibrated Smoothed Classifiers for Certified Robustness

abstract: Many experiments compare count outcomes among treatment groups. Examples include the number of successful signups in conversion rate experiments or the number of errors produced by software versions in canary tests. Observations typically arrive in a sequence and practitioners wish to continuously monitor their experiments, sequentially testing hypotheses while maintaining Type I error probabilities under optional stopping and continuation. These goals are frequently complicated in practice by non-stationary time dynamics. We provide practical solutions through sequential tests of multinomial hypotheses, hypotheses about many inhomogeneous Bernoulli processes and hypotheses about many time-inhomogeneous Poisson counting processes. For estimation, we further provide confidence sequences for multinomial probability vectors, all contrasts among probabilities of inhomogeneous Bernoulli processes and all contrasts among intensities of time-inhomogeneous Poisson counting processes. Together, these provide an ``anytime-valid'' inference framework for a wide variety of experiments dealing with count outcomes, which we illustrate with several industry applications.

paragraphs: Experiments often compare counts, such as successful signups or software errors, while observations keep arriving. Practitioners want to inspect the results repeatedly and decide when to stop or continue. The statistical challenge is to preserve control over false positive probabilities despite those decisions, including settings where the processes generating observations change over time.

The paper develops sequential hypothesis tests for multinomial data, multiple inhomogeneous Bernoulli processes, and multiple time-inhomogeneous Poisson counting processes. These cover category counts, binary outcomes, and counts arising over time. The framework explicitly addresses optional stopping and continuation rather than requiring the experiment to be inspected only at a predetermined endpoint.

For estimation, the authors also construct confidence sequences: uncertainty statements designed to remain valid across repeated observation times. These cover multinomial probability vectors and all contrasts among the relevant Bernoulli probabilities or Poisson intensities. Industry applications illustrate how testing and estimation fit together into an anytime-valid framework for monitoring count-based experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper provides sequential tests and confidence sequences for monitoring count experiments while preserving statistical validity under optional stopping and continuation.

title: Anytime-Valid Inference For Multinomial Count Data

abstract: Greedy best-first search (GBFS) and A* search (A*) are popular algorithms for path-finding on large graphs. Both use so-called heuristic functions, which estimate how close a vertex is to the goal. While heuristic functions have been handcrafted using domain knowledge, recent studies demonstrate that learning heuristic functions from data is effective in many applications. Motivated by this emerging approach, we study the sample complexity of learning heuristic functions for GBFS and A*. We build on a recent framework called \textit{data-driven algorithm design} and evaluate the \textit{pseudo-dimension} of a class of utility functions that measure the performance of parameterized algorithms. Assuming that a vertex set of size $n$ is fixed, we present $\mathrm{O}(n\lg n)$ and $\mathrm{O}(n^2\lg n)$ upper bounds on the pseudo-dimensions for GBFS and A*, respectively, parameterized by heuristic function values. The upper bound for A* can be improved to $\mathrm{O}(n^2\lg d)$ if every vertex has a degree of at most $d$ and to $\mathrm{O}(n \lg n)$ if edge weights are integers bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also give $\Omega(n)$ lower bounds for GBFS and A*, which imply that our bounds for GBFS and A* under the integer-weight condition are tight up to a $\lg n$ factor. Finally, we discuss a case where the performance of A* is measured by the suboptimality and show that we can sometimes obtain a better guarantee by combining a parameter-dependent worst-case bound with a sample complexity bound.

The upper bound for A* can be improved to $\mathrm{O}(n^2\lg d)$ if every vertex has a degree of at most $d$ and to $\mathrm{O}(n \lg n)$ if edge weights are integers bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Finally, we discuss a case where the performance of A* is measured by the suboptimality and show that we can sometimes obtain a better guarantee by combining a parameter-dependent worst-case bound with a sample complexity bound.

paragraphs: Greedy best-first search and A* use heuristic functions to estimate how close a graph vertex is to a goal. As these functions are increasingly learned from data, a natural question is how much data is needed to learn useful heuristics. This paper studies that question through the data-driven algorithm design framework.

The analysis measures the pseudo-dimension of utility functions describing search performance as heuristic values change. For a fixed vertex set of size n, the authors prove upper bounds of O(n log n) for greedy best-first search and O(n² log n) for A*. A* admits sharper bounds when vertex degrees are bounded or edge weights are polynomially bounded integers.

Both algorithms have lower bounds of Ω(n), making the greedy best-first bound and the integer-weight A* bound tight up to a logarithmic factor. The authors also examine A* performance measured by suboptimality. In some cases, combining a parameter-dependent worst-case guarantee with a sample complexity guarantee gives a better result than relying on the learning bound alone.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the learning complexity of search heuristics for greedy best-first search and A*, with stronger results under specific graph conditions.

title: Sample Complexity of Learning Heuristic Functions for Greedy-Best-First and A* Search

abstract: A cursory reading of the literature suggests that we have made a lot of progress in designing effective adversarial defenses for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Yet, the standard methodology has a serious flaw – virtually all of the defenses are evaluated against non-adaptive attacks leading to overly optimistic robustness estimates. We perform a thorough robustness analysis of 7 of the most popular defenses spanning the entire spectrum of strategies, i.e., aimed at improving the graph, the architecture, or the training. The results are sobering – most defenses show no or only marginal improvement compared to an undefended baseline. We advocate using custom adaptive attacks as a gold standard and we outline the lessons we learned from successfully designing such attacks. Moreover, our diverse collection of perturbed graphs forms a (black-box) unit test offering a first glance at a model's robustness.

paragraphs: A defense against adversarial manipulation should withstand attacks that account for how the defense works. This paper argues that evaluations of graph neural network defenses have generally missed that requirement. Testing with non-adaptive attacks can make a defense appear stronger because the attack does not specifically challenge the protection being evaluated.

The authors analyze seven popular defenses covering changes to the graph, the network architecture, and the training procedure. They design adaptive attacks for these defenses and examine robustness under those attacks. Most evaluated defenses offer no improvement, or only marginal improvement, over an undefended baseline. This challenges the apparent progress suggested by the earlier evaluation methodology.

The paper recommends custom adaptive attacks as the standard for evaluating robustness and shares lessons from constructing them. It also provides a diverse collection of perturbed graphs that can serve as a black-box unit test. That collection offers an initial robustness check, while the broader finding emphasizes the importance of testing a defense against attacks tailored to it.
summary.tldr: Adaptive attacks reveal that most of seven evaluated graph neural network defenses provide little or no robustness improvement.

title: Are Defenses for Graph Neural Networks Robust?

abstract: Adversarial training is one important algorithm to achieve robust machine learning models. However, numerous empirical results show a great performance degradation from clean training to adversarial training (e.g., 90+\% vs 67\% testing accuracy on CIFAR-10 dataset), which does not match the theoretical guarantee delivered by the existing studies. Such a gap inspires us to explore the existence of an (asymptotic) phase transition phenomenon with respect to the attack strength: adversarial training is as well behaved as clean training in the small-attack regime, but there is a sharp transition from clean training to adversarial training in the large-attack regime. We validate this conjecture in linear regression models, and conduct comprehensive experiments in deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Adversarial training is intended to make models robust, yet empirical studies can show a substantial drop in test accuracy compared with ordinary training. This paper starts from the mismatch between that observed degradation and existing theoretical guarantees. It asks whether attack strength changes the behavior of training in a more abrupt way than those guarantees suggest.

The proposed explanation is an asymptotic phase transition. When attacks are small, adversarial training can behave as well as clean training. In a larger-attack regime, the authors propose that a sharp transition occurs. The important distinction is between qualitatively different regimes, rather than assuming that increasing attack strength always produces a similar, gradual change.

The authors validate this conjecture in linear regression models and conduct extensive experiments with deep neural networks. The abstract therefore supports a result in the regression setting alongside an empirical investigation in more complex models. The work offers a way to interpret the gap between favorable theory and degraded performance: conclusions about adversarial training may depend critically on which attack-strength regime is being studied.
summary.tldr: The paper validates an attack-strength-dependent phase transition in linear regression and investigates it experimentally in deep networks.

title: Phase Transition from Clean Training to Adversarial Training

abstract: Great efforts have been devoted to causal discovery from observational data, and it is well known that introducing some background knowledge attained from experiments or human expertise can be very helpful. However, it remains unknown that \emph{what causal relations are identifiable given background knowledge in the presence of latent confounders}. In this paper, we solve the problem with sound and complete orientation rules when the background knowledge is given in a \emph{local} form. Furthermore, based on the solution to the problem, this paper proposes a general active learning framework for causal discovery in the presence of latent confounders, with its effectiveness and efficiency validated by experiments.
