In this paper, we solve the problem with sound and complete orientation rules when the background knowledge is given in a \emph{local} form. Furthermore, based on the solution to the problem, this paper proposes a general active learning framework for causal discovery in the presence of latent confounders, with its effectiveness and efficiency validated by experiments.

paragraphs: Causal discovery uses observational data to investigate which variables influence others. Background knowledge from experiments or human expertise can help resolve uncertainty, but unobserved confounders complicate what can be established. This paper asks which causal relationships become identifiable when such hidden variables are present and additional knowledge is available.

The authors solve this identification problem for background knowledge supplied in a local form. They provide sound and complete orientation rules. Soundness means that the rules support valid causal orientations in the stated setting; completeness means that they recover the orientations identifiable within that setting. The local form of the knowledge is part of the scope of the result.

Building on these rules, the paper proposes a general active-learning framework for causal discovery with latent confounders. This connects the identification result to a learning process that can make use of additional information. Experiments validate the framework's effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution combines a characterization of what can be inferred with a framework for using that characterization during discovery.
summary.tldr: Sound and complete rules identify causal orientations from local background knowledge despite latent confounders and support an active-learning framework.

title: Sound and Complete Causal Identification with Latent Variables Given Local Background Knowledge

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated an impressive ability to generate code for various programming tasks. In many instances, LLMs can generate a correct program for a task when given numerous trials. Consequently, a recent trend is to do large scale sampling of programs using a model and then filtering/ranking the programs based on the program execution on a small number of known unit tests to select one candidate solution. However, these approaches assume that the unit tests are given and assume the ability to safely execute the generated programs (which can do arbitrary dangerous operations such as file manipulations). Both of the above assumptions are impractical in real-world software development. In this paper, we propose CodeRanker, a neural ranker that can predict the correctness of a sampled program without executing it. Our CodeRanker is fault-aware i.e., it is trained to predict different kinds of execution information such as predicting the exact compile/runtime error type (e.g., an IndexError or a TypeError). We show that CodeRanker can significantly increase the pass@1 accuracy of various code generation models (including Codex, GPT-Neo, GPT-J) on APPS, HumanEval and MBPP datasets.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models can sometimes produce a correct solution if allowed many attempts. Selecting that solution from the candidates is another problem. Existing approaches often run generated programs against known unit tests, which requires both available tests and a way to execute potentially dangerous code safely.

CodeRanker learns to rank sampled programs by predicted correctness without executing them at selection time. Its training is fault-aware: it predicts execution-related information, including specific compilation or runtime error types such as IndexError and TypeError. This gives the ranking model a more detailed training signal about program failures than an undifferentiated correctness judgment.

The authors report significant improvements in pass@1 accuracy for several code generators, including Codex, GPT-Neo, and GPT-J, on APPS, HumanEval, and MBPP. Here, the benefit concerns the correctness of the single candidate ultimately selected. The results support learned ranking as a way to improve candidate selection when execution-based filtering is impractical. Predicting correctness remains distinct from certifying that a program is correct.
summary.tldr: CodeRanker improves selection among generated programs by learning correctness and fault predictions without executing candidates.

title: Fault-Aware Neural Code Rankers

abstract: General Value Function (GVF) is a powerful tool to represent both the {\em predictive} and {\em retrospective} knowledge in reinforcement learning (RL). In practice, often multiple interrelated GVFs need to be evaluated jointly with pre-collected off-policy samples. In the literature, the gradient temporal difference (GTD) learning method has been adopted to evaluate GVFs in the off-policy setting, but such an approach may suffer from a large estimation error even if the function approximation class is sufficiently expressive. Moreover, none of the previous work have formally established the convergence guarantee to the ground truth GVFs under the function approximation settings. In this paper, we address both issues through the lens of a class of GVFs with causal filtering, which cover a wide range of RL applications such as reward variance, value gradient, cost in anomaly detection, stationary distribution gradient, etc. We propose a new algorithm called GenTD for off-policy GVFs evaluation and show that GenTD learns multiple interrelated multi-dimensional GVFs as efficiently as a single canonical scalar value function. We further show that unlike GTD, the learned GVFs by GenTD are guaranteed to converge to the ground truth GVFs as long as the function approximation power is sufficiently large. To our best knowledge, GenTD is the first off-policy GVF evaluation algorithm that has global optimality guarantee.

paragraphs: General value functions let a reinforcement learning agent represent knowledge about both future and past behavior. Applications may require several interdependent quantities to be estimated together using previously collected data from a different policy. This paper examines how to perform that off-policy evaluation accurately with function approximation.

The authors identify a problem with gradient temporal difference learning: estimates can remain substantially wrong even when the approximation class is expressive enough. They develop GenTD through a class of general value functions with causal filtering. The framework covers quantities such as reward variance, value gradients, anomaly-detection costs, and gradients of stationary distributions.

GenTD is shown to learn multiple interrelated, multidimensional value functions as efficiently as a single ordinary scalar value function. Its convergence to the true general value functions is guaranteed when function approximation power is sufficiently large. That condition is central to the result. The contribution combines joint evaluation efficiency with a global optimality guarantee for the studied off-policy framework.
summary.tldr: GenTD jointly evaluates interrelated off-policy general value functions, with convergence to the truth given sufficient approximation power.

title: A Unifying Framework of Off-Policy General Value Function Evaluation

abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) are widely used in many sub-fields of natural language processing (NLP) and generally known as excellent few-shot learners with task-specific exemplars. Notably, chain of thought (CoT) prompting, a recent technique for eliciting complex multi-step reasoning through step-by-step answer examples, achieved the state-of-the-art performances in arithmetics and symbolic reasoning, difficult system-2 tasks that do not follow the standard scaling laws for LLMs. While these successes are often attributed to LLMs' ability for few-shot learning, we show that LLMs are decent zero-shot reasoners by simply adding ``Let's think step by step'' before each answer. Experimental results demonstrate that our Zero-shot-CoT, using the same single prompt template, significantly outperforms zero-shot LLM performances on diverse benchmark reasoning tasks including arithmetics (MultiArith, GSM8K, AQUA-RAT, SVAMP), symbolic reasoning (Last Letter, Coin Flip), and other logical reasoning tasks (Date Understanding, Tracking Shuffled Objects), without any hand-crafted few-shot examples, e.g. increasing the accuracy on MultiArith from 17.7% to 78.7% and GSM8K from 10.4% to 40.7% with large-scale InstructGPT model (text-davinci-002), as well as similar magnitudes of improvements with another off-the-shelf large model, 540B parameter PaLM. The versatility of this single prompt across very diverse reasoning tasks hints at untapped and understudied fundamental zero-shot capabilities of LLMs, suggesting high-level, multi-task broad cognitive capabilities may be extracted by simple prompting. We hope our work not only serves as the minimal strongest zero-shot baseline for the challenging reasoning benchmarks, but also highlights the importance of carefully exploring and analyzing the enormous zero-shot knowledge hidden inside LLMs before crafting finetuning datasets or few-shot exemplars.

This paper tests a simpler intervention: adding “Let's think step by step” before the answer, without providing worked examples. The resulting approach, Zero-shot-CoT, uses the same prompt template across different reasoning tasks.

The authors also report improvements of similar magnitude with the 540-billion-parameter PaLM model. These results show that a brief instruction can substantially change measured reasoning performance in the tested models.

The broader implication is that useful capabilities may remain hidden when evaluation relies on an ordinary zero-shot prompt. The authors interpret the prompt's versatility as evidence suggesting broader, underexplored reasoning capabilities, rather than establishing universal reasoning ability. Their work motivates examining what pretrained models can already do with simple prompting before investing in task-specific examples or fine-tuning data.
summary.tldr: A simple step-by-step instruction substantially improves zero-shot reasoning performance across several benchmarks without supplying worked examples.

title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners

abstract: The visual world can be parsimoniously characterized in terms of distinct entities with sparse interactions. Discovering this compositional structure in dynamic visual scenes has proven challenging for end-to-end computer vision approaches unless explicit instance-level supervision is provided. Slot-based models leveraging motion cues have recently shown great promise in learning to represent, segment, and track objects without direct supervision, but they still fail to scale to complex real-world multi-object videos. In an effort to bridge this gap, we take inspiration from human development and hypothesize that information about scene geometry in the form of depth signals can facilitate object-centric learning. We introduce SAVi++, an object-centric video model which is trained to predict depth signals from a slot-based video representation. By further leveraging best practices for model scaling, we are able to train SAVi++ to segment complex dynamic scenes recorded with moving cameras, containing both static and moving objects of diverse appearance on naturalistic backgrounds, without the need for segmentation supervision. Finally, we demonstrate that by using sparse depth signals obtained from LiDAR, SAVi++ is able to learn emergent object segmentation and tracking from videos in the real-world Waymo Open dataset.

paragraphs: Object-centric video learning aims to represent a scene as distinct entities that can be segmented and tracked. Earlier slot-based approaches using motion cues struggle with complex real-world videos. SAVi++ explores whether depth information can supply the geometric signal needed to learn object structure in scenes containing more varied appearances, backgrounds, and camera movement.

The model learns a slot-based video representation by predicting depth signals. Combined with practices for scaling the model, this training enables segmentation of dynamic scenes recorded by moving cameras, including both stationary and moving objects. The approach does not require segmentation supervision, though depth prediction supplies a training signal about the structure of the scene.

The authors also demonstrate learning from sparse LiDAR depth measurements in the real-world Waymo Open dataset. Object segmentation and tracking emerge from this training setup. The result supports the hypothesis that scene geometry can help organize video representations around objects, extending object-centric learning toward complex conditions where motion-based slot models had struggled.
summary.tldr: SAVi++ learns to segment and track objects in complex videos by predicting depth from slot-based representations without segmentation supervision.

title: SAVi++: Towards End-to-End Object-Centric Learning from Real-World Videos

abstract: Recently, contrastiveness-based augmentation surges a new climax in the computer vision domain, where some operations, including rotation, crop, and flip, combined with dedicated algorithms, dramatically increase the model generalization and robustness. Following this trend, some pioneering attempts employ the similar idea to graph data. Nevertheless, unlike images, it is much more difficult to design reasonable augmentations without changing the nature of graphs. Although exciting, the current graph contrastive learning does not achieve as promising performance as visual contrastive learning. We conjecture the current performance of graph contrastive learning might be limited by the violation of the label-invariant augmentation assumption. In light of this, we propose a label-invariant augmentation for graph-structured data to address this challenge. Different from the node/edge modification and subgraph extraction, we conduct the augmentation in the representation space and generate the augmented samples in the most difficult direction while keeping the label of augmented data the same as the original samples. In the semi-supervised scenario, we demonstrate our proposed method outperforms the classical graph neural network based methods and recent graph contrastive learning on eight benchmark graph-structured data, followed by several in-depth experiments to further explore the label-invariant augmentation in several aspects.

paragraphs: Data augmentation creates variations of training examples to improve learning. For graphs, however, modifying nodes or edges can change the property that determines the graph's label. The authors conjecture that violations of the assumption that augmentation preserves labels may help explain why graph contrastive learning has not matched the promise seen in visual contrastive learning.

They propose augmenting graphs in representation space, where the model encodes their information, instead of directly modifying graph structure or extracting subgraphs. The method generates examples in the most challenging direction while preserving the original label. Its aim is to expose the learner to difficult variations without changing what the example is supposed to represent.

In semi-supervised graph classification, the approach outperforms classical graph neural network methods and recent graph contrastive methods on eight benchmarks. Additional experiments explore aspects of label-preserving augmentation. These results support the proposed representation-space method, while the explanation that label changes constrain existing approaches remains framed as the authors' motivating conjecture.
summary.tldr: The paper creates challenging, label-preserving augmentations in graph representation space and reports improved semi-supervised classification on eight benchmarks.

title: Label-invariant Augmentation for Semi-Supervised Graph Classification

abstract: Recently, a new trend of exploring training sparsity has emerged, which remove parameters during training, leading to both training and inference efficiency improvement. This line of works primarily aims to obtain a single sparse model under a pre-defined large sparsity ratio. It leads to a static/fixed sparse inference model that is not capable of adjusting or re-configuring its computation complexity (i.e., inference structure, latency) after training for real-world varying and dynamic hardware resource availability. To enable such run-time or post-training network morphing, the concept of `dynamic inference' or `training-once-for-all' has been proposed to train a single network consisting of multiple sub-nets once, but each sub-net could perform the same inference function with different computing complexity. However, the traditional dynamic inference training method requires a joint training scheme with multi-objective optimization, which suffers from very large training overhead. In this work, for the first time, we propose a novel alternating sparse training (AST) scheme to train multiple sparse sub-nets for dynamic inference without extra training cost compared to the case of training a single sparse model from scratch. Furthermore, to mitigate the interference of weight update among sub-nets, we propose gradient correction within the inner-group iterations to reduce their weight update interference. We validate the proposed AST on multiple datasets against state-of-the-art sparse training method, which shows that AST achieves similar or better accuracy, but only needs to train once to get multiple sparse sub-nets with different sparsity ratios. More importantly, compared with the traditional joint training based dynamic inference training methodology, the large training overhead is completely eliminated without affecting the accuracy of each sub-net.

paragraphs: Sparse training can reduce training and inference costs by removing parameters, but it commonly produces one model with a fixed computational footprint. That is restrictive when available hardware resources change after training. Dynamic inference addresses this by providing several subnetworks that perform the same task at different computational costs.

Training those subnetworks together traditionally introduces substantial overhead through joint optimization. Alternating Sparse Training, or AST, instead trains multiple sparse subnetworks without extra training cost relative to training a single sparse model from scratch. A gradient correction procedure within inner-group iterations reduces interference between the subnetworks' weight updates.

Across multiple datasets, AST achieves similar or better accuracy than the compared sparse training methods while producing subnetworks with several sparsity levels in one training run. Compared with traditional joint training for dynamic inference, the authors report eliminating its large overhead without reducing individual subnetwork accuracy. The result makes post-training adjustment of computation compatible with the reported cost of training one sparse model.
summary.tldr: AST trains multiple sparse subnetworks at the reported cost of training one, using gradient correction to reduce update interference.

title: Get More at Once: Alternating Sparse Training with Gradient Correction

abstract: Object-oriented reinforcement learning (OORL) is a promising way to improve the sample efficiency and generalization ability over standard RL. Recent works that try to solve OORL tasks without additional feature engineering mainly focus on learning the object representations and then solving tasks via reasoning based on these object representations. However, none of these works tries to explicitly model the inherent similarity between different object instances of the same category. Objects of the same category should share similar functionalities; therefore, the category is the most critical property of an object. Following this insight, we propose a novel framework named Object-Category Aware Reinforcement Learning (OCARL), which utilizes the category information of objects to facilitate both perception and reasoning. OCARL consists of three parts: (1) Category-Aware Unsupervised Object Discovery (UOD), which discovers the objects as well as their corresponding categories; (2) Object-Category Aware Perception, which encodes the category information and is also robust to the incompleteness of (1) at the same time; (3) Object-Centric Modular Reasoning, which adopts multiple independent and object-category-specific networks when reasoning based on objects. Our experiments show that OCARL can improve both the sample efficiency and generalization in the OORL domain.

paragraphs: Object-oriented reinforcement learning represents an environment through its objects and reasons about them to choose actions. This paper focuses on information that individual object representations can overlook: different instances of the same category often have similar functions. The proposed OCARL framework explicitly uses category information in both perception and reasoning.

OCARL has three components. An unsupervised discovery stage identifies objects and their categories. A perception stage encodes category information while remaining robust to incompleteness in that discovery process. Finally, modular reasoning uses multiple independent networks associated with object categories, giving category distinctions a direct role in how the agent reasons.

Experiments in the object-oriented reinforcement learning domain show improvements in both sample efficiency and generalization. These findings support using shared category structure in addition to recognizing individual objects. The design also acknowledges that object discovery may be incomplete, rather than requiring the perception stage to rely on a perfect discovered inventory. The overall contribution is an integrated framework that carries category information from discovery through representation to decision-making.
summary.tldr: OCARL uses object categories throughout perception and reasoning to improve reported reinforcement learning sample efficiency and generalization.

title: Object-Category Aware Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Post-hoc explanation techniques on graph neural networks (GNNs) provide economical solutions for opening the black-box graph models without model retraining. Many GNN explanation variants have achieved state-of-the-art explaining results on a diverse set of benchmarks, while they rarely provide theoretical analysis for their inherent properties and explanatory capability. In this work, we propose $\underline{\text{S}}$tructure-$\underline{\text{A}}$ware Shapley-based $\underline{\text{M}}$ultipiece $\underline{\text{E}}$xplanation (SAME) method to address the structure-aware feature interactions challenges for GNNs explanation. Specifically, SAME leverages an expansion-based Monte Carlo tree search to explore the multi-grained structure-aware connected substructure. Afterward, the explanation results are encouraged to be informative of the graph properties by optimizing the combination of distinct single substructures. With the consideration of fair feature interactions in the process of investigating multiple connected important substructures, the explanation provided by SAME has the potential to be as explainable as the theoretically optimal explanation obtained by the Shapley value within polynomial time. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic benchmarks show that SAME improves the previous state-of-the-art fidelity performance by 12.9\% on BBBP, 7.01\% on MUTAG, 42.3\% on Graph-SST2, 38.9\% on Graph-SST5, 11.3\% on BA-2Motifs and 18.2\% on BA-Shapes under the same testing condition. Code is available at https://github.com/same2023neurips/same.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network requires accounting for how connected features interact, not merely identifying isolated important elements. SAME produces explanations after training, without retraining the predictive model. Its goal is to identify multiple connected graph pieces whose combined contribution helps explain the model’s behavior.

The method uses expansion-based Monte Carlo tree search to explore connected substructures at different scales. It then optimizes combinations of distinct substructures so the resulting explanation captures informative graph properties. Shapley-based reasoning guides its treatment of feature interactions, connecting the search for useful pieces with a principled notion of fair contribution.

The authors argue that this treatment has the potential to match the explanatory quality of a theoretically optimal Shapley explanation within polynomial time; this is not stated as an unconditional equivalence. Experiments report higher fidelity than previous leading methods across six real-world and synthetic benchmarks under matched testing conditions. The findings support considering several interacting graph pieces when seeking explanations that reflect a model’s predictions.
summary.tldr: SAME explains graph neural networks through combinations of connected substructures, using Shapley-based interactions to guide informative explanations.

title: SAME: Uncovering GNN Black Box with Structure-aware Shapley-based Multipiece Explanations

abstract: Spiking neural networks are becoming increasingly popular for their low energy requirement in real-world tasks with accuracy comparable to traditional ANNs. SNN training algorithms face the loss of gradient information and non-differentiability due to the Heaviside function in minimizing the model loss over model parameters. To circumvent this problem, the surrogate method employs a differentiable approximation of the Heaviside function in the backward pass, while the forward pass continues to use the Heaviside as the spiking function. We propose to use the zeroth-order technique at the local or neuron level in training SNNs, motivated by its regularizing and potential energy-efficient effects and establish a theoretical connection between it and the existing surrogate methods. We perform experimental validation of the technique on standard static datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100) and neuromorphic datasets (DVS-CIFAR-10, DVS-Gesture, N-Caltech-101, NCARS) and obtain results that offer improvement over the state-of-the-art results. The proposed method also lends itself to efficient implementations of the back-propagation method, which could provide 3-4 times overall speedup in training time. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/BhaskarMukhoty/LocalZO}.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are attractive because they can combine low energy requirements with accuracy comparable to conventional neural networks. Training them is difficult because the step function that produces spikes does not provide the gradient information ordinary training relies on. A common workaround uses the actual spike function for prediction and a differentiable substitute when propagating training signals backward.

This paper proposes applying a zeroth-order technique locally, at the level of individual neurons. The motivation includes regularizing effects and the possibility of more energy-efficient training. The authors also establish a theoretical connection to existing surrogate-gradient methods, helping relate the proposed training approach to the workaround already used for spiking networks.

Experiments cover both static image datasets and neuromorphic datasets, including CIFAR, ImageNet-100, and event-based recognition tasks. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art results in their evaluation. They also describe compatibility with efficient backpropagation implementations that could yield an overall training speedup of three to four times. That speedup is presented as a possibility enabled by implementation, while the energy benefit is likewise a motivation rather than a quantified finding.
summary.tldr: Neuron-level zeroth-order training improves reported spiking-network results and could support faster, more energy-efficient implementations.

title: Direct Training of SNN using Local Zeroth Order Method

abstract: Previous work on user-level differential privacy (DP) [Ghazi et al. NeurIPS 2021, Bun et al. STOC 2023] obtained generic algorithms that work for various learning tasks. However, their focus was on the *example-rich* regime, where the users have so many examples that each user could themselves solve the problem. In this work we consider the *example-scarce* regime, where each user has only a few examples, and obtain the following results:* For approximate-DP, we give a generic transformation of any item-level DP algorithm to a user-level DP algorithm. Roughly speaking, the latter gives a (multiplicative) savings of $O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\sqrt{m})$ in terms of the number of users required for achieving the same utility, where $m$ is the number of examples per user. This algorithm, while recovering most known bounds for specific problems, also gives new bounds, e.g., for PAC learning. * For pure-DP, we present a simple technique for adapting the exponential mechanism [McSherry & Talwar, FOCS 2007] to the user-level setting. This gives new bounds for a variety of tasks, such as private PAC learning, hypothesis selection, and distribution learning. For some of these problems, we show that our bounds are near-optimal.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects a person's contribution across their examples. Earlier generic learning approaches focused on settings where each person had enough examples to solve the learning problem individually. This paper instead studies the example-scarce setting, where each user contributes only a few examples and learning must make effective use of information across users.

For approximate differential privacy, the authors provide a generic transformation from an item-level private algorithm to a user-level private algorithm. Roughly, with m examples per user, the result yields a square-root-of-m multiplicative saving in the required number of users for the same utility, with dependence on privacy parameters. It recovers most known problem-specific bounds and supplies new ones, including for PAC learning.

For pure differential privacy, the paper adapts the exponential mechanism to the user-level setting. This produces new bounds for private PAC learning, hypothesis selection, and distribution learning. Some of these bounds are shown to be near-optimal. Together, the results establish generic approaches for obtaining useful user-level protection even when individual users have limited data.
summary.tldr: The paper develops generic user-level private learning methods for settings where each user contributes only a few examples.

title: User-Level Differential Privacy With Few Examples Per User

abstract: In many applications, e.g. in healthcare and e-commerce, the goal of a contextual bandit may be to learn an optimal treatment assignment policy at the end of the experiment. That is, to minimize simple regret. However, this objective remains understudied. We propose a new family of computationally efficient bandit algorithms for the stochastic contextual bandit setting, where a tuning parameter determines the weight placed on cumulative regret minimization (where we establish near-optimal minimax guarantees) versus simple regret minimization (where we establish state-of-the-art guarantees). Our algorithms work with any function class, are robust to model misspecification, and can be used in continuous arm settings. This flexibility comes from constructing and relying on “conformal arm sets" (CASs). CASs provide a set of arms for every context, encompassing the context-specific optimal arm with a certain probability across the context distribution. Our positive results on simple and cumulative regret guarantees are contrasted with a negative result, which shows that no algorithm can achieve instance-dependent simple regret guarantees while simultaneously achieving minimax optimal cumulative regret guarantees.

paragraphs: A contextual-bandit experiment can pursue two different goals: make good decisions throughout the experiment or learn a strong policy to use afterward. Cumulative regret measures the first concern, while simple regret measures the quality of the final policy. This paper introduces efficient algorithms with a tuning parameter controlling how much emphasis each goal receives.

The algorithms use conformal arm sets, which assign candidate actions to each context. Across the context distribution, these sets contain the context-specific best action with a specified probability. This coverage property supports algorithms that accommodate any function class, tolerate model misspecification, and extend to continuous action spaces. The guarantee concerns coverage across contexts rather than certainty for every individual context.

The authors establish near-optimal minimax cumulative-regret guarantees and state-of-the-art simple-regret guarantees. They also prove a boundary: no algorithm can combine instance-dependent simple-regret guarantees with minimax-optimal cumulative-regret guarantees. The work therefore provides a way to tune the two objectives while identifying a theoretical restriction on how strong both types of guarantee can be simultaneously.
summary.tldr: Conformal arm sets support contextual-bandit algorithms that trade off final-policy quality against performance during learning, with guarantees and an impossibility result.

title: Proportional Response: Contextual Bandits for Simple and Cumulative Regret Minimization

abstract: We propose Deep Patch Visual Odometry (DPVO), a new deep learning system for monocular Visual Odometry (VO). DPVO uses a novel recurrent network architecture designed for tracking image patches across time. Recent approaches to VO have significantly improved the state-of-the-art accuracy by using deep networks to predict dense flow between video frames. However, using dense flow incurs a large computational cost, making these previous methods impractical for many use cases. Despite this, it has been assumed that dense flow is important as it provides additional redundancy against incorrect matches. DPVO disproves this assumption, showing that it is possible to get the best accuracy and efficiency by exploiting the advantages of sparse patch-based matching over dense flow. DPVO introduces a novel recurrent update operator for patch based correspondence coupled with differentiable bundle adjustment. On Standard benchmarks, DPVO outperforms all prior work, including the learning-based state-of-the-art VO-system (DROID) using a third of the memory while running 3x faster on average. Code is available at https://github.com/princeton-vl/DPVO

paragraphs: Deep Patch Visual Odometry estimates camera motion from video captured by a single camera. Recent learning-based approaches had improved accuracy by predicting dense motion between frames, but that computation is expensive. Dense matching was also thought important because its many correspondences provide redundancy when some matches are wrong. This paper investigates whether sparse patch tracking can deliver both accuracy and efficiency.

DPVO uses a recurrent network designed to follow image patches over time. Its update operator refines patch correspondences and works together with differentiable bundle adjustment. The architecture therefore couples learned matching with geometric refinement, making sparse patch observations the basis of the motion-estimation system.

On the standard benchmarks reported in the abstract, DPVO outperforms prior methods, including DROID. Relative to that learning-based system, it uses one-third of the memory and runs three times faster on average. These results demonstrate that dense flow is not required to achieve leading accuracy in the evaluated setting, making sparse matching a practical route to lower computational cost.
summary.tldr: DPVO tracks sparse image patches to achieve strong monocular motion estimation with one-third of DROID's memory and threefold average speed.

title: Deep Patch Visual Odometry

abstract: Diagnosing and cleaning data is a crucial step for building robust machine learning systems. However, identifying problems within large-scale datasets with real-world distributions is challenging due to the presence of complex issues such as label errors, under-representation, and outliers. In this paper, we propose a unified approach for identifying the problematic data by utilizing a largely ignored source of information: a relational structure of data in the feature-embedded space. To this end, we present scalable and effective algorithms for detecting label errors and outlier data based on the relational graph structure of data. We further introduce a visualization tool that provides contextual information of a data point in the feature-embedded space, serving as an effective tool for interactively diagnosing data. We evaluate the label error and outlier/out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performances of our approach on the large-scale image, speech, and language domain tasks, including ImageNet, ESC-50, and SST2. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art detection performance on all tasks considered and demonstrates its effectiveness in debugging large-scale real-world datasets across various domains. We release codes at https://github.com/snu-mllab/Neural-Relation-Graph.

paragraphs: Large datasets can contain incorrect labels and unusual examples that undermine reliable learning. This paper uses relationships among examples in feature space to identify such problems. Its central idea is that the relational structure surrounding a data point provides useful evidence for diagnosing label errors and outliers.

The authors turn that structure into a graph and develop scalable detection algorithms around it. They also introduce an interactive visualization tool that shows a point in the context of the feature representation. The framework therefore supports both automated detection and human inspection, helping users examine how a flagged example relates to other data.

Evaluation spans image, speech, and language tasks, including ImageNet, ESC-50, and SST2. The method achieves state-of-the-art label-error and outlier or out-of-distribution detection performance on all tasks considered. These results support relational information as a useful shared basis for debugging datasets across modalities, with the visualization providing contextual information alongside the detection algorithms.
summary.tldr: Neural Relation Graph uses relationships in feature space to detect mislabeled examples and outliers across image, speech, and language datasets.

title: Neural Relation Graph: A Unified Framework for Identifying Label Noise and Outlier Data

abstract: Offline inverse reinforcement learning (Offline IRL) aims to recover the structure of rewards and environment dynamics that underlie observed actions in a fixed, finite set of demonstrations from an expert agent. Accurate models of expertise in executing a task has applications in safety-sensitive applications such as clinical decision making and autonomous driving. However, the structure of an expert's preferences implicit in observed actions is closely linked to the expert's model of the environment dynamics (i.e. the ``world''). Thus, inaccurate models of the world obtained from finite data with limited coverage could compound inaccuracy in estimated rewards. To address this issue, we propose a bi-level optimization formulation of the estimation task wherein the upper level is likelihood maximization based upon a conservative model of the expert's policy (lower level). The policy model is conservative in that it maximizes reward subject to a penalty that is increasing in the uncertainty of the estimated model of the world. We propose a new algorithmic framework to solve the bi-level optimization problem formulation and provide statistical and computational guarantees of performance for the associated optimal reward estimator. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art offline IRL and imitation learning benchmarks by a large margin, over the continuous control tasks in MuJoCo and different datasets in the D4RL benchmark.

paragraphs: Offline inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards and environment dynamics from a fixed set of expert demonstrations. These two estimates are closely linked: interpreting why an expert chose an action depends on what consequences the expert expected. With finite data and limited coverage, errors in the learned world model can therefore distort inferred rewards.

The paper addresses this dependency through a two-level optimization problem. The upper level maximizes the likelihood of the demonstrations using a policy model defined at the lower level. That policy model is conservative: it maximizes reward while paying a penalty that grows with uncertainty in the estimated environment dynamics.

The authors provide an algorithmic framework for solving this formulation, together with statistical and computational guarantees for the associated optimal reward estimator. Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and D4RL datasets show large improvements over state-of-the-art offline inverse reinforcement learning and imitation-learning benchmarks. The central idea is to make uncertainty about the world directly influence the policy model used to infer the expert's preferences.
summary.tldr: A two-level likelihood framework uses uncertainty-penalized policy modeling to improve reward inference from fixed expert demonstrations.

title: When Demonstrations meet Generative World Models: A Maximum Likelihood Framework for Offline Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Contract design involves a principal who establishes contractual agreements about payments for outcomes that arise from the actions of an agent. In this paper, we initiate the study of deep learning for the automated design of optimal contracts. We introduce a novel representation: the Discontinuous ReLU (DeLU) network, which models the principal's utility as a discontinuous piecewise affine function of the design of a contract where each piece corresponds to the agent taking a particular action. DeLU networks implicitly learn closed-form expressions for the incentive compatibility constraints of the agent and the utility maximization objective of the principal, and support parallel inference on each piece through linear programming or interior-point methods that solve for optimal contracts. We provide empirical results that demonstrate success in approximating the principal's utility function with a small number of training samples and scaling to find approximately optimal contracts on problems with a large number of actions and outcomes.

paragraphs: Contract design asks how a principal should pay for outcomes when those payments influence an agent's actions. The difficulty is that changing a contract can change which action the agent chooses, producing abrupt changes in the principal's utility. This paper introduces a deep learning approach that explicitly represents that discontinuous structure.

Its Discontinuous ReLU network, or DeLU, describes utility using separate affine pieces, each corresponding to a particular agent action. The network implicitly learns both the conditions under which an action serves the agent's interests and the principal's utility objective. These learned pieces support parallel optimization through linear programming or interior-point methods.

This representation connects learning a utility function with searching for a good contract: the learned structure can be used directly in optimization. The reported experiments show that DeLU approximates utility with relatively few training samples and scales to problems containing many actions and outcomes. The resulting contracts are approximately optimal, making the empirical contribution one of scalable approximation rather than an unconditional claim of exact recovery.
summary.tldr: DeLU networks represent discontinuous contract utilities and support scalable searches for approximately optimal contracts.

title: Deep Contract Design via Discontinuous Networks

abstract: Invariant graph representation learning aims to learn the invariance among data from different environments for out-of-distribution generalization on graphs. As the graph environment partitions are usually expensive to obtain, augmenting the environment information has become the de facto approach. However, the usefulness of the augmented environment information has never been verified. In this work, we find that it is fundamentally impossible to learn invariant graph representations via environment augmentation without additional assumptions. Therefore, we develop a set of minimal assumptions, including variation sufficiency and variation consistency, for feasible invariant graph learning. We then propose a new framework Graph invAriant Learning Assistant (GALA). GALA incorporates an assistant model that needs to be sensitive to graph environment changes or distribution shifts. The correctness of the proxy predictions by the assistant model hence can differentiate the variations in spurious subgraphs. We show that extracting the maximally invariant subgraph to the proxy predictions provably identifies the underlying invariant subgraph for successful OOD generalization under the established minimal assumptions. Extensive experiments on datasets including DrugOOD with various graph distribution shifts confirm the effectiveness of GALA.

paragraphs: Invariant graph learning seeks patterns that remain useful when the environment changes. Because labels identifying graph environments are expensive to obtain, methods often create additional environment information through augmentation. This paper examines whether that generated information is actually sufficient to reveal stable graph structure.

The authors establish that environment augmentation alone cannot identify invariant graph representations without additional assumptions. They introduce minimal assumptions that include variation sufficiency and variation consistency. Their framework, GALA, then uses an assistant model that is deliberately sensitive to environmental changes. Whether its proxy predictions are correct helps distinguish changes in spurious subgraphs.

GALA extracts a subgraph that is maximally invariant to those proxy predictions. Under the stated assumptions, the authors prove that this procedure identifies the underlying invariant subgraph, supporting out-of-distribution generalization. Experiments across graph distribution shifts, including DrugOOD, demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution connects a practical learning strategy to explicit conditions under which augmented information can reveal invariance.
summary.tldr: GALA uses an environment-sensitive assistant to identify invariant graph structure under explicit assumptions that environment augmentation alone cannot replace.

title: Does Invariant Graph Learning via Environment Augmentation Learn Invariance?

abstract: Face recognition systems are widely deployed in safety-critical applications, including law enforcement, yet they exhibit bias across a range of socio-demographic dimensions, such as gender and race. Conventional wisdom dictates that model biases arise from biased training data. As a consequence, previous works on bias mitigation largely focused on pre-processing the training data, adding penalties to prevent bias from effecting the model during training, or post-processing predictions to debias them, yet these approaches have shown limited success on hard problems such as face recognition. In our work, we discover that biases are actually inherent to neural network architectures themselves. Following this reframing, we conduct the first neural architecture search for fairness, jointly with a search for hyperparameters. Our search outputs a suite of models which Pareto-dominate all other high-performance architectures and existing bias mitigation methods in terms of accuracy and fairness, often by large margins, on the two most widely used datasets for face identification, CelebA and VGGFace2. Furthermore, these models generalize to other datasets and sensitive attributes. We release our code, models and raw data files at https://github.com/dooleys/FR-NAS.

paragraphs: Face-recognition systems can perform unevenly across demographic groups. Many mitigation efforts focus on training data, training penalties, or changes to predictions. This paper identifies neural network architecture itself as a source of bias, making the model’s structural design an additional target for improving fairness.

The authors conduct a neural architecture search explicitly aimed at fairness, combined with a search over hyperparameters. This evaluates model design and training choices together, seeking architectures that improve the relationship between recognition accuracy and fairness. The approach shifts part of the mitigation effort toward selecting a better model structure before relying on interventions around a fixed architecture.

On CelebA and VGGFace2, the resulting suite of models is reported to Pareto-dominate the compared high-performance architectures and existing mitigation methods in accuracy and fairness, often by large margins. Pareto dominance indicates improvement without sacrificing the other criterion. The authors also report generalization to other datasets and sensitive attributes. These findings establish architecture search as a promising fairness intervention in the evaluated settings, expanding the set of model-development decisions relevant to demographic performance.
summary.tldr: Joint architecture and hyperparameter search produces face-recognition models with better accuracy–fairness tradeoffs in the reported evaluations.

title: Rethinking Bias Mitigation: Fairer Architectures Make for Fairer Face Recognition

abstract: Recognizing human actions in videos requires spatial and temporal understanding. Most existing action recognition models lack a balanced spatio-temporal understanding of videos. In this work, we propose a novel two-stream architecture, called Cross-Attention in Space and Time (CAST), that achieves a balanced spatio-temporal understanding of videos using only RGB input. Our proposed bottleneck cross-attention mechanism enables the spatial and temporal expert models to exchange information and make synergistic predictions, leading to improved performance. We validate the proposed method with extensive experiments on public benchmarks with different characteristics: EPIC-Kitchens-100, Something-Something-V2, and Kinetics-400. Our method consistently shows favorable performance across these datasets, while the performance of existing methods fluctuates depending on the dataset characteristics. The code is available at https://github.com/KHU-VLL/CAST.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a video requires understanding both what appears in individual frames and how the scene changes over time. The paper argues that many action-recognition models do not balance these two demands well. CAST addresses this with separate spatial and temporal expert models that work together using RGB video input.

The key connection between the two streams is a bottleneck cross-attention mechanism. It allows the spatial expert and temporal expert to exchange information, so their predictions can draw on each other’s understanding. The architecture therefore gives each stream a distinct role while explicitly providing a way to coordinate those roles during recognition.

The authors evaluate CAST on EPIC-Kitchens-100, Something-Something-V2, and Kinetics-400, benchmarks with different characteristics. They report consistently favorable performance across all three, whereas existing methods vary more with the dataset. This pattern supports the value of balanced spatial and temporal processing: exchanging information between experts helps the model perform well across the evaluated video settings, without requiring input beyond RGB.
summary.tldr: CAST lets spatial and temporal video experts exchange information through cross-attention, producing consistently favorable action-recognition results across three benchmarks.

title: CAST: Cross-Attention in Space and Time for Video Action Recognition

abstract: Generative diffusion models and many stochastic models in science and engineering naturally live in infinite dimensions before discretisation. To incorporate observed data for statistical and learning tasks, one needs to condition on observations. While recent work has treated conditioning linear processes in infinite dimensions, conditioning non-linear processes in infinite dimensions has not been explored. This paper conditions function valued stochastic processes without prior discretisation. To do so, we use an infinite-dimensional version of Girsanov's theorem to condition a function-valued stochastic process, leading to a stochastic differential equation (SDE) for the conditioned process involving the score. We apply this technique to do time series analysis for shapes of organisms in evolutionary biology, where we discretise via the Fourier basis and then learn the coefficients of the score function with score matching methods.

paragraphs: Many stochastic models describe evolving functions rather than fixed lists of numbers. Before numerical discretization, these models naturally occupy infinite-dimensional spaces. Incorporating observations requires conditioning the stochastic process on those data. The paper addresses this task for nonlinear processes, extending beyond the linear setting treated in earlier work.

The central move is to condition the function-valued process before discretizing it. The authors use an infinite-dimensional version of Girsanov's theorem to derive a stochastic differential equation for the conditioned process. That equation involves the score, a quantity that also becomes the object of learning in their application. This establishes the conditioning construction at the level of functions themselves.

The application analyzes time series of organism shapes in evolutionary biology. After deriving the conditioned process, the authors discretize it using a Fourier basis and learn the score function's coefficients with score matching. The order of operations matters: the mathematical conditioning is formulated in infinite dimensions, while a finite representation is introduced afterward for computation.
summary.tldr: The paper derives observation-conditioned nonlinear diffusion processes in function space before discretization, then applies the method to evolving organism shapes.

title: Conditioning non-linear and infinite-dimensional diffusion processes

abstract: A major challenge of the long measurement times in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), an important medical imaging technology, is that patients may move during data acquisition. This leads to severe motion artifacts in the reconstructed images and volumes. In this paper, we propose MotionTTT a deep learning-based test-time-training (TTT) method for accurate motion estimation. The key idea is that a neural network trained for motion-free reconstruction has a small loss if there is no motion, thus optimizing over motion parameters passed through the reconstruction network enables accurate estimation of motion. The estimated motion parameters enable to correct for the motion and to reconstruct accurate motion-corrected images. Our method uses 2D reconstruction networks to estimate rigid motion in 3D, and constitutes the first deep learning based method for 3D rigid motion estimation towards 3D-motion-corrected MRI. We show that our method can provably reconstruct motion parameters for a simple signal and neural network model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for both retrospectively simulated motion and prospectively collected real motion-corrupted data. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/MLI-lab/MRI_MotionTTT}.

paragraphs: Movement during an MRI scan can introduce severe artifacts into reconstructed images and volumes. MotionTTT estimates that movement at test time so the reconstruction can account for it. Its key idea is to use a network trained for motion-free reconstruction as a guide for finding motion parameters.

The approach relies on the reconstruction network producing a small loss when motion is absent. It therefore optimizes motion parameters through the network, seeking parameters that make the reconstruction consistent with that behavior. Although the reconstruction networks operate in two dimensions, the method estimates rigid motion in three dimensions and uses those estimates to reconstruct corrected images.

The paper proves motion-parameter recovery for a simplified signal and neural network model. It also evaluates the method using both retrospectively simulated movement and prospectively collected measurements containing real movement. Together, these results provide a theoretical demonstration in a simple setting and empirical support on motion-corrupted data for the proposed route to three-dimensional motion correction.
summary.tldr: MotionTTT optimizes three-dimensional rigid motion estimates through two-dimensional reconstruction networks to correct motion-corrupted MRI.

title: MotionTTT: 2D Test-Time-Training Motion Estimation for 3D Motion Corrected MRI

abstract: Popular zero-shot models suffer due to artifacts inherited from pretraining. One particularly detrimental issue, caused by unbalanced web-scale pretraining data, is mismatched label distribution. Existing approaches that seek to repair the label distribution are not suitable in zero-shot settings, as they have mismatching requirements, such as needing access to labeled downstream task data or knowledge of the true label balance in the pretraining distribution. We sidestep these challenges and introduce a simple and lightweight approach to adjust pretrained model predictions via optimal transport. Our technique requires only an estimate of the label distribution of a downstream task. Theoretically, we characterize the improvement produced by our procedure under certain mild conditions and provide bounds on the error caused by misspecification. Empirically, we validate our method in a wide array of zero-shot image and text classification tasks, improving accuracy by 4.8% and 15.9% on average, and beating baselines like prior matching---often by significant margins---in 17 out of 21 datasets.

paragraphs: OTTER addresses a mismatch between the label distribution reflected in a pretrained zero-shot model and the distribution needed for a downstream task. Unbalanced web-scale pretraining data can leave models with harmful prediction tendencies. Existing correction methods may require labeled downstream examples or knowledge of pretraining label frequencies, requirements that do not fit the intended zero-shot setting.

The proposed method adjusts pretrained predictions through optimal transport. Its required task-specific input is an estimate of the downstream label distribution. This makes the correction lightweight while retaining an explicit dependency on that estimate. The theoretical analysis characterizes improvements under certain mild conditions and bounds the error introduced when the distribution estimate is misspecified.

Experiments cover zero-shot image and text classification, reporting average accuracy improvements of 4.8% and 15.9%, respectively. OTTER also beats baselines such as prior matching on 17 of 21 datasets, often by substantial margins. The results support distribution adjustment as a practical way to improve pretrained predictions, while the theory makes clear that its guarantees are conditional and account for imperfect estimates.
summary.tldr: OTTER uses optimal transport and an estimated downstream label distribution to improve zero-shot classification predictions.

title: OTTER: Effortless Label Distribution Adaptation of Zero-shot Models

abstract: The goal of this paper is to improve the generality and accuracy of open-vocabulary object counting in images. To improve the generality, we repurpose an open-vocabulary detection foundation model (GroundingDINO) for the counting task, and also extend its capabilities by introducing modules to enable specifying the target object to count by visual exemplars. In turn, these new capabilities -- being able to specify the target object by multi-modalites (text and exemplars) -- lead to an improvement in counting accuracy. We make three contributions: First, we introduce the first open-world counting model, CountGD, where the prompt can be specified by a text description or visual exemplars or both; Second, we show that the performance of the model significantly improves the state of the art on multiple counting benchmarks -- when using text only, CountGD outperforms all previous text-only works, and when using both text and visual exemplars, we outperform all previous models; Third, we carry out a preliminary study into different interactions between the text and visual exemplar prompts, including the cases where they reinforce each other and where one restricts the other. The code and an app to test the model are available at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/vgg/research/countgd/.

paragraphs: Counting objects in an image depends on specifying which objects should count. CountGD supports three ways to express that target: a text description, visual examples, or both together. The paper aims to make open-vocabulary counting more general and accurate by giving users these complementary ways to describe what they want.

The method adapts GroundingDINO, an existing open-vocabulary object detection foundation model, for counting. It adds modules that accept visual exemplars, extending the model beyond text-based target descriptions. The authors also study how the two prompt types interact, including cases where they reinforce the same interpretation and cases where one narrows the meaning of the other.

Across multiple counting benchmarks, the authors report that text-only CountGD outperforms previous text-only approaches, while its combined text-and-example version outperforms previous models. These results connect the expanded interface to improved counting accuracy. The interaction study is preliminary, but it also highlights that combining prompts can help define the intended counting task more precisely.
summary.tldr: CountGD adapts an open-vocabulary detector to count objects specified by text, visual examples, or both, improving results across multiple benchmarks.

title: CountGD: Multi-Modal Open-World Counting

abstract: PAC-Bayes learning is a comprehensive setting for (i) studying the generalisation ability of learning algorithms and (ii) deriving new learning algorithms by optimising a generalisation bound. However, optimising generalisation bounds might not always be viable for tractable or computational reasons, or both. For example, iteratively querying the empirical risk might prove computationally expensive.In response, we introduce a novel principled strategy for building an iterative learning algorithm via the optimisation of a sequence of surrogate training objectives, inherited from PAC-Bayes generalisation bounds. The key argument is to replace the empirical risk (seen as a function of hypotheses) in the generalisation bound by its projection onto a constructible low dimensional functional space: these projections can be queried much more efficiently than the initial risk. On top of providing that generic recipe for learning via surrogate PAC-Bayes bounds, we (i) contribute theoretical results establishing that iteratively optimising our surrogates implies the optimisation of the original generalisation bounds, (ii) instantiate this strategy to the framework of meta-learning, introducing a meta-objective offering a closed form expression for meta-gradient, (iii) illustrate our approach with numerical experiments inspired by an industrial biochemical problem.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayes theory can assess generalization and guide learning by making a generalization bound the objective to optimize. Direct optimization can nevertheless be computationally difficult, especially when repeatedly evaluating empirical risk is expensive. This paper develops an iterative alternative that uses a sequence of more tractable surrogate objectives derived from those bounds.

The key construction treats empirical risk as a function over hypotheses and projects it into a low-dimensional space of functions that can be constructed explicitly. The resulting projection can be queried much more cheaply than the original risk. The authors provide theoretical results establishing that iterative optimization of their surrogates implies optimization of the original generalization bounds.

They also apply the strategy to meta-learning, introducing an objective whose meta-gradient has a closed-form expression. Numerical experiments inspired by an industrial biochemical problem illustrate the approach. The contribution combines a general recipe, a theoretical connection to the original objective, and a concrete learning application, showing how cheaper intermediate calculations can retain a principled relationship to generalization-bound optimization.
summary.tldr: Surrogate PAC-Bayes replaces expensive risk evaluations with low-dimensional approximations while retaining a theoretical link to optimizing the original generalization bounds.

title: Learning via Surrogate PAC-Bayes

abstract: Power efficiency is plateauing in the standard digital electronics realm such that new hardware, models, and algorithms are needed to reduce the costs of AI training. The combination of energy-based analog circuits and the Equilibrium Propagation (EP) algorithm constitutes a compelling alternative compute paradigm for gradient-based optimization of neural nets. Existing analog hardware accelerators, however, typically incorporate digital circuitry to sustain auxiliary non-weight-stationary operations, mitigate analog device imperfections, and leverage existing digital platforms. Such heterogeneous hardware lacks a supporting theoretical framework. In this work, we introduce \emph{Feedforward-tied Energy-based Models} (ff-EBMs), a hybrid model comprised of feedforward and energy-based blocks housed on digital and analog circuits. We derive a novel algorithm to compute gradients end-to-end in ff-EBMs by backpropagating and ``eq-propagating'' through feedforward and energy-based parts respectively, enabling EP to be applied flexibly on realistic architectures. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on ff-EBMs using Deep Hopfield Networks (DHNs) as energy-based blocks, and show that a standard DHN can be arbitrarily split into any uniform size while maintaining or improving performance with increases in simulation speed of up to four times. We then train ff-EBMs on ImageNet32 where we establish a new state-of-the-art performance for the EP literature (46 top-1 \%). Our approach offers a principled, scalable, and incremental roadmap for the gradual integration of self-trainable analog computational primitives into existing digital accelerators.

paragraphs: Analog energy-based circuits offer an alternative route to neural-network training, but practical accelerators also rely on digital computation. This combination needs a training framework that connects the two kinds of components. The paper introduces feedforward-tied energy-based models, which combine digital feedforward blocks with analog energy-based blocks.

The authors derive an end-to-end gradient algorithm that uses backpropagation through feedforward components and Equilibrium Propagation through energy-based components. This allows the two training mechanisms to operate within one model. The approach gives Equilibrium Propagation a role in mixed architectures, supporting gradual integration of analog computational blocks into existing digital systems.

The authors show that a standard network can be divided into blocks of any uniform size while maintaining or improving performance, with simulation speedups reaching fourfold. On ImageNet32, the hybrid models achieve 46% top-1 performance, reported as a new best result in the Equilibrium Propagation literature. The speed finding concerns simulation; the broader contribution is a principled gradient framework for training hybrid digital and analog architectures.
summary.tldr: A hybrid gradient algorithm connects backpropagation and Equilibrium Propagation to train models combining digital feedforward and analog energy-based blocks.

title: Towards training digitally-tied analog blocks via hybrid gradient computation

abstract: Addressing intermittent client availability is critical for the real-world deployment of federated learning algorithms. Most prior work either overlooks the potential non-stationarity in the dynamics of client unavailability or requires substantial memory/computation overhead. We study federated learning in the presence of heterogeneous and non-stationary client availability, which may occur when the deployment environments are uncertain, or the clients are mobile. The impacts of heterogeneity and non-stationarity on client unavailability can be significant, as we illustrate using FedAvg, the most widely adopted federated learning algorithm. We propose FedAWE, which includes novel algorithmic structures that (i) compensate for missed computations due to unavailability with only $O(1)$ additional memory and computation with respect to standard FedAvg, and (ii) evenly diffuse local updates within the federated learning system through implicit gossiping, despite being agnostic to non-stationary dynamics. We show that FedAWE converges to a stationary point of even non-convex objectives while achieving the desired linear speedup property. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments over diversified client unavailability dynamics on real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often operate with devices that connect intermittently. Availability can differ across clients and change over time, especially when clients move or deployment conditions are uncertain. This paper studies both effects together and illustrates how they can significantly affect FedAvg, a widely used federated learning algorithm.

The proposed method, FedAWE, compensates for computations missed while a client is unavailable. It does so with only constant additional memory and computation relative to standard FedAvg. A second component spreads local updates evenly through the system using implicit gossiping. The method does not require knowledge of the changing dynamics that govern client availability.

The authors show convergence to a stationary point for nonconvex objectives and establish a linear speedup property. A stationary-point result describes a convergence target without asserting that the algorithm reaches a global optimum. Experiments on real-world datasets with varied availability dynamics support the analysis. The contribution combines adaptation to unreliable participation with limited added computational and memory demands.
summary.tldr: FedAWE handles unequal and changing client availability through missed-computation compensation and implicit gossiping with constant added overhead.

title: Efficient Federated Learning against Heterogeneous and Non-stationary Client Unavailability

abstract: Reinforcement learning based fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on human preferences has been shown to enhance both their capabilities and safety behavior. However, in cases related to safety, without precise instructions to human annotators, the data collected may cause the model to become overly cautious, or to respond in an undesirable style, such as being judgmental. Additionally, as model capabilities and usage patterns evolve, there may be a costly need to add or relabel data to modify safety behavior. We propose a novel preference modeling approach that utilizes AI feedback and only requires a small amount of human data. Our method, Rule Based Rewards (RBR), uses a collection of rules for desired or undesired behaviors (e.g. refusals should not be judgmental) along with a LLM grader. In contrast to prior methods using AI feedback, our method uses fine-grained, composable, LLM-graded few-shot prompts as reward directly in RL training, resulting in greater control, accuracy and ease of updating. We show that RBRs are an effective training method, achieving an F1 score of 97.1, compared to a human-feedback baseline of 91.7, resulting in much higher safety-behavior accuracy through better balancing usefulness and safety.

paragraphs: Training language models from human preferences can improve safety, but unclear annotation instructions can also encourage excessive caution or undesirable response styles. Updating those behaviors may require costly changes to the training data. Rule Based Rewards addresses this problem by expressing desired and undesired behaviors as rules that an LLM grader can evaluate.

The method uses fine-grained, composable prompts with examples to grade responses and supply rewards directly during reinforcement learning. For instance, a rule can specify that a refusal should avoid being judgmental. The approach requires only a small amount of human data and is designed to make safety behavior more controllable, accurately assessed, and easier to update.

The authors report a safety-behavior F1 score of 97.1, compared with 91.7 for a human-feedback baseline. They attribute the improvement to a better balance between usefulness and safety. The contribution is a direct route from explicit behavioral requirements to training rewards, with the reported evaluation showing that this structure can improve the accuracy of learned safety behavior.
summary.tldr: Rule Based Rewards turns explicit, LLM-graded behavior rules into reinforcement-learning rewards, improving reported safety-behavior accuracy with little human data.

title: Rule Based Rewards for Language Model Safety

abstract: We propose a method for metric-scale monocular depth estimation. Inferring depth from a single image is an ill-posed problem due to the loss of scale from perspective projection during the image formation process. Any scale chosen is a bias, typically stemming from training on a dataset; hence, existing works have instead opted to use relative (normalized, inverse) depth. Our goal is to recover metric-scaled depth maps through a linear transformation. The crux of our method lies in the observation that certain objects (e.g., cars, trees, street signs) are typically found or associated with certain types of scenes (e.g., outdoor). We explore whether language descriptions can be used to transform relative depth predictions to those in metric scale. Our method, RSA , takes as input a text caption describing objects present in an image and outputs the parameters of a linear transformation which can be applied globally to a relative depth map to yield metric-scaled depth predictions. We demonstrate our method on recent general-purpose monocular depth models on indoors (NYUv2, VOID) and outdoors (KITTI). When trained on multiple datasets, RSA can serve as a general alignment module in zero-shot settings. Our method improves over common practices in aligning relative to metric depth and results in predictions that are comparable to an upper bound of fitting relative depth to ground truth via a linear transformation. Code is available at: https://github.com/Adonis-galaxy/RSA.

Many depth models therefore predict relative depth rather than distances in metric units. RSA investigates whether a description of the objects in an image can help align those relative predictions with metric depth.

The method uses a text caption to predict the parameters of a linear transformation applied across the entire relative depth map. Its motivation is that objects are associated with particular scene types: the objects named in a caption can provide contextual information relevant to scale. RSA supplies an alignment module for an existing depth prediction.

The authors demonstrate the approach with general-purpose depth models on indoor NYUv2 and VOID data and outdoor KITTI data. With training across multiple datasets, it can also act as a zero-shot alignment module. Reported predictions improve on common alignment practices and approach the reference obtained by fitting relative depth directly to ground truth with a linear transformation.
summary.tldr: RSA uses image captions to predict a global linear transformation that converts relative depth estimates into metric-scaled predictions.

title: RSA: Resolving Scale Ambiguities in Monocular Depth Estimators through Language Descriptions

abstract: In many social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences, treatment effect estimation is a crucial step in understanding the impact of an intervention, policy, or treatment. In recent years, an increasing emphasis has been placed on heterogeneity in treatment effects, leading to the development of various methods for estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). These approaches hinge on a crucial identifying condition of no unmeasured confounding, an assumption that is not always guaranteed in observational studies or randomized control trials with non-compliance. In this paper, we proposed a general framework for estimating CATE with a possible unmeasured confounder using Instrumental Variables. We also construct estimators that exhibit greater efficiency and robustness against various scenarios of model misspecification. The efficacy of the proposed framework is demonstrated through simulation studies and a real data example.
