The problem structure allows us to reformulate it as a convex-concave saddle point problem. We propose a stochastic primal-dual coordinate method, which alternates between maximizing over one (or more) randomly chosen dual variable and minimizing over the primal variable. We also develop an extension to non-smooth and non-strongly convex loss functions, and an extension with better convergence rate on unnormalized data. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that the SPDC method has comparable or better performance than several state-of-the-art optimization methods.

paragraphs: Regularized empirical risk minimization trains a predictor by balancing its fit to observed data with a penalty on the model. This paper studies a generic convex version of that problem for linear predictors. It uses the problem's structure to rewrite training as a convex-concave saddle-point problem involving primal and dual variables.

The proposed stochastic primal-dual coordinate method, SPDC, alternates between maximizing over one or more randomly selected dual variables and minimizing over the primal variable. Random coordinate selection makes partial dual updates part of the main optimization procedure. The saddle-point formulation supplies a coordinated way to connect these updates to changes in the predictor.

The authors also develop extensions for nonsmooth losses and losses that are not strongly convex, together with an extension offering a better convergence rate on unnormalized data. Theoretical analysis and experiments show comparable or better performance than several existing leading optimization methods. The result is a family of stochastic optimization procedures whose formulation supports both convergence analysis and adaptation to different loss properties.
summary.tldr: SPDC trains regularized linear predictors through alternating primal updates and random dual-coordinate updates, with theoretical and empirical performance benefits.

title: Stochastic Primal-Dual Coordinate Method for Regularized Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: We introduce new families of Integral Probability Metrics (IPM) for training Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). Our IPMs are based on matching statistics of distributions embedded in a finite dimensional feature space. Mean and covariance feature matching IPMs allow for stable training of GANs, which we will call McGan. McGan minimizes a meaningful loss between distributions.
originalAbstract: We introduce new families of Integral Probability Metrics (IPM) for training Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). Our IPMs are based on matching statistics of distributions embedded in a finite dimensional feature space. Mean and covariance feature matching IPMs allow for stable training of GANs, which we will call McGan. McGan minimizes a meaningful loss between distributions.

paragraphs: McGan approaches generative adversarial network training through a statistical comparison between distributions. The paper introduces families of integral probability metrics, which provide a loss for comparing the distribution of generated examples with the distribution being modeled. The comparison takes place after distributions are represented in a finite-dimensional feature space.

The proposed metrics focus on feature means and covariances. Means describe average feature values, while covariances describe how features vary together. Matching these statistics gives the training objective a concrete interpretation: generated and target distributions are compared through selected properties of their feature representations. Both average behavior and relationships among features therefore enter the formulation.

The authors state that these mean- and covariance-matching metrics allow stable GAN training and give McGan a meaningful loss between distributions. The contribution centers on how the training objective is defined. By expressing the discrepancy through feature statistics, the method connects the quantity being minimized to identifiable statistical differences between generated data and the data the model seeks to reproduce.
summary.tldr: McGan trains GANs using distribution metrics that match feature means and covariances, supporting stable training with a meaningful loss.

title: McGan: Mean and Covariance Feature Matching GAN

abstract: We study revenue optimization learning algorithms for repeated posted-price auctions where a seller interacts with a single strategic buyer that holds a fixed private valuation for a good and seeks to maximize his cumulative discounted surplus. We propose a novel algorithm that never decreases offered prices and has a tight strategic regret bound of $\Theta(\log\log T)$. This result closes the open research question on the existence of a no-regret horizon-independent weakly consistent pricing. We also show that the property of non-decreasing prices is nearly necessary for a weakly consistent algorithm to be a no-regret one.
originalAbstract: We study revenue optimization learning algorithms for repeated posted-price auctions where a seller interacts with a single strategic buyer that holds a fixed private valuation for a good and seeks to maximize his cumulative discounted surplus. We propose a novel algorithm that never decreases offered prices and has a tight strategic regret bound of $\Theta(\log\log T)$. This result closes the open research question on the existence of a no-regret horizon-independent weakly consistent pricing. We also show that the property of non-decreasing prices is nearly necessary for a weakly consistent algorithm to be a no-regret one.

paragraphs: In repeated posted-price auctions, a seller learns how to price a good while a buyer may strategically accept or reject offers. The buyer in this paper has a fixed private valuation and optimizes discounted surplus across interactions. This makes the learning problem different from estimating willingness to pay from an immediately truthful response.

The authors introduce a pricing algorithm whose offered prices never decrease. Its strategic regret has a tight Θ(log log T) bound, where T is the number of rounds. The method is horizon-independent, so its operation does not require knowing the eventual interaction length in advance, and it satisfies the paper’s weak-consistency requirement.

This establishes the existence of a no-regret pricing strategy with those properties, resolving the stated open question. The paper also shows that nondecreasing prices are nearly necessary for weakly consistent no-regret algorithms. Both conclusions belong to the specific repeated-auction model with one strategic buyer and a fixed valuation, rather than a general market with changing or competing buyers.
summary.tldr: A nondecreasing-price strategy achieves tight doubly logarithmic strategic regret without knowing the auction horizon.

title: Weakly Consistent Optimal Pricing Algorithms in Repeated Posted-Price Auctions with Strategic Buyer

abstract: We analyze the loss landscape and expressiveness of practical deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with shared weights and max pooling layers. We show that such CNNs produce linearly independent features at a “wide” layer which has more neurons than the number of training samples. This condition holds e.g. for the VGG network. Furthermore, we provide for such wide CNNs necessary and sufficient conditions for global minima with zero training error. For the case where the wide layer is followed by a fully connected layer we show that almost every critical point of the empirical loss is a global minimum with zero training error. Our analysis suggests that both depth and width are very important in deep learning. While depth brings more representational power and allows the network to learn high level features, width smoothes the optimization landscape of the loss function in the sense that a sufficiently wide network has a well-behaved loss surface with almost no bad local minima.

Furthermore, we provide for such wide CNNs necessary and sufficient conditions for global minima with zero training error. paragraphs: This paper examines both what deep convolutional networks can represent and the shape of the loss surface used to train them. The analysis includes shared weights and max pooling, connecting the theory to practical CNN architectures. Its central architectural condition is a wide layer containing more neurons than there are training examples.

The authors show that such networks produce linearly independent features at the wide layer and give necessary and sufficient conditions for global minima with zero training error. For the case in which a fully connected layer follows the wide layer, they further show that almost every critical point of the empirical loss is a global minimum with zero training error.

These findings suggest complementary roles for depth and width. Depth increases representational power and supports higher-level features, while sufficient width improves the optimization landscape in the stated sense of having almost no bad local minima. The conclusions concern the analyzed architecture and training loss; the qualification about almost every critical point is part of the result.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes expressivity and training-loss results showing how sufficiently wide layers can give deep CNNs favorable optimization landscapes.

title: Optimization Landscape and Expressivity of Deep CNNs

abstract: We present a novel family of deep neural architectures, named partially exchangeable networks (PENs) that leverage probabilistic symmetries. By design, PENs are invariant to block-switch transformations, which characterize the partial exchangeability properties of conditionally Markovian processes. Moreover, we show that any block-switch invariant function has a PEN-like representation. The DeepSets architecture is a special case of PEN and we can therefore also target fully exchangeable data. We employ PENs to learn summary statistics in approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). When comparing PENs to previous deep learning methods for learning summary statistics, our results are highly competitive, both considering time series and static models. Indeed, PENs provide more reliable posterior samples even when using less training data.

paragraphs: This paper designs neural networks around probabilistic symmetries in data. Its partially exchangeable networks, or PENs, are unchanged by block-switch transformations associated with conditionally Markovian processes. Encoding that invariance in the architecture makes the network respect a specific form of structure in the data it processes.

The authors also establish a representation result: any function invariant to those block switches has a PEN-like representation. DeepSets appears as a special case, so the family includes architectures for fully exchangeable data as well. This connects the proposed network design to both partial and full exchangeability within a common framework.

The application is learning summary statistics for approximate Bayesian computation, where those summaries support posterior inference. Comparisons with earlier deep-learning methods are highly competitive across time-series and static models. The authors report more reliable posterior samples even with less training data. These findings support using the relevant probabilistic symmetry as an architectural guide when learning summaries for the studied inference problems.
summary.tldr: PENs encode partial-exchangeability symmetries and learn effective summary statistics for approximate Bayesian computation, even with less training data.

title: Partially Exchangeable Networks and Architectures for Learning Summary Statistics in Approximate Bayesian Computation

abstract: A popular line of recent research incorporates ML advice in the design of online algorithms to improve their performance in typical instances. These papers treat the ML algorithm as a black-box, and redesign online algorithms to take advantage of ML predictions. In this paper, we ask the complementary question: can we redesign ML algorithms to provide better predictions for online algorithms? We explore this question in the context of the classic rent-or-buy problem, and show that incorporating optimization benchmarks in ML loss functions leads to significantly better performance, while maintaining a worst-case adversarial result when the advice is completely wrong. We support this finding both through theoretical bounds and numerical simulations.
originalAbstract: A popular line of recent research incorporates ML advice in the design of online algorithms to improve their performance in typical instances. These papers treat the ML algorithm as a black-box, and redesign online algorithms to take advantage of ML predictions. In this paper, we ask the complementary question: can we redesign ML algorithms to provide better predictions for online algorithms? We explore this question in the context of the classic rent-or-buy problem, and show that incorporating optimization benchmarks in ML loss functions leads to significantly better performance, while maintaining a worst-case adversarial result when the advice is completely wrong. We support this finding both through theoretical bounds and numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Online algorithms make decisions as information arrives, so predictions about future events can improve their choices. Much work in this area treats the predictor as a fixed component and changes the decision algorithm around it. This paper investigates how training the predictor for the downstream decision problem can improve the resulting system.

The authors study the classic rent-or-buy problem, where a decision maker chooses between continuing to rent and paying to buy. Their approach incorporates optimization benchmarks into the machine-learning loss function. This makes the training objective reflect how predictions affect the online algorithm's performance, connecting prediction quality to the decisions those predictions support.

The paper supports this approach with theoretical bounds and numerical simulations, reporting significantly better performance in the studied setting. It also retains a worst-case adversarial guarantee when the advice is completely wrong. The result shows how tailoring prediction training to an online optimization task can improve performance while preserving protection against highly unreliable advice.
summary.tldr: Training predictions around the rent-or-buy decision objective improves online performance while retaining a worst-case guarantee for completely wrong advice.

title: Customizing ML Predictions for Online Algorithms

abstract: Learned dynamics models combined with both planning and policy learning algorithms have shown promise in enabling artificial agents to learn to perform many diverse tasks with limited supervision. However, one of the fundamental challenges in using a learned forward dynamics model is the mismatch between the objective of the learned model (future state reconstruction), and that of the downstream planner or policy (completing a specified task). This issue is exacerbated by vision-based control tasks in diverse real-world environments, where the complexity of the real world dwarfs model capacity. In this paper, we propose to direct prediction towards task relevant information, enabling the model to be aware of the current task and encouraging it to only model relevant quantities of the state space, resulting in a learning objective that more closely matches the downstream task. Further, we do so in an entirely self-supervised manner, without the need for a reward function or image labels. We find that our method more effectively models the relevant parts of the scene conditioned on the goal, and as a result outperforms standard task-agnostic dynamics models and model-free reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A learned dynamics model predicts what will happen next, while a planner or policy uses predictions to accomplish a task. These objectives need not align: reconstructing an entire future scene can require modeling details that do little to help achieve the goal. The mismatch becomes especially challenging for visual control when the environment is more complex than the model can represent.

The authors make prediction aware of the current task. Their approach directs learning toward relevant parts of the state, encouraging the model to spend its capacity on quantities that matter for the goal. They develop this objective in a self-supervised way, without requiring a reward function or image labels for the proposed learning approach.

The reported findings show that conditioning on the goal helps the model represent relevant scene content more effectively. The method also outperforms standard task-agnostic dynamics models and model-free reinforcement learning in the authors’ evaluation. These results support aligning predictive learning with the information a downstream task actually needs.
summary.tldr: Goal-aware, self-supervised prediction focuses dynamics models on task-relevant information and improves the reported control results.

title: Goal-Aware Prediction: Learning to Model What Matters

abstract: Training autonomous agents able to generalize to multiple tasks is a key target of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) research. In parallel to improving DRL algorithms themselves, Automatic Curriculum Learning (ACL) study how teacher algorithms can train DRL agents more efficiently by adapting task selection to their evolving abilities. While multiple standard benchmarks exist to compare DRL agents, there is currently no such thing for ACL algorithms. Thus, comparing existing approaches is difficult, as too many experimental parameters differ from paper to paper. In this work, we identify several key challenges faced by ACL algorithms. Based on these, we present TeachMyAgent (TA), a benchmark of current ACL algorithms leveraging procedural task generation. It includes 1) challenge-specific unit-tests using variants of a procedural Box2D bipedal walker environment, and 2) a new procedural Parkour environment combining most ACL challenges, making it ideal for global performance assessment. We then use TeachMyAgent to conduct a comparative study of representative existing approaches, showcasing the competitiveness of some ACL algorithms that do not use expert knowledge. We also show that the Parkour environment remains an open problem. We open-source our environments, all studied ACL algorithms (collected from open-source code or re-implemented), and DRL students in a Python package available at https://github.com/flowersteam/TeachMyAgent.

paragraphs: Automatic curriculum learning uses a teacher algorithm to select tasks as a reinforcement-learning agent's abilities change. Comparing such teachers is difficult when studies use different experimental setups. TeachMyAgent addresses this problem by providing a benchmark organized around key challenges in curriculum learning and using procedurally generated tasks.

The benchmark includes focused tests built from variants of a procedural Box2D bipedal walker environment. It also introduces a procedural Parkour environment that combines most of the identified challenges for broader assessment. This organization allows evaluation of particular difficulties alongside evaluation in a setting where several difficulties occur together.

The authors compare representative curriculum methods and find that some approaches without expert knowledge are competitive. They also report that Parkour remains an open problem, preserving a demanding target for future methods. The released Python package includes the environments, studied curriculum algorithms, and reinforcement-learning students. The contribution is a common experimental foundation for studying task selection, with initial comparisons showing both competitive existing approaches and a substantial remaining challenge.
summary.tldr: TeachMyAgent benchmarks curriculum-learning algorithms with focused procedural tests and a challenging Parkour environment that remains an open problem.

title: TeachMyAgent: a Benchmark for Automatic Curriculum Learning in Deep RL

abstract: We propose a novel approximation hierarchy for cardinality-constrained, convex quadratic programs that exploits the rank-dominating eigenvectors of the quadratic matrix. Each level of approximation admits a min-max characterization whose objective function can be optimized over the binary variables analytically, while preserving convexity in the continuous variables. Exploiting this property, we propose two scalable optimization algorithms, coined as the “best response" and the “dual program", that can efficiently screen the potential indices of the nonzero elements of the original program. We show that the proposed methods are competitive with the existing screening methods in the current sparse regression literature, and it is particularly fast on instances with high number of measurements in experiments with both synthetic and real datasets.

Each level of approximation admits a min-max characterization whose objective function can be optimized over the binary variables analytically, while preserving convexity in the continuous variables. Exploiting this property, we propose two scalable optimization algorithms, coined as the “best response" and the “dual program", that can efficiently screen the potential indices of the nonzero elements of the original program. paragraphs: A cardinality constraint limits how many variables in an optimization solution can be nonzero. This paper studies convex quadratic objectives with that additional sparsity requirement. It builds a hierarchy of approximations using the dominant eigenvectors of the quadratic matrix, so the matrix's leading directions guide how the optimization problem is simplified.

Each approximation has a min-max formulation with a useful separation between discrete and continuous choices. The binary variables can be optimized analytically while the problem retains convexity in its continuous variables. The authors use this property to develop two scalable algorithms, called best response and dual program, for screening candidate locations of nonzero entries.

Screening helps narrow the indices that need attention in the original sparse problem. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the proposed methods are competitive with existing screening approaches in sparse regression. They are particularly fast on instances with many measurements. The contribution is therefore an approximation-based route to efficient screening, supported by favorable results in that high-measurement setting.
summary.tldr: A principal-component approximation hierarchy enables scalable screening for sparse quadratic optimization, with particularly fast reported results on high-measurement problems.

title: Principal Component Hierarchy for Sparse Quadratic Programs

abstract: Storing information in DNA molecules is of great interest because of its advantages in longevity, high storage density, and low maintenance cost. A key step in the DNA storage pipeline is to efficiently cluster the retrieved DNA sequences according to their similarities. Levenshtein distance is the most suitable metric on the similarity between two DNA sequences, but it is inferior in terms of computational complexity and less compatible with mature clustering algorithms. In this work, we propose a novel deep squared Euclidean embedding for DNA sequences using Siamese neural network, squared Euclidean embedding, and chi-squared regression. The Levenshtein distance is approximated by the squared Euclidean distance between the embedding vectors, which is fast calculated and clustering algorithm friendly. The proposed approach is analyzed theoretically and experimentally. The results show that the proposed embedding is efficient and robust.

paragraphs: DNA storage requires grouping retrieved DNA sequences according to their similarity. The paper identifies Levenshtein distance as particularly suitable for comparing these sequences, but costly to compute and awkward to combine with established clustering algorithms. This creates a practical bottleneck between recovering sequences and organizing them into useful groups.

The proposed solution learns a vector representation of each sequence. It combines a Siamese neural network, squared Euclidean embedding, and chi-squared regression so that the squared distance between two vectors approximates the sequences' Levenshtein distance. Sequence comparison can then use vector arithmetic, while clustering can operate in a representation better matched to familiar algorithms.

The approach matters because it seeks to retain the useful similarity information of the original distance while changing how that information is computed and consumed. The authors analyze the embedding theoretically and experimentally, reporting efficiency and robustness. The result is an approximation rather than an exact replacement for Levenshtein distance, with the stated findings supporting its usefulness for the DNA sequence clustering step.
summary.tldr: A learned DNA sequence embedding approximates Levenshtein distance with fast squared Euclidean comparisons suited to clustering.

title: Deep Squared Euclidean Approximation to the Levenshtein Distance for DNA Storage

abstract: In the last years decision-focused learning framework, also known as predict-and-optimize, have received increasing attention. In this setting, the predictions of a machine learning model are used as estimated cost coefficients in the objective function of a discrete combinatorial optimization problem for decision making. Decision-focused learning proposes to train the ML models, often neural network models, by directly optimizing the quality of decisions made by the optimization solvers. Based on a recent work that proposed a noise contrastive estimation loss over a subset of the solution space, we observe that decision-focused learning can more generally be seen as a learning-to-rank problem, where the goal is to learn an objective function that ranks the feasible points correctly. This observation is independent of the optimization method used and of the form of the objective function. We develop pointwise, pairwise and listwise ranking loss functions, which can be differentiated in closed form given a subset of solutions. We empirically investigate the quality of our generic methods compared to existing decision-focused learning approaches with competitive results. Furthermore, controlling the subset of solutions allows controlling the runtime considerably, with limited effect on regret.

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains a predictive model according to the quality of the decisions its predictions support. In the setting studied here, predicted values become cost coefficients in a discrete optimization problem. The paper reframes this process as learning to rank feasible solutions: the learned objective should place the better decisions ahead of worse ones.

This viewpoint does not depend on a particular optimization method or objective-function form. Building on it, the authors develop pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ranking losses. Given a subset of feasible solutions, these losses have derivatives available in closed form. The subset supplies the alternatives against which the model learns how its predictions affect the ordering of decisions.

Empirical comparisons find the resulting generic methods competitive with existing decision-focused approaches. The experiments also show that choosing the solution subset provides substantial control over runtime with limited impact on regret. This makes the ranking formulation useful both as an explanation of the learning goal and as a practical way to adjust computation while preserving decision quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Viewing decision-focused learning as ranking feasible solutions yields differentiable losses and practical runtime control with competitive empirical decision quality.

title: Decision-Focused Learning: Through the Lens of Learning to Rank

abstract: Estimating counterfactual outcomes over time from observational data is relevant for many applications (e.g., personalized medicine). Yet, state-of-the-art methods build upon simple long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, thus rendering inferences for complex, long-range dependencies challenging. In this paper, we develop a novel Causal Transformer for estimating counterfactual outcomes over time. Our model is specifically designed to capture complex, long-range dependencies among time-varying confounders. For this, we combine three transformer subnetworks with separate inputs for time-varying covariates, previous treatments, and previous outcomes into a joint network with in-between cross-attentions. We further develop a custom, end-to-end training procedure for our Causal Transformer. Specifically, we propose a novel counterfactual domain confusion loss to address confounding bias: it aims to learn adversarial balanced representations, so that they are predictive of the next outcome but non-predictive of the current treatment assignment. We evaluate our Causal Transformer based on synthetic and real-world datasets, where it achieves superior performance over current baselines. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work proposing transformer-based architecture for estimating counterfactual outcomes from longitudinal data.

paragraphs: Estimating counterfactual outcomes means predicting what would happen under a different treatment history. For observations collected over time, this requires accounting for changing variables that influence both treatment assignment and outcomes. The paper develops a transformer architecture to capture complex dependencies across long histories, which can be challenging for the LSTM-based methods it discusses.

The Causal Transformer combines three subnetworks, separately processing time-varying covariates, previous treatments, and previous outcomes. Cross-attention connects these streams so that the model can represent interactions among them. Its custom training procedure includes a counterfactual domain confusion loss, intended to make learned representations useful for predicting the next outcome while making the current treatment difficult to predict.

That training objective aims to reduce confounding bias by balancing representations across treatment assignments. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than the compared baselines. The stated contribution therefore combines a model for long-range temporal relationships with a training mechanism directed at confounding, supported by empirical improvements in counterfactual outcome estimation.
summary.tldr: The Causal Transformer combines interacting temporal subnetworks with a balancing loss to improve counterfactual outcome estimation.

title: Causal Transformer for Estimating Counterfactual Outcomes

abstract: Vision models typically rely on fine-tuning general-purpose models pre-trained on large, static datasets. These general-purpose models only capture the knowledge within their pre-training datasets, which are tiny, out-of-date snapshots of the Internet—where billions of images are uploaded each day. We suggest an alternate approach: rather than hoping our static datasets transfer to our desired tasks after large-scale pre-training, we propose dynamically utilizing the Internet to quickly train a small-scale model that does extremely well on a target dataset. Our approach, called Internet Explorer, explores the web in a self-supervised manner to progressively find relevant examples that improve performance on a desired target dataset. It cycles between searching for images on the Internet with text queries, self-supervised training on downloaded images, determining which images were useful, and prioritizing what to search for next. We evaluate Internet Explorer across several datasets and show that it outperforms or matches CLIP oracle performance using just a single GPU desktop to actively query the Internet for 30-40 hours.

paragraphs: Vision models commonly adapt a general-purpose model trained on a large, fixed image collection. This paper explores a different approach: actively find training images on the web that are useful for a particular target dataset. The motivation is that a static pretraining collection contains only a limited snapshot of the visual information available online.

Internet Explorer repeatedly searches for images using text queries, downloads them, and trains through self-supervision. It then assesses which images were useful and uses that information to prioritize future searches. Data collection and representation learning form a feedback loop, allowing the training material to become progressively more relevant to the target.

Across several datasets, the method matches or exceeds the reported CLIP oracle performance after actively querying the Internet for 30–40 hours on a desktop with one GPU. These findings support targeted web exploration as a practical way to train a small-scale model for a desired dataset. The demonstrated strength lies in directing data acquisition toward the task.
summary.tldr: Internet Explorer alternates web search and self-supervised training to build task-focused visual representations on a single-GPU desktop.

title: Internet Explorer: Targeted Representation Learning on the Open Web

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been found to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, raising security concerns about their deployment in mission-critical applications. While existing defense methods have demonstrated promising results, it is still not clear how to effectively remove backdoor-associated neurons in backdoored DNNs. In this paper, we propose a novel defense called Reconstructive Neuron Pruning (RNP) to expose and prune backdoor neurons via an unlearning and then recovering process. Specifically, RNP first unlearns the neurons by maximizing the model’s error on a small subset of clean samples and then recovers the neurons by minimizing the model’s error on the same data. In RNP, unlearning is operated at the neuron level while recovering is operated at the filter level, forming an asymmetric reconstructive learning procedure. We show that such an asymmetric process on only a few clean samples can effectively expose and prune the backdoor neurons implanted by a wide range of attacks, achieving a new state-of-the-art defense performance. Moreover, the unlearned model at the intermediate step of our RNP can be directly used to improve other backdoor defense tasks including backdoor removal, trigger recovery, backdoor label detection, and backdoor sample detection. Code is available at https://github.com/bboylyg/RNP.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks implant unwanted behavior in neural networks, creating a need to identify and remove the neurons associated with that behavior. Reconstructive Neuron Pruning, or RNP, approaches this through a deliberate unlearning-and-recovery process. It uses a small collection of clean samples to expose backdoor-related neurons before pruning them.

The first stage increases the model’s error on the clean samples to unlearn at the neuron level. The second reduces error on those same samples, but performs recovery at the filter level. This asymmetry is the central design choice: the two stages operate at different levels of the network while using the same clean data.

The authors show that this procedure can expose and prune backdoor neurons from a wide range of attacks using only a few clean samples, reporting state-of-the-art defense performance. They also find that the intermediate unlearned model can improve backdoor removal, trigger recovery, backdoor label detection, and backdoor sample detection. The intermediate stage therefore supplies useful information beyond its role in the final pruning procedure.
summary.tldr: RNP exposes backdoor neurons by unlearning at the neuron level and recovering at the filter level before pruning.

title: Reconstructive Neuron Pruning for Backdoor Defense

abstract: We study contextual combinatorial bandits with probabilistically triggered arms (C$^2$MAB-T) under a variety of smoothness conditions that capture a wide range of applications, such as contextual cascading bandits and contextual influence maximization bandits. Under the triggering probability modulated (TPM) condition, we devise the C$^2$-UCB-T algorithm and propose a novel analysis that achieves an $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{KT})$ regret bound, removing a potentially exponentially large factor $O(1/p_{\min})$, where $d$ is the dimension of contexts, $p_{\min}$ is the minimum positive probability that any arm can be triggered, and batch-size $K$ is the maximum number of arms that can be triggered per round. Under the variance modulated (VM) or triggering probability and variance modulated (TPVM) conditions, we propose a new variance-adaptive algorithm VAC$^2$-UCB and derive a regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T})$, which is independent of the batch-size $K$. As a valuable by-product, our analysis technique and variance-adaptive algorithm can be applied to the CMAB-T and C$^2$MAB setting, improving existing results there as well. We also include experiments that demonstrate the improved performance of our algorithms compared with benchmark algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions in which context informs a combined action, and the action activates individual options only probabilistically. Applications include cascading recommendations and influence maximization. The central challenge is learning good decisions when an option’s contribution depends partly on whether it is activated at all. The authors analyze this problem under several smoothness conditions.

Under triggering probability modulated smoothness, their C²-UCB-T algorithm achieves regret of order d√(KT), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here, d measures context dimension, K is the maximum number of options activated per round, and T is the number of rounds. The analysis removes an inverse minimum-triggering-probability factor that could otherwise be exponentially large.

Under variance modulated or triggering probability and variance modulated conditions, the variance-adaptive VAC²-UCB algorithm achieves order d√T regret, again suppressing logarithmic factors. This bound removes dependence on K under those conditions. The techniques also improve results in related bandit settings, while synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate better performance than benchmark algorithms.
summary.tldr: New contextual combinatorial bandit algorithms improve regret guarantees by accounting for triggering probabilities and, under suitable conditions, variance.

title: Contextual Combinatorial Bandits with Probabilistically Triggered Arms

abstract: We present a detailed study of $H$-consistency bounds for score-based ranking. These are upper bounds on the target loss estimation error of a predictor in a hypothesis set $H$, expressed in terms of the surrogate loss estimation error of that predictor. We will show that both in the general pairwise ranking scenario and in the bipartite ranking scenario, there are no meaningful $H$-consistency bounds for most hypothesis sets used in practice including the family of linear models and that of the neural networks, which satisfy the equicontinuous property with respect to the input. To come up with ranking surrogate losses with theoretical guarantees, we show that a natural solution consists of resorting to a pairwise abstention loss in the general pairwise ranking scenario, and similarly, a bipartite abstention loss in the bipartite ranking scenario, to abstain from making predictions at some limited cost $c$. For surrogate losses of these abstention loss functions, we give a series of $H$-consistency bounds for both the family of linear functions and that of neural networks with one hidden-layer. Our experimental results illustrate the effectiveness of ranking with abstention.

paragraphs: Ranking models are often trained with a convenient surrogate loss instead of the loss that directly measures incorrect ordering. This paper asks whether reducing surrogate error guarantees a reduction in ranking error within a particular model family. H-consistency bounds formalize that connection by bounding target-loss estimation error using surrogate-loss estimation error.

The authors find a substantial obstruction in both general pairwise ranking and bipartite ranking. For most practical hypothesis sets covered by their equicontinuity condition, including linear models and neural networks, meaningful bounds of this kind do not exist. The result concerns a specific theoretical guarantee and the model classes satisfying the stated property.

The proposed response is to allow abstention: a ranker may decline to make a prediction at a limited cost. For surrogate losses corresponding to these abstention objectives, the paper derives H-consistency bounds for linear functions and neural networks with one hidden layer. Experiments illustrate the effectiveness of ranking with abstention. Allowing a paid refusal therefore changes the ranking objective in a way that makes useful theoretical guarantees possible.
summary.tldr: Allowing ranking models to abstain at a cost enables H-consistency guarantees where common ranking objectives lack meaningful bounds for many practical model classes.

title: $H$-Consistency Bounds for Pairwise Misranking Loss Surrogates

abstract: Supervised learning is often affected by a covariate shift in which the marginal distributions of instances (covariates $x$) of training and testing samples $p_\text{tr}(x)$ and $p_\text{te}(x)$ are different but the label conditionals coincide. Existing approaches address such covariate shift by either using the ratio $p_\text{te}(x)/p_\text{tr}(x)$ to weight training samples (reweighted methods) or using the ratio $p_\text{tr}(x)/p_\text{te}(x)$ to weight testing samples (robust methods). However, the performance of such approaches can be poor under support mismatch or when the above ratios take large values. We propose a minimax risk classification (MRC) approach for covariate shift adaptation that avoids such limitations by weighting both training and testing samples. In addition, we develop effective techniques that obtain both sets of weights and generalize the conventional kernel mean matching method. We provide novel generalization bounds for our method that show a significant increase in the effective sample size compared with reweighted methods. The proposed method also achieves enhanced classification performance in both synthetic and empirical experiments.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions, while the relationship between inputs and labels remains the same. Standard correction methods weight either training examples or test examples using a ratio of those distributions. Such ratios can become very large, and mismatched distribution supports can make these approaches perform poorly.

This paper proposes weighting both sides through minimax risk classification. Instead of placing the whole adaptation burden on one set of weights, the method uses weights for both training and test samples. The authors develop procedures to obtain these weights that generalize kernel mean matching, connecting their approach to an established distribution-matching technique.

The theoretical contribution is a set of generalization bounds showing a substantially larger effective sample size than reweighting training examples alone. This concerns how much statistical information the weighted data provide, rather than an increase in the number of collected examples. Synthetic and empirical experiments also show improved classification performance, supporting the usefulness of double weighting within the covariate-shift setting.
summary.tldr: Weighting both training and test samples improves covariate-shift adaptation, with stronger effective-sample-size bounds and better reported classification results.

title: Double-Weighting for Covariate Shift Adaptation

abstract: Large language models have achieved impressive performance on various natural language processing tasks. However, so far they have been evaluated primarily on benchmarks where all information in the input context is relevant for solving the task. In this work, we investigate the distractibility of large language models, i.e., how the model prediction can be distracted by irrelevant context. In particular, we introduce Grade-School Math with Irrelevant Context (GSM-IC), an arithmetic reasoning dataset with irrelevant information in the problem description. We use this benchmark to measure the distractibility of different prompting techniques for large language models, and find that the model is easily distracted by irrelevant information. We also identify several approaches for mitigating this deficiency, such as decoding with self-consistency and adding to the prompt an instruction that tells the language model to ignore the irrelevant information.

paragraphs: A model may solve a reasoning problem when every supplied detail is useful yet struggle when the same kind of task includes unrelated information. This paper investigates that sensitivity to irrelevant context. It focuses on an evaluation gap: many existing benchmarks primarily present inputs whose information is relevant to the task.

The authors introduce Grade-School Math with Irrelevant Context, or GSM-IC, an arithmetic reasoning dataset that includes unnecessary information in problem descriptions. They use it to compare the distractibility of different prompting techniques. The evaluation asks whether a model can identify and use the information needed for a calculation while disregarding other details.

The results show that irrelevant information can readily distract the evaluated language models. The paper also identifies ways to reduce this problem, including self-consistency decoding and an explicit instruction to ignore irrelevant context. These are reported as mitigations. The broader significance is that reasoning performance depends partly on selecting relevant information, so success on clean problem descriptions does not fully capture the behavior tested by GSM-IC.
summary.tldr: GSM-IC shows that irrelevant context can disrupt language-model arithmetic reasoning, while certain prompting and decoding approaches mitigate the problem.

title: Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context

abstract: We show that deep belief networks with binary hidden units can approximate any multivariate probability density under very mild integrability requirements on the parental density of the visible nodes. The approximation is measured in the $L^q$-norm for $q\in[1,\infty]$ ($q=\infty$ corresponding to the supremum norm) and in Kullback-Leibler divergence. Furthermore, we establish sharp quantitative bounds on the approximation error in terms of the number of hidden units.
originalAbstract: We show that deep belief networks with binary hidden units can approximate any multivariate probability density under very mild integrability requirements on the parental density of the visible nodes. The approximation is measured in the $L^q$-norm for $q\in[1,\infty]$ ($q=\infty$ corresponding to the supremum norm) and in Kullback-Leibler divergence. Furthermore, we establish sharp quantitative bounds on the approximation error in terms of the number of hidden units.

paragraphs: This paper studies how well deep belief networks with binary hidden units can represent probability densities involving multiple variables. Its main result establishes universal approximation under mild integrability requirements on the parental density of the visible nodes. Subject to those requirements, the network family can approximate any multivariate probability density.

The authors assess approximation using several mathematical measures. These include Lq norms across the range from q equal to one through infinity, with the infinity case measuring the largest pointwise discrepancy. They also establish approximation in Kullback–Leibler divergence. Covering both kinds of measures gives more than one precise interpretation of how closely a network can match a density.

The paper goes beyond showing that approximation is possible by proving sharp bounds relating approximation error to the number of hidden units. This connects representational capacity to network size in a quantitative way. The result therefore addresses both the breadth of densities these networks can represent and how their approximation guarantees depend on the hidden-unit budget.
summary.tldr: Deep belief networks with binary hidden units have conditional universal density-approximation guarantees and sharp error bounds tied to hidden-unit count.

title: Quantitative Universal Approximation Bounds for Deep Belief Networks

abstract: Instruction-following agents must ground language into their observation and action spaces. Learning to ground language is challenging, typically requiring domain-specific engineering or large quantities of human interaction data. To address this challenge, we propose using pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise embodied agents. We combine ideas from model distillation and hindsight experience replay (HER), using a VLM to retroactively generate language describing the agent’s behavior. Simple prompting allows us to control the supervision signal, teaching an agent to interact with novel objects based on their names (e.g., planes) or their features (e.g., colors) in a 3D rendered environment. Fewshot prompting lets us teach abstract category membership, including pre-existing categories (food vs toys) and ad-hoc ones (arbitrary preferences over objects). Our work outlines a new and effective way to use internet-scale VLMs, repurposing the generic language grounding acquired by such models to teach task-relevant groundings to embodied agents.

paragraphs: An instruction-following agent must connect words to what it observes and what it can do. Establishing those connections often requires specialized engineering or substantial human interaction data. This paper investigates using a pretrained vision-language model as a source of supervision, transferring its existing language grounding into an embodied agent's task environment.

The method combines model distillation with hindsight experience replay. After an agent acts, the vision-language model generates language describing that behavior. These retrospective descriptions become supervision for learning connections between language and action. Prompting controls which aspects of the behavior the descriptions emphasize, allowing the same source model to teach different task-relevant meanings.

In a rendered 3D environment, the authors teach interactions with novel objects using object names or features such as color. With a few prompting examples, they also teach familiar abstract categories and newly specified categories based on arbitrary preferences. The findings show how broad visual-language knowledge can be repurposed into more specific embodied groundings through supervision generated from the agent's own behavior.
summary.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model teaches embodied agents language grounding by retrospectively describing their behavior.

title: Distilling Internet-Scale Vision-Language Models into Embodied Agents

abstract: Offline goal-conditioned RL (GCRL) offers a way to train general-purpose agents from fully offline datasets. In addition to being conservative within the dataset, the generalization ability to achieve unseen goals is another fundamental challenge for offline GCRL. However, to the best of our knowledge, this problem has not been well studied yet. In this paper, we study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of offline GCRL both theoretically and empirically to identify factors that are important. In a number of experiments, we observe that weighted imitation learning enjoys better generalization than pessimism-based offline RL method. Based on this insight, we derive a theory for OOD generalization, which characterizes several important design choices. We then propose a new offline GCRL method, Generalizable Offline goAl-condiTioned RL (GOAT), by combining the findings from our theoretical and empirical studies. On a new benchmark containing 9 independent identically distributed (IID) tasks and 17 OOD tasks, GOAT outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to pursue different goals using a fixed dataset. Remaining conservative around recorded experience is one challenge; achieving goals outside the training distribution is another. This paper investigates that second challenge through both experiments and theory, asking which design choices support generalization to unseen goals.

Across a number of experiments, weighted imitation learning generalizes better than a pessimism-based offline reinforcement-learning method. The authors use this observation to develop a theory of out-of-distribution generalization that characterizes several important design choices. They then combine the theoretical and empirical findings into GOAT, a new offline goal-conditioned learning method.

Evaluation uses a new benchmark with nine tasks drawn from the training distribution and 17 out-of-distribution tasks. GOAT outperforms current leading methods by a large margin on that benchmark. The results support the paper’s combined design approach and show why unseen-goal performance deserves explicit attention when developing agents from offline data, beyond the concern of staying close to recorded behavior.
summary.tldr: GOAT combines theoretical and empirical insights about offline goal generalization to improve performance on unseen-goal benchmarks.

title: What is Essential for Unseen Goal Generalization of Offline Goal-conditioned RL?

abstract: Diffusion models show promising generation capability for a variety of data. Despite their high generation quality, the inference for diffusion models is still time-consuming due to the numerous sampling iterations required. To accelerate the inference, we propose ReDi, a simple yet learning-free Retrieval-based Diffusion sampling framework. From a precomputed knowledge base, ReDi retrieves a trajectory similar to the partially generated trajectory at an early stage of generation, skips a large portion of intermediate steps, and continues sampling from a later step in the retrieved trajectory. We theoretically prove that the generation performance of ReDi is guaranteed. Our experiments demonstrate that ReDi improves the model inference efficiency by 2$\times$ speedup. Furthermore, ReDi is able to generalize well in zero-shot cross-domain image generation such as image stylization. The code and demo for ReDi is available at https://github.com/zkx06111/ReDiffusion.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality data, but their many sampling iterations make inference slow. ReDi accelerates generation by reusing information from previously computed sampling trajectories. Its retrieval-based approach does not require learning an additional acceleration mechanism, although it does rely on a precomputed knowledge base.

Early in generation, ReDi compares the partially generated trajectory with trajectories in that knowledge base. It retrieves a similar one, skips a substantial stretch of intermediate sampling steps, and resumes from a later point along the retrieved trajectory. The key idea is to use a relevant stored continuation to avoid computing every intermediate step anew.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for generation performance and report a twofold inference speedup in experiments. They also find that ReDi generalizes well to zero-shot image generation across domains, including image stylization. These findings support trajectory retrieval as a practical route to faster diffusion sampling, with the reported efficiency gain coming from bypassing steps rather than executing the full sampling process.
summary.tldr: ReDi retrieves stored diffusion trajectories to skip intermediate sampling steps, delivering a reported twofold inference speedup without additional learning.

title: ReDi: Efficient Learning-Free Diffusion Inference via Trajectory Retrieval

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) remains difficult to scale to many agents. Recent MARL using Mean Field Control (MFC) provides a tractable and rigorous approach to otherwise difficult cooperative MARL. However, the strict MFC assumption of many independent, weakly-interacting agents is too inflexible in practice. We generalize MFC to instead simultaneously model many similar and few complex agents – as Major-Minor Mean Field Control (M3FC). Theoretically, we give approximation results for finite agent control, and verify the sufficiency of stationary policies for optimality together with a dynamic programming principle. Algorithmically, we propose Major-Minor Mean Field MARL (M3FMARL) for finite agent systems instead of the limiting system. The algorithm is shown to approximate the policy gradient of the underlying M3FC MDP. Finally, we demonstrate its capabilities experimentally in various scenarios. We observe a strong performance in comparison to state-of-the-art policy gradient MARL methods.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows. Mean field control offers a tractable approach, but its assumption of many independent, weakly interacting agents is restrictive. This paper extends the framework to systems containing many similar agents alongside a small number of more complex agents.

The resulting Major-Minor Mean Field Control framework, M3FC, comes with approximation results for finite-agent control. The authors also establish that stationary policies are sufficient for optimality and provide a dynamic programming principle. These results supply a theoretical basis for decision making in the expanded model, including a connection between the mean field formulation and finite systems.

For learning, the paper introduces M3FMARL, an algorithm operating on finite-agent systems instead of directly on the limiting system. It is shown to approximate the policy gradient of the underlying M3FC decision process. Experiments across several scenarios show strong performance compared with state-of-the-art policy-gradient multi-agent methods, supporting the framework’s practical relevance for mixed populations of agents.
summary.tldr: Major-Minor Mean Field Control extends scalable cooperative learning to populations with many similar agents and a few complex ones.

title: Major-Minor Mean Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Bayesian Neural Networks(BNNs) with high-dimensional parameters pose a challenge for posterior inference due to the multi-modality of the posterior distributions. Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo(SGMCMC) with cyclical learning rate scheduling is a promising solution, but it requires a large number of sampling steps to explore high-dimensional multi-modal posteriors, making it computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose a meta-learning strategy to build SGMCMC which can efficiently explore the multi-modal target distributions. Our algorithm allows the learned SGMCMC to quickly explore the high-density region of the posterior landscape. Also, we show that this exploration property is transferrable to various tasks, even for the ones unseen during a meta-training stage. Using popular image classification benchmarks and a variety of downstream tasks, we demonstrate that our method significantly improves the sampling efficiency, achieving better performance than vanilla SGMCMC without incurring significant computational overhead.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks require inference over distributions of model parameters. Those distributions can have many high-density regions in a high-dimensional space, making them difficult to explore. Stochastic gradient MCMC with cyclical learning rates is promising, but reaching different regions can require many sampling steps.

This paper proposes meta-learning an SGMCMC strategy that explores multimodal target distributions more efficiently. The learned procedure is designed to move quickly through high-density regions of the posterior landscape. Learning how to explore addresses the cost of obtaining useful samples, rather than relying only on a prescribed learning-rate schedule.

The authors show that the learned exploration behavior transfers across tasks, including tasks absent from meta-training. Experiments on image classification benchmarks and other downstream tasks report substantially improved sampling efficiency and better performance than vanilla SGMCMC, without significant computational overhead. These findings suggest that exploration behavior learned during meta-training can remain useful beyond its original tasks and reduce the sampling burden of Bayesian neural-network inference in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned SGMCMC strategy explores multimodal posteriors more efficiently and transfers that exploration behavior to unseen tasks.

title: Learning to Explore for Stochastic Gradient MCMC

abstract: Autoregressive language models are the currently dominant paradigm for text generation, however they have some fundamental limitations that cannot be remedied by scale—for example inherently sequential and unidirectional generation. While alternate classes of models have been explored, we have limited mathematical understanding of their fundamental power and limitations. In this paper we focus on Generative Masked Language Models (GMLMs), a non-autoregressive paradigm in which we train a model to fit conditional probabilities of the data distribution via masking, which are subsequently used as inputs to a Markov Chain to draw samples from the model. These models empirically strike a promising speed-quality trade-off as each step can be typically parallelized by decoding the entire sequence in parallel. We develop a mathematical framework for analyzing and improving such models which sheds light on questions of sample complexity and inference speed and quality. Empirically, we adapt the T5 model for iteratively-refined parallel decoding, achieving 2-3x speedup in machine translation with minimal sacrifice in quality compared with autoregressive models. We run careful ablation experiments to give recommendations on key design choices, and make fine-grained observations on the common error modes in connection with our theory. Our mathematical analyses and empirical observations characterize both potentials and limitations of this approach, and can be applied to future works on improving understanding and performance of GMLMs. We released codes for our experiments.

paragraphs: Autoregressive text generation proceeds sequentially in one direction. This paper examines generative masked language models as an alternative that can typically update an entire sequence in parallel at each decoding step. These models learn conditional probabilities through masking, then use those probabilities within a Markov chain to generate samples.

The authors develop a mathematical framework addressing how much data the models require and how inference choices affect speed and quality. The framework supports analysis and improvement of the approach, while the experiments examine concrete design decisions and common errors. Connecting those observations to theory helps characterize both the benefits and the difficulties of iterative parallel generation.

For a practical demonstration, the authors adapt T5 to perform parallel decoding with iterative refinement. In machine translation, they report a two- to three-fold speedup with a small quality sacrifice relative to autoregressive models. Ablation experiments inform design recommendations. The result supports a promising speed-quality trade-off in the evaluated setting, alongside a framework for understanding where this generation strategy succeeds or struggles.
summary.tldr: A theoretical and empirical study of masked text generation reports two- to three-fold faster translation through iterative parallel decoding with minimal quality loss.

title: Promises and Pitfalls of Generative Masked Language Modeling: Theoretical Framework and Practical Guidelines

abstract: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) of latent variable models is often recast as the minimization of a free energy functional over an extended space of parameters and probability distributions. This perspective was recently combined with insights from optimal transport to obtain novel particle-based algorithms for fitting latent variable models to data. Drawing inspiration from prior works which interpret ‘momentum-enriched’ optimization algorithms as discretizations of ordinary differential equations, we propose an analogous dynamical-systems-inspired approach to minimizing the free energy functional. The result is a dynamical system that blends elements of Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient method, the underdamped Langevin diffusion, and particle methods. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the continuous-time system minimizes the functional. By discretizing the system, we obtain a practical algorithm for MLE in latent variable models. The algorithm outperforms existing particle methods in numerical experiments and compares favourably with other MLE algorithms.

paragraphs: Maximum likelihood fitting for latent-variable models can be reformulated as minimizing a free-energy functional over model parameters and probability distributions. Earlier work used this viewpoint together with optimal transport to construct particle-based fitting algorithms. This paper develops that line of work by introducing momentum through a dynamical-systems formulation.

The proposed continuous-time system combines elements of Nesterov acceleration, underdamped Langevin diffusion, and particle methods. The guiding idea comes from interpreting momentum-based optimization algorithms as discrete versions of differential equations. Here, that connection is extended to the larger optimization space involved in free-energy minimization for latent-variable models.

Under suitable assumptions, the authors prove that the continuous-time system minimizes the functional. They then discretize it to obtain a practical maximum likelihood algorithm. Numerical experiments show that this algorithm outperforms existing particle methods and compares favorably with other maximum likelihood approaches. The theory establishes the continuous-time result under its assumptions, while the experiments demonstrate the practical value of the resulting discrete algorithm in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: A momentum-based dynamical system yields a practical particle algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation with favorable numerical results.

title: Momentum Particle Maximum Likelihood

abstract: Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces, which is practical for learning solution operators of PDEs and other scientific modeling applications. Among them, the Fourier neural operator (FNO) is a popular architecture that performs global convolutions in the Fourier space. However, such global operations are often prone to over-smoothing and may fail to capture local details. In contrast, convolutional neural networks (CNN) can capture local features but are limited to training and inference at a single resolution. In this work, we present a principled approach to operator learning that can capture local features under two frameworks by learning differential operators and integral operators with locally supported kernels. Specifically, inspired by stencil methods, we prove that we obtain differential operators under an appropriate scaling of the kernel values of CNNs. To obtain local integral operators, we utilize suitable basis representations for the kernels based on discrete-continuous convolutions. Both these approaches preserve the properties of operator learning and, hence, the ability to predict at any resolution. Adding our layers to FNOs significantly improves their performance, reducing the relative L2-error by 34-72% in our experiments, which include a turbulent 2D Navier-Stokes and the spherical shallow water equations.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, making them useful for scientific problems such as predicting solutions of partial differential equations. Fourier neural operators use global operations that can oversmooth local details. This paper develops local operator layers that preserve the ability to make predictions at different resolutions while capturing finer spatial information.

The authors pursue two constructions. One learns differential operators, proving that appropriately scaling CNN kernel values yields such operators, inspired by stencil methods. The other learns integral operators with locally supported kernels using suitable basis representations. Both constructions retain the properties of operator learning, bringing local processing into a framework that supports prediction at any resolution.

The results support combining global and local operations for these scientific modeling tasks. The theoretical constructions explain how local layers can fit the operator setting, while the experiments show their practical contribution to accuracy.
summary.tldr: Local differential and integral operator layers improve Fourier neural operators while preserving prediction across resolutions.

title: Neural Operators with Localized Integral and Differential Kernels

abstract: Permutation symmetries of deep networks make basic operations like model merging and similarity estimation challenging. In many cases, aligning the weights of the networks, i.e., finding optimal permutations between their weights, is necessary. Unfortunately, weight alignment is an NP-hard problem. Prior research has mainly focused on solving relaxed versions of the alignment problem, leading to either time-consuming methods or sub-optimal solutions. To accelerate the alignment process and improve its quality, we propose a novel framework aimed at learning to solve the weight alignment problem, which we name Deep-Align. To that end, we first prove that weight alignment adheres to two fundamental symmetries and then, propose a deep architecture that respects these symmetries. Notably, our framework does not require any labeled data. We provide a theoretical analysis of our approach and evaluate Deep-Align on several types of network architectures and learning setups. Our experimental results indicate that a feed-forward pass with Deep-Align produces better or equivalent alignments compared to those produced by current optimization algorithms. Additionally, our alignments can be used as an effective initialization for other methods, leading to improved solutions with a significant speedup in convergence.

paragraphs: Deep networks can represent equivalent computations with differently ordered internal units. These permutation symmetries complicate operations such as comparing models or merging their weights, because corresponding parts may occupy different positions. Finding the optimal alignment is NP-hard, and earlier relaxed approaches can be slow or produce suboptimal matches.

Deep-Align learns to perform weight alignment. The authors first prove that the alignment problem follows two fundamental symmetries, then design a neural architecture that respects them. The framework requires no labeled data. Its structure therefore incorporates mathematical properties of the task while learning how to produce useful permutations.

Across several network architectures and learning settings, a single feed-forward pass produces alignments that are better than or equivalent to those from the evaluated optimization algorithms. The resulting alignments also serve as effective starting points for other methods, improving solutions and substantially accelerating convergence. These empirical findings support Deep-Align as both a direct alignment method and an initialization strategy, without implying that it solves every instance optimally.
summary.tldr: Deep-Align learns symmetry-respecting weight alignments without labeled data and produces strong alignments in a single feed-forward pass.

title: Equivariant Deep Weight Space Alignment

abstract: We propose Embodied AI (E-AI) as the next fundamental step in the pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), juxtaposing it against current AI advancements, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs). We traverse the evolution of the embodiment concept across diverse fields (philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, and robotics) to highlight how E-AI distinguishes itself from the classical paradigm of static learning. By broadening the scope of E-AI, we introduce a theoretical framework based on cognitive architectures, emphasizing perception, action, memory, and learning as essential components of an embodied agent. This framework is aligned with Friston’s active inference principle, offering a comprehensive approach to E-AI development. Despite the progress made in the field of AI, substantial challenges, such as the formulation of a novel AI learning theory and the innovation of advanced hardware, persist. Our discussion lays down a foundational guideline for future E-AI research. Highlighting the importance of creating E-AI agents capable of seamless communication, collaboration, and coexistence with humans and other intelligent entities within real-world environments, we aim to steer the AI community towards addressing the multifaceted challenges and seizing the opportunities that lie ahead in the quest for AGI.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that embodied AI should be a fundamental next step toward artificial general intelligence. It places agents' engagement with real environments at the center of that proposal. To develop the argument, the authors trace ideas about embodiment across philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, and robotics, contrasting this perspective with static learning.

The proposed theoretical framework draws on cognitive architectures and treats perception, action, memory, and learning as essential parts of an embodied agent. It aligns these components with the active inference principle. The framework is intended to guide development by considering these capabilities together, rather than treating intelligence only as performance on a fixed learning task.

The paper identifies substantial work ahead, including new learning theory and advances in hardware. It also emphasizes agents that can communicate, collaborate, and coexist with humans and other intelligent entities in real-world environments. Its contribution is a research agenda and conceptual foundation: the authors advocate embodiment as a direction toward AGI, rather than report an experimental demonstration that embodiment achieves it.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates embodied AI and proposes a framework connecting perception, action, memory, and learning to guide future research.

title: Position: A Call for Embodied AI

abstract: Motivated by the growing theoretical understanding of neural networks that employ the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) as their activation function, we revisit the use of ReLU activation functions for learning implicit neural representations (INRs). Inspired by second order B-spline wavelets, we incorporate a set of simple constraints to the ReLU neurons in each layer of a deep neural network (DNN) to remedy the spectral bias. This in turn enables its use for various INR tasks. Empirically, we demonstrate that, contrary to popular belief, one can learn state-of-the-art INRs based on a DNN composed of only ReLU neurons. Next, by leveraging recent theoretical works which characterize the kinds of functions ReLU neural networks learn, we provide a way to quantify the regularity of the learned function. This offers a principled approach to selecting the hyperparameters in INR architectures. We substantiate our claims through experiments in signal representation, super resolution, and computed tomography, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of our method. The code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/joeshenouda/relu-inrs.
