paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode signals through a neural network's learned function. This paper revisits whether networks using only ReLU activations can perform these tasks effectively. The obstacle it addresses is spectral bias, which makes learning different frequency components uneven and can hinder detailed signal representation.

Inspired by second-order B-spline wavelets, the authors impose simple constraints on ReLU neurons in every layer. These constraints remedy the spectral bias and make the resulting networks useful for implicit representation tasks. Experiments show that this construction can achieve state-of-the-art representations using only ReLU neurons, establishing their sufficiency within the proposed approach.

The paper also uses existing theory about the functions learned by ReLU networks to quantify the regularity of the learned function. This gives a principled basis for choosing architecture hyperparameters. Experiments in signal representation, super resolution, and computed tomography support the method's effectiveness across different tasks. The overall contribution combines a practical architectural modification with a theoretical tool for understanding and selecting the resulting representation.
summary.tldr: Wavelet-inspired constraints enable ReLU-only networks to learn state-of-the-art implicit representations and support principled analysis of function regularity.

title: ReLUs Are Sufficient for Learning Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Exploiting invariant relations and mitigating spurious correlation (a.k.a., shortcut) between representation and target across varied data distributions can tackle the challenging out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization problem. In personalized federated learning (PFL), heterogeneous data distribution across local clients offers the inherent prerequisites to extract the invariant features that maintain invariant relation with target. Nevertheless, personalized features are closely entangled with spurious features in PFL since they exhibit similar variability across different clients, which makes preserving personalization knowledge and eliminating shortcuts two conflicting objectives in PFL. To address the above challenge, we analyse the heterogeneous data generation on local clients through the lens of structured causal model and propose a crucial causal signature which can distinguish personalized features from spurious features with global invariant features as the anchor. Then the causal signature is quantified as an information-theoretic constraint that facilitates the shortcut-averse personalized invariant learning on each client. Theoretical analysis demonstrates our method, FedPIN, can yield a tighter bound on generalization error than the prevalent PFL approaches when train-test distribution shift exists on clients. Moreover, we provide a theoretical guarantee on the convergence rate of FedPIN in this paper. The results of extensive experiments show that our method can achieve superior OOD generalization performance compared with the state-of-the-art competitors.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must accommodate differences between clients while avoiding misleading correlations that fail when data distributions change. This creates a difficult distinction: useful personalized features and unreliable shortcuts can both vary across clients. Removing everything that varies could therefore discard the very information needed for personalization.

The authors analyze client data generation through a structured causal model. They propose a causal signature that uses globally invariant features as an anchor to distinguish personalized information from spurious information. They then express this signature as an information-theoretic constraint, which guides each client toward personalized representations that avoid shortcuts. The resulting method is called FedPIN.

The theoretical analysis shows that FedPIN can obtain a tighter generalization-error bound than prevalent personalized federated approaches when clients experience a training-to-test distribution shift. The paper also provides a convergence-rate guarantee. Experiments report stronger out-of-distribution generalization than state-of-the-art competitors, supporting the value of separating useful client-specific information from correlations that merely happen to hold during training.
summary.tldr: FedPIN uses a causal, information-theoretic constraint to preserve client personalization while reducing shortcuts that undermine generalization under distribution shifts.

title: Causally Motivated Personalized Federated Invariant Learning with Shortcut-Averse Information-Theoretic Regularization

abstract: We investigate the potential of patent data for improving the antibody humanness prediction using a multi-stage, multi-loss training process. Humanness serves as a proxy for the immunogenic response to antibody therapeutics, one of the major causes of attrition in drug discovery and a challenging obstacle for their use in clinical settings. We pose the initial learning stage as a weakly-supervised contrastive-learning problem, where each antibody sequence is associated with possibly multiple identifiers of function and the objective is to learn an encoder that groups them according to their patented properties. We then freeze a part of the contrastive encoder and continue training it on the patent data using the cross-entropy loss to predict the humanness score of a given antibody sequence. We illustrate the utility of the patent data and our approach by performing inference on three different immunogenicity datasets, unseen during training. Our empirical results demonstrate that the learned model consistently outperforms the alternative baselines and establishes new state-of-the-art on five out of six inference tasks, irrespective of the used metric.

paragraphs: Antibody humanness is used as a proxy for the immune response that an antibody therapeutic might provoke. Such responses are a major obstacle in drug development and clinical use. This paper investigates whether information contained in patents can improve humanness prediction through a training process that combines multiple stages and objectives.

The first stage uses weakly supervised contrastive learning. Each antibody sequence can carry several identifiers describing its function, and the encoder learns to group sequences according to their patented properties. The authors then freeze part of this encoder and continue training on patent data with a cross-entropy objective to predict humanness scores. This connects representations of patented properties to the final prediction task.

Evaluation uses three immunogenicity datasets that were unseen during training. The learned model consistently outperforms the alternative baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on five of six inference tasks across the metrics used. These results support the value of patent data for the prediction problem, while humanness remains a proxy for immunogenic response.
summary.tldr: Multistage learning from antibody patents improves humanness prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results on five of six evaluated inference tasks.

title: Improving Antibody Humanness Prediction using Patent Data

abstract: Active domain adaptation has shown promising results in enhancing unsupervised domain adaptation (DA), by actively selecting and annotating a small amount of unlabeled samples from the target domain. Despite its effectiveness in boosting overall performance, the gain usually concentrates on the categories that are readily improvable, while challenging categories that demand the utmost attention are often overlooked by existing models. To alleviate this discrepancy, we propose a novel category-aware active DA method that aims to boost the adaptation for the individual category without adversely affecting others. Specifically, our approach identifies the unlabeled data that are most important for the recognition of the targeted category. Our method assesses the impact of each unlabeled sample on the recognition loss of the target data via the influence function, which allows us to directly evaluate the sample importance, without relying on indirect measurements used by existing methods. Comprehensive experiments and in-depth explorations demonstrate the efficacy of our method on category-aware active DA over three datasets.

paragraphs: Active domain adaptation improves a model in a new domain by choosing a small number of examples for annotation. An overall improvement can conceal uneven progress: categories that are easy to improve may receive most of the benefit, while difficult categories remain poorly recognized. This paper makes the category needing improvement an explicit part of the selection problem.

The method identifies unlabeled examples that matter most for recognizing a targeted category. It uses an influence function to assess how each example affects recognition loss on target-domain data. This gives the selection procedure a direct connection to the prediction objective, rather than relying on an indirect measure of which examples might be useful.

Experiments across three datasets support the method's effectiveness for category-aware adaptation. The intended benefit is more deliberate allocation of a limited annotation effort, with the aim of improving an individual category without harming others. The reported evidence supports that approach; the abstract does not present the no-harm objective as a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: The method uses influence estimates to choose target-domain examples for annotation that support recognition of a particular category.

title: Category-Aware Active Domain Adaptation

abstract: Learning new knowledge frequently occurs in our dynamically changing world, e.g., humans culturally evolve by continuously acquiring new abilities to sustain their survival, leveraging collective intelligence rather than a large number of individual attempts. The effective learning paradigm during cultural evolution is termed socialized learning (SL). Consequently, a straightforward question arises: Can multi-agent systems acquire more new abilities like humans? In contrast to most existing methods that address continual learning and multi-agent collaboration, our emphasis lies in a more challenging problem: we prioritize the knowledge in the original expert classes, and as we adeptly learn new ones, the accuracy in the original expert classes stays superior among all in a directional manner. Inspired by population genetics and cognitive science, leading to unique and complete development, we propose Multi-Agent Socialized Collaboration (MASC), which achieves SL through interactions among multiple agents. Specifically, we introduce collective collaboration and reciprocal altruism modules, organizing collaborative behaviors, promoting information sharing, and facilitating learning and knowledge interaction among individuals. We demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-agent collaboration in an extensive empirical study. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.com/yxjdarren/SL.

paragraphs: This paper studies how multiple learning agents can acquire new abilities through interaction while preserving their existing expertise. Its motivating analogy is socialized learning in human cultural evolution, where collective intelligence supports learning. The target goes beyond simply adding new classes: performance on original expert classes is explicitly prioritized.

The proposed Multi-Agent Socialized Collaboration framework, MASC, draws inspiration from population genetics and cognitive science. It includes collective collaboration and reciprocal altruism modules that organize collaboration, share information, and support knowledge exchange among agents. These mechanisms aim to let agents learn new classes while maintaining the stated directional advantage on their original areas of expertise.

An extensive empirical study demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-agent collaboration for this objective. The central contribution is a learning setup and framework that treat continued specialization and acquisition of new abilities as linked goals. Information exchange is therefore organized around making agents better learners while preserving the importance of the expert knowledge they already hold.
summary.tldr: MASC organizes multi-agent knowledge sharing to learn new classes while prioritizing agents' original expertise.

title: Socialized Learning: Making Each Other Better Through Multi-Agent Collaboration

abstract: The growing Machine Learning (ML) services require extensive collections of user data, which may inadvertently include people’s private information irrelevant to the services. Various studies have been proposed to protect private attributes by removing them from the data while maintaining the utilities of the data for downstream tasks. Nevertheless, as we theoretically and empirically show in the paper, these methods reveal severe vulnerability because of a common weakness rooted in their adversarial training based strategies. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach, PASS, designed to stochastically substitute the original sample with another one according to certain probabilities, which is trained with a novel loss function soundly derived from information-theoretic objective defined for utility-preserving private attributes protection. The comprehensive evaluation of PASS on various datasets of different modalities, including facial images, human activity sensory signals, and voice recording datasets, substantiates PASS’s effectiveness and generalizability.

paragraphs: Data collected for a machine-learning service can contain private attributes unrelated to the service's intended task. Protecting those attributes requires preserving useful information while limiting what the data reveal about private characteristics. This paper theoretically and empirically identifies a shared vulnerability in protection methods based on adversarial training.

PASS addresses that vulnerability by learning to replace an original sample with another sample according to a probability distribution. Protection therefore operates through stochastic substitution. The replacement probabilities are trained using a new loss derived from an information-theoretic objective that explicitly combines private-attribute protection with preservation of downstream utility.

The authors evaluate PASS on facial images, human-activity sensor signals, and voice recordings. Results across these different modalities support its effectiveness and generalizability. The variety of data matters because the proposed mechanism is intended to protect attributes without being tied to a single input format. The central contribution is an alternative to adversarial removal strategies, with a principled training objective for choosing substitutions that retain task-relevant information while protecting private attributes.
summary.tldr: PASS learns probabilistic sample substitutions to protect private attributes while preserving downstream utility across several data modalities.

title: PASS: Private Attributes Protection with Stochastic Data Substitution

abstract: The multi-agent linear bandit setting is a well-known setting for which designing efficient collaboration between agents remains challenging. This paper studies the impact of data sharing among agents on regret minimization. Unlike most existing approaches, our contribution does not rely on any assumptions on the bandit parameters structure. Our main result formalizes the trade-off between the bias and uncertainty of the bandit parameter estimation for efficient collaboration. This result is the cornerstone of the Bandit Adaptive Sample Sharing (BASS) algorithm, whose efficiency over the current state-of-the-art is validated through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, when agents’ parameters display a cluster structure, our algorithm accurately recovers them.

paragraphs: In a multi-agent linear bandit problem, several agents learn which actions produce good outcomes. Sharing observations can make learning more efficient, but another agent’s data may reflect different underlying parameters. Collaboration must therefore account for whether additional evidence improves an estimate or pulls it toward an inappropriate value.

The paper formalizes this tension as a trade-off between estimation bias and uncertainty. That result provides the foundation for Bandit Adaptive Sample Sharing, or BASS. Unlike most existing approaches discussed in the abstract, the method does not require assumptions about structural relationships among agents’ bandit parameters. Its collaboration strategy is grounded in the estimation trade-off instead.

Theoretical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support BASS’s efficiency relative to current state-of-the-art methods. The authors also show that when agents’ parameters have a cluster structure, the algorithm accurately recovers those clusters. This conditional finding is useful: the method can exploit such organization when present without requiring it as a starting assumption.
summary.tldr: BASS adapts data sharing between bandit agents by balancing estimation bias and uncertainty without assuming a parameter structure.

title: Adaptive Sample Sharing for Multi Agent Linear Bandits

abstract: Bilevel optimization is characterized by a two-level optimization structure, where the upper-level problem is constrained by optimal lower-level solutions, and such structures are prevalent in real-world problems. The constraint by optimal lower-level solutions poses significant challenges, especially in noisy, constrained, and derivative-free settings, as repeating lower-level optimizations is sample inefficient and predicted lower-level solutions may be suboptimal. We present BILevel Bayesian Optimization (BILBO), a novel Bayesian optimization algorithm for general bilevel problems with blackbox functions, which optimizes both upper- and lower-level problems simultaneously, without the repeated lower-level optimization required by existing methods. BILBO samples from confidence-bounds based trusted sets, which bounds the suboptimality on the lower level. Moreover, BILBO selects only one function query per iteration, where the function query selection strategy incorporates the uncertainty of estimated lower-level solutions and includes a conditional reassignment of the query to encourage exploration of the lower-level objective. The performance of BILBO is theoretically guaranteed with a sublinear regret bound for commonly used kernels and is empirically evaluated on several synthetic and real-world problems.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems: an upper-level choice must respect an optimal solution to a lower-level problem. This becomes especially expensive when functions are noisy, constrained, or accessible only through evaluations. Repeatedly solving the lower problem consumes samples, while relying on an estimated solution risks using one that is suboptimal.

BILBO tackles both levels simultaneously through Bayesian optimization. It samples within trusted sets constructed from confidence bounds, which bound lower-level suboptimality. Each iteration makes only one function query. The query-selection strategy accounts for uncertainty in estimated lower-level solutions and can conditionally redirect the query to encourage exploration of the lower-level objective.

This design makes deciding what to evaluate part of the coupled optimization procedure, reducing dependence on repeated lower-level searches. The authors prove a sublinear regret bound for commonly used kernels and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world problems. The theoretical result supplies a qualified performance guarantee, while the experiments examine the algorithm’s behavior on concrete bilevel tasks.
summary.tldr: BILBO jointly optimizes both levels of a black-box bilevel problem using confidence-based trusted sets and one function query per iteration.

title: BILBO: BILevel Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Detecting anomalies with limited supervision is challenging due to the scarcity of labeled anomalies, which often fail to capture the diversity of abnormal behaviors. We propose Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection via Dual-Tailed Kernel (WSAD-DT), a novel framework that learns robust latent representations to distinctly separate anomalies from normal samples under weak supervision. WSAD-DT introduces two centroids—one for normal samples and one for anomalies—and leverages a dual-tailed kernel scheme: a light-tailed kernel to compactly model in-class points and a heavy-tailed kernel to main- tain a wider margin against out-of-class instances. To preserve intra-class diversity, WSAD-DT in- corporates kernel-based regularization, encouraging richer representations within each class. Furthermore, we devise an ensemble strategy that partition unlabeled data into diverse subsets, while sharing the limited labeled anomalies among these partitions to maximize their impact. Empirically, WSAD-DT achieves state-of-the-art performance on several challenging anomaly detection benchmarks, outperforming leading ensemble-based methods such as XGBOD.

paragraphs: A small collection of labeled anomalies rarely represents the full range of abnormal behavior. Weakly supervised anomaly detection must therefore use those scarce labels without collapsing all unusual cases into an overly narrow representation. WSAD-DT builds a latent geometry intended to separate normal and anomalous examples while preserving variation within each group.

The method uses separate normal and anomaly centroids. A light-tailed kernel compacts in-class points, while a heavy-tailed kernel maintains separation from out-of-class instances. Kernel-based regularization preserves within-class diversity. An ensemble partitions unlabeled data into varied subsets while sharing the limited labeled anomalies across those partitions.

Experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmarks and outperform leading ensemble methods such as XGBOD. The contribution combines representation geometry and data reuse under sparse supervision. The abstract does not claim detection of every unseen anomaly type, so the benchmark gains should be interpreted within the abnormal behaviors and data conditions evaluated.
summary.tldr: Dual-tailed kernels and an ensemble strategy improve anomaly separation while reusing scarce labeled anomalies and preserving class diversity.

title: Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection via Dual-Tailed Kernel

abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs on tabular classification tasks can lead to the phenomenon of fine-tuning multiplicity where equally well-performing models make conflicting predictions on the same input. Fine-tuning multiplicity can arise due to variations in the training process, e.g., seed, weight initialization, minor changes to training data, etc., raising concerns about the reliability of Tabular LLMs in high-stakes applications such as finance, hiring, education, healthcare. Our work formalizes this unique challenge of fine-tuning multiplicity in Tabular LLMs and proposes a novel measure to quantify the consistency of individual predictions without expensive model retraining. Our measure quantifies a prediction’s consistency by analyzing (sampling) the model’s local behavior around that input in the embedding space. Interestingly, we show that sampling in the local neighborhood can be leveraged to provide probabilistic guarantees on prediction consistency under a broad class of fine-tuned models, i.e., inputs with sufficiently high local stability (as defined by our measure) also remain consistent across several fine-tuned models with high probability. We perform experiments on multiple real-world datasets to show that our local stability measure preemptively captures consistency under actual multiplicity across several fine-tuned models, outperforming competing measures.

paragraphs: Two language models fine-tuned for tabular classification can achieve similar overall performance while disagreeing on the same individual case. Training seeds, initialization, or small data changes can produce this fine-tuning multiplicity. The paper formalizes the problem and asks how to assess the consistency of a prediction without repeatedly training alternative models.

The proposed measure samples the model's behavior near an input in embedding space. It quantifies how stable the prediction is under these local variations. The central idea is to use this accessible local behavior to anticipate agreement across fine-tuned models, reducing the need for expensive retraining solely to assess consistency.

The authors establish probabilistic guarantees for a broad class of fine-tuned models: inputs with sufficiently high local stability remain consistent across several such models with high probability. This is a conditional guarantee, not certainty for every prediction. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that the measure anticipates actual cross-model consistency better than competing measures, supporting its use as an indicator of prediction reliability under training variation.
summary.tldr: Local embedding-space stability estimates prediction consistency across fine-tuned tabular LLMs, with conditional probabilistic guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: Quantifying Prediction Consistency Under Fine-tuning Multiplicity in Tabular LLMs

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is crucial for safe deployment, yet existing methods assume specific preference models like Bradley-Terry model. This assumption leads to statistical inconsistency, where more data doesn’t guarantee convergence to true human preferences. To address this critical gap, we introduce a novel alignment method Direct Density Ratio Optimization (DDRO). DDRO directly estimates the density ratio between preferred and unpreferred output distributions, circumventing the need for explicit human preference modeling. We theoretically prove that DDRO is statistically consistent, ensuring convergence to the true preferred distribution as the data size grows, regardless of the underlying preference structure. Experiments demonstrate that DDRO achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness and potential for significant improvement. DDRO unlocks the potential for truly data-driven alignment, paving the way for more reliable and human-aligned LLMs.

paragraphs: Preference alignment methods often assume a particular mathematical model of how people choose between outputs. This paper argues that assumptions such as the Bradley–Terry model can create statistical inconsistency: collecting more preference data need not make the learned result converge to the true preferences. The issue concerns the method's eventual target, not just its performance with limited data.

Direct Density Ratio Optimization, or DDRO, instead estimates the ratio between distributions of preferred and unpreferred outputs. This makes the distinction between those distributions the direct learning target. It avoids specifying an explicit model of the human preference process as an intermediate step.

The authors prove statistical consistency, with convergence to the true preferred distribution as the amount of data grows, regardless of the underlying preference structure. They also report better experimental performance than existing approaches. The theoretical result gives an asymptotic justification for the method, while the experiments support its practical promise. Together, these contributions address both the statistical formulation of alignment and its observed effectiveness.
summary.tldr: DDRO directly estimates preferred-to-unpreferred output density ratios and is proved statistically consistent without an explicit human preference model.

title: Direct Density Ratio Optimization: A Statistically Consistent Approach to Aligning Large Language Models

abstract: The success of deep networks is crucially attributed to their ability to capture latent features within a representation space. In this work, we investigate whether the underlying learned features of a model can be efficiently retrieved through feedback from an agent, such as a large language model (LLM), in the form of relative triplet comparisons. These features may represent various constructs, including dictionaries in LLMs or components of a covariance matrix of Mahalanobis distances. We analyze the feedback complexity associated with learning a feature matrix in sparse settings. Our results establish tight bounds when the agent is permitted to construct activations and demonstrate strong upper bounds in sparse scenarios when the agent’s feedback is limited to distributional information. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on two distinct applications: feature recovery from Recursive Feature Machine-trained models and dictionary extraction from sparse autoencoders trained on Large Language Models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether hidden features learned by a model can be recovered efficiently from an agent's feedback. The feedback consists of relative triplet comparisons, providing comparative judgments rather than direct access to the feature matrix. The features may describe dictionaries in language models or components associated with a learned distance function.

The authors analyze how much feedback is needed when the feature structure is sparse. They distinguish two access settings. When the agent can construct activations, they establish tight complexity bounds. When feedback is restricted to distributional information, they establish strong upper bounds in sparse scenarios. This distinction matters because the available form of interaction changes what recovery guarantees can be established.

Experiments test the theory in two applications: recovering features from models trained with Recursive Feature Machines and extracting dictionaries from sparse autoencoders trained on large language models. The contribution links sparse feature recovery to an explicit accounting of feedback requirements, with empirical validation in both applications. The guarantees remain differentiated by the agent's access and the sparsity setting.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the comparison feedback needed to recover sparse hidden features, with guarantees that depend on the agent's access to activations.

title: The Complexity of Learning Sparse Superposed Features with Feedback

abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) is a critical research area that seeks to decode human emotions from diverse data modalities. However, existing machine learning methods predominantly rely on predefined emotion taxonomies, which fail to capture the inherent complexity, subtlety, and multi-appraisal nature of human emotional experiences, as demonstrated by studies in psychology and cognitive science. To overcome this limitation, we advocate for introducing the concept of open vocabulary into MER. This paradigm shift aims to enable models to predict emotions beyond a fixed label space, accommodating a flexible set of categories to better reflect the nuanced spectrum of human emotions. To achieve this, we propose a novel paradigm: Open-Vocabulary MER (OV-MER), which enables emotion prediction without being confined to predefined spaces. However, constructing a dataset that encompasses the full range of emotions for OV-MER is practically infeasible; hence, we present a comprehensive solution including a newly curated database, novel evaluation metrics, and a preliminary benchmark. By advancing MER from basic emotions to more nuanced and diverse emotional states, we hope this work can inspire the next generation of MER, enhancing its generalizability and applicability in real-world scenarios. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/zeroQiaoba/AffectGPT.

paragraphs: Emotion-recognition systems commonly choose among a predetermined set of categories. That setup can make subtle or complex emotional states difficult to express, even when several forms of input provide useful evidence. This paper proposes open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition, allowing predictions beyond a fixed inventory of emotion labels.

The contribution includes a newly curated database, evaluation metrics, and a preliminary benchmark for studying this setting. These components are important because changing the permissible output space also changes what training and evaluation must accommodate. The authors explicitly recognize that building a dataset covering the full range of human emotions is practically infeasible.

The proposed resources therefore establish a way to investigate flexible emotion prediction without claiming exhaustive emotional coverage. The work’s stated ambition is to encourage systems that represent more nuanced and diverse emotional states and eventually generalize more effectively in real-world use. Its central contribution is the task formulation and supporting evaluation infrastructure; those broader improvements are presented as goals for the research direction.
summary.tldr: OV-MER introduces a task, dataset, and evaluation framework for recognizing emotions beyond predefined category lists.

title: OV-MER: Towards Open-Vocabulary Multimodal Emotion Recognition

abstract: Counterfactual image generation presents significant challenges, including preserving identity, maintaining perceptual quality, and ensuring faithfulness to an underlying causal model. While existing auto-encoding frameworks admit semantic latent spaces which can be manipulated for causal control, they struggle with scalability and fidelity. Advancements in diffusion models present opportunities for improving counterfactual image editing, having demonstrated state-of-the-art visual quality, human-aligned perception and representation learning capabilities. Here, we present a suite of diffusion-based causal mechanisms, introducing the notions of spatial, semantic and dynamic abduction. We propose a general framework that integrates semantic representations into diffusion models through the lens of Pearlian causality to edit images via a counterfactual reasoning process. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to consider high-level semantic identity preservation for diffusion counterfactuals and to demonstrate how semantic control enables principled trade-offs between faithful causal control and identity preservation.

paragraphs: Counterfactual image generation asks how an image would change under an intervention governed by a causal model. Producing a convincing result requires more than visual quality: the edit should follow the intended causal relationship while retaining relevant aspects of the original image’s identity. The paper treats these requirements as connected parts of the generation problem.

The authors introduce diffusion-based causal mechanisms and three notions of abduction: spatial, semantic, and dynamic. Their general framework brings semantic representations into diffusion models using Pearlian causal reasoning. Here, abduction concerns reasoning from an observed image about the underlying information needed to construct a counterfactual version of that same observation.

The central contribution is explicit control over high-level semantic identity during counterfactual editing. The authors demonstrate that semantic control supports principled trade-offs between preserving identity and following causal interventions faithfully. They describe this treatment of semantic identity in diffusion counterfactuals as a first to their knowledge. The result frames identity preservation as something to reason about and balance, rather than simply assume from realistic-looking images.
summary.tldr: This framework uses semantic representations in diffusion models to balance causal faithfulness and identity preservation during counterfactual image editing.

title: Diffusion Counterfactual Generation with Semantic Abduction

abstract: In recent years, there has been a trend in the field of Reinforcement Learning (RL) towards large action models trained offline on large-scale datasets via sequence modeling. Existing models are primarily based on the Transformer architecture, which results in powerful agents. However, due to slow inference times, Transformer-based approaches are impractical for real-time applications, such as robotics. Recently, modern recurrent architectures, such as xLSTM and Mamba, have been proposed that exhibit parallelization benefits during training similar to the Transformer architecture while offering fast inference. In this work, we study the aptitude of these modern recurrent architectures for large action models. Consequently, we propose a Large Recurrent Action Model (LRAM) with an xLSTM at its core that comes with linear-time inference complexity and natural sequence length extrapolation abilities. Experiments on 432 tasks from 6 domains show that LRAM compares favorably to Transformers in terms of performance and speed.

paragraphs: Large action models learn how to act from previously collected datasets by treating behavior as a sequence modeling problem. Transformers have produced capable agents in this setting, but their inference speed creates difficulties for applications that need timely responses, including robotics. This paper investigates whether modern recurrent architectures can offer a better combination of action quality and execution speed.

The proposed Large Recurrent Action Model, or LRAM, uses xLSTM as its central architecture. The motivation is that modern recurrent models can retain training parallelization benefits similar to transformers while supporting fast inference. LRAM has linear-time inference complexity and naturally supports extrapolation to sequence lengths beyond those encountered during training.

The authors evaluate the approach on 432 tasks spanning six domains and report favorable performance and speed compared with transformers. These findings support recurrent architectures as a practical option for large action models, connecting architectural efficiency with the demands of robotics rather than treating prediction quality as the only consideration.
summary.tldr: LRAM uses xLSTM to combine fast recurrent inference with competitive action-model performance across 432 tasks.

title: A Large Recurrent Action Model: xLSTM enables Fast Inference for Robotics Tasks

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at reasoning and planning when trained on chain-of-thought (CoT) data, where the step-by-step thought process is explicitly outlined by text tokens. However, this results in lengthy inputs where many words support textual coherence rather than core reasoning information, and processing these inputs consumes substantial computation resources. In this work, we propose a hybrid representation of the reasoning process, where we partially abstract away the initial reasoning steps using latent discrete tokens generated by VQ-VAE, significantly reducing the length of reasoning traces. We explore the use of latent trace abstractions in two scenarios: 1) training the model from scratch for the Keys-Finding Maze problem, 2) fine-tuning LLMs on this hybrid data with an extended vocabulary including unseen latent tokens, for both logical and mathematical reasoning problems. To facilitate effective learning, we introduce a simple training procedure that randomly mixes latent and text tokens, which enables fast adaptation to new latent tokens. Our approach consistently outperforms the baselines methods in various benchmarks, such as Math (+4.2%, Llama-3.2-1B), GSM8K (+4.1%, Llama-3.2-3B), and Fresh-Gaokao-Math-2023 (+13.3%, Llama-3.1-8B) with an average reduction of 17% in reasoning trace’s length.

title: Token Assorted: Mixing Latent and Text Tokens for Improved Language Model Reasoning

abstract: With the growing availability of multi-domain time series data, there is an increasing demand for general forecasting models pre-trained on multi-source datasets to support diverse downstream prediction scenarios. Existing time series foundation models primarily focus on scaling up pre-training datasets and model sizes to enhance generalization performance. In this paper, we take a different approach by addressing two critical aspects of general forecasting models: (1) how to derive unified representations from heterogeneous multi-domain time series data, and (2) how to effectively capture domain-specific features to enable adaptive transfer across various downstream scenarios. To address the first aspect, we propose Decomposed Frequency Learning as the pre-training task, which leverages frequency-based masking and reconstruction to decompose coupled semantic information in time series, resulting in unified representations across domains. For the second aspect, we introduce the Time Series Register, which captures domain-specific representations during pre-training and enhances adaptive transferability to downstream tasks. Our model achieves the state-of-the-art forecasting performance on seven real-world benchmarks, demonstrating remarkable few-shot and zero-shot capabilities.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general forecasting model around two complementary needs: finding representations shared across different time-series domains and retaining information specific to each domain. Both matter when pretraining on heterogeneous datasets and transferring to new prediction settings. The approach focuses on representation design and adaptation as routes to better generalization.

For shared representations, the authors introduce Decomposed Frequency Learning. This pretraining task masks and reconstructs frequency-based information to separate semantic content that is coupled together in the original series. For domain-specific information, they introduce the Time Series Register, which captures representations during pretraining that help the model adapt to downstream tasks.

The two components address how a model can share knowledge while remaining responsive to differences between forecasting settings. On seven real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art forecasting performance and strong few-shot and zero-shot capabilities. These findings support treating cross-domain commonality and domain-specific adaptation as distinct, jointly useful parts of a general time-series forecasting model.
summary.tldr: Frequency-based pretraining and a domain-specific register combine shared time-series representations with adaptive transfer for general forecasting.

title: Towards a General Time Series Forecasting Model with Unified Representation and Adaptive Transfer

abstract: Graph generation models have shown significant potential across various domains. However, despite their success, these models often inherit societal biases, limiting their adoption in real-world applications. Existing research on fairness in graph generation primarily addresses structural bias, overlooking the critical issue of feature bias. To address this gap, we propose FDGen, a novel approach that defines and mitigates both feature and structural biases in graph generation models. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of how bias sources in graph data contribute to disparities in graph generation tasks. Experimental results on four real-world datasets demonstrate that FDGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving notable improvements in fairness while maintaining competitive generation performance.

paragraphs: Graph generation models can reproduce societal biases present in the data from which they learn. This paper distinguishes two places those biases can appear: graph structure and graph features. It argues that previous fairness research in graph generation has concentrated on structural bias, leaving feature bias insufficiently addressed despite its relevance to generated outputs.

FDGen is designed to define and mitigate both forms of bias within graph generation. This broadens the fairness objective beyond the pattern of connections to include the information represented through features. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis connecting sources of bias in graph data to disparities in generation tasks, giving the method an analytical account of the problem it targets.

Experiments on four real-world datasets report better fairness than state-of-the-art methods while retaining competitive generation performance. The stated result suggests that addressing both bias sources can improve fairness without sacrificing competitiveness on generation quality in those evaluations. The paper's contribution is this combined treatment of structural and feature bias, supported by theory and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: FDGen addresses both feature and structural bias in graph generation, improving fairness while maintaining competitive generation performance.

title: FDGen: A Fairness-Aware Graph Generation Model

abstract: Many large-scale systems rely on high-quality deep representations (embeddings) to facilitate tasks like retrieval, search, and generative modeling. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) recently emerged as a solution for adaptive embedding lengths, but it requires full model retraining and suffers from noticeable performance degradations at short lengths. In this paper, we show that sparse coding offers a compelling alternative for achieving adaptive representation with minimal overhead and higher fidelity. We propose Contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR), a method that specifies pre-trained embeddings into a high-dimensional but selectively activated feature space. By leveraging lightweight autoencoding and task-aware contrastive objectives, CSR preserves semantic quality while allowing flexible, cost-effective inference at different sparsity levels. Extensive experiments on image, text, and multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that CSR consistently outperforms MRL in terms of both accuracy and retrieval speed—often by large margins—while also cutting training time to a fraction of that required by MRL. Our results establish sparse coding as a powerful paradigm for adaptive representation learning in real-world applications where efficiency and fidelity are both paramount. Code is available at this URL.

paragraphs: Embedding-based systems need representations that balance useful information against storage and computation. Matryoshka Representation Learning addresses this through adjustable embedding lengths, but the abstract identifies full model retraining and reduced performance at short lengths as drawbacks. This paper investigates sparse coding as another way to make representations adapt to different computational budgets.

Contrastive Sparse Representation, or CSR, maps pretrained embeddings into a larger feature space in which only selected features are active. A lightweight autoencoder and task-aware contrastive objectives aim to retain semantic information. Adaptation comes from changing the level of sparsity, allowing inference to use different amounts of active information without requiring the same approach as shortening a dense embedding.

Across image, text, and multimodal benchmarks, CSR consistently outperforms Matryoshka Representation Learning in accuracy and retrieval speed, often substantially, while taking a fraction of its training time. These results support sparse representations as a practical alternative for the tested settings. The central finding is that a high-dimensional representation can still support efficient inference when its activity is selective.
summary.tldr: CSR converts pretrained embeddings into selectively active features, improving accuracy, retrieval speed, and training efficiency over Matryoshka learning in the reported benchmarks.

title: Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation

abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) has achieved remarkable success due to its large-scale pretraining on general domains, but it still faces challenges when applying it to downstream distant domains that have only scarce training data, which gives rise to the Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning (CDFSL) task. Inspired by Self-Attention’s insensitivity to token orders, we find an interesting phenomenon neglected in current works: disrupting the continuity of image tokens (i.e., making pixels not smoothly transited across patches) in ViT leads to a noticeable performance decline in the general (source) domain but only a marginal decrease in downstream target domains. This questions the role of image tokens’ continuity in ViT’s generalization under large domain gaps. In this paper, we delve into this phenomenon for an interpretation. We find continuity aids ViT in learning larger spatial patterns, which are harder to transfer than smaller ones, enlarging domain distances. Meanwhile, it implies that only smaller patterns within each patch could be transferred under extreme domain gaps. Based on this interpretation, we further propose a simple yet effective method for CDFSL that better disrupts the continuity of image tokens, encouraging the model to rely less on large patterns and more on smaller ones. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method in reducing domain gaps and outperforming state-of-the-art works. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/shuaiyi308/ReCIT.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether continuity between image patches helps vision transformers transfer to very different domains with little labeled data. The authors disrupt the smooth visual transitions across patch boundaries and observe a substantial performance drop in the source domain, but only a small decrease in downstream target domains.

Their interpretation is that continuity helps the model learn larger spatial patterns, which transfer less readily than smaller patterns under large domain gaps. In the extreme-gap settings discussed, the findings suggest that transferable information may be concentrated in patterns contained within individual patches. This connects an image representation choice to the scale of visual structure the model learns to use.

Based on that interpretation, the authors propose a method that further disrupts token continuity, encouraging less reliance on large patterns and greater reliance on smaller ones. Experiments report reduced domain gaps and improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution shows how sacrificing a source-domain cue can improve transfer when that cue mainly supports patterns that do not carry well into distant target domains.
summary.tldr: Disrupting continuity between image patches encourages smaller-scale visual patterns and improves few-shot transfer across large domain gaps.

title: Revisiting Continuity of Image Tokens for Cross-domain Few-shot Learning

abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions is fundamental in machine learning and statistics. As datasets grow larger, computational efficiency becomes increasingly important, particularly in reducing adaptive complexity, namely the number of sequential rounds required for sampling algorithms. While recent works have introduced several parallelizable techniques, they often exhibit suboptimal convergence rates and remain significantly weaker than the latest lower bounds for log-concave sampling. To address this, we propose a novel parallel sampling method that improves adaptive complexity dependence on dimension $d$ reducing it from $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^2 d)$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log d)$. Our approach builds on parallel simulation techniques from scientific computing.

paragraphs: Sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions is a basic operation in machine learning and statistics. This paper focuses on adaptive complexity: how many rounds of computation must occur sequentially. That distinction matters for parallel algorithms, because work within one round may proceed together, while later rounds must wait for earlier results. Reducing these dependencies is a separate efficiency objective from reducing total work.

The authors propose a sampling method built on parallel simulation techniques from scientific computing. Their motivation is that existing parallelizable approaches still have suboptimal convergence behavior and a substantial gap relative to lower bounds for log-concave sampling. The contribution targets the dependence of sequential-round complexity on the distribution's dimension, denoted by d.

The stated improvement reduces that dependence from O-tilde(log² d) to O-tilde(log d). This removes one logarithmic factor from the reported dimension dependence of adaptive complexity. The result concerns the sequential structure of sampling computation; it supplies a theoretical advance in how parallel simulation can organize high-dimensional sampling with fewer dependent rounds.
summary.tldr: A parallel simulation-based sampling method improves dimension-dependent sequential-round complexity from O-tilde(log² d) to O-tilde(log d).

title: Parallel Simulation for Log-concave Sampling and Score-based Diffusion Models

abstract: This position paper proposes a “Right to AI,” which asserts that individuals and communities should meaningfully participate in the development and governance of the AI systems that shape their lives. Motivated by the increasing deployment of AI in critical domains and inspired by Henri Lefebvre's concept of the “Right to the City,” we reconceptualize AI as a societal infrastructure, rather than merely a product of expert design. In this paper, we critically evaluate how generative agents, large-scale data extraction, and diverse cultural values bring new complexities to AI oversight. The paper proposes that grassroots participatory methodologies can mitigate biased outcomes and enhance social responsiveness. It asserts that data is socially produced and should be managed and owned collectively. Drawing on Sherry Arnstein’s Ladder of Citizen Participation and analyzing nine case studies, the paper develops a four-tier model for the Right to AI that situates the current paradigm and envisions an aspirational future. It proposes recommendations for inclusive data ownership, transparent design processes, and stakeholder-driven oversight. We also discuss market-led and state-centric alternatives and argue that participatory approaches offer a better balance between technical efficiency and democratic legitimacy.

The authors examine complications created by generative agents, large-scale data extraction, and differing cultural values. The framework makes their proposed right more concrete as an agenda for institutional design.
summary.tldr: The proposed Right to AI centers meaningful public participation, collective data ownership, and stakeholder oversight in AI development and governance.

title: Position: The Right to AI

abstract: Benchmarks for LLM-assisted theorem proving in Lean are often treated as intrinsically reliable because every solved instance comes with a machine-checked proof. However, the kernel only checks that a proof establishes a formal statement; it does not verify that the statement faithfully encodes the intended informal problem, nor that evaluation harnesses are robust to trivial or adversarial solutions. We audit five widely used Lean theorem-proving benchmarks and their forks, using corpus-scale static checkers to surface 4,833 findings, including 398 mechanically certified issues such as counterexamples, vacuous theorems, and unsound axioms. We also document semantic defects such as missing hypotheses, problem simplification, incomplete or incorrect translations, and Lean-specific specification hazards. Beyond dataset construction, we survey evaluation-time failure modes and show, on corrected subsets, that defects can both inflate and deflate reported prover scores. We propose a fault taxonomy, a suite of automated checkers and recall-oriented semantic-audit prompts, and release standards to guide the creation of formal math datasets and make evaluation more reproducible and trustworthy. Our checkers, audit prompts, and corrected dataset snapshots are available at https://github.com/Shashi456/atp-checkers.

paragraphs: A machine-checked proof establishes a formal statement, but the statement may still misrepresent the intended mathematical problem. This paper audits that gap in Lean theorem-proving benchmarks. It also examines evaluation machinery, where trivial or adversarial solutions can undermine what a reported success actually measures.

The authors audit five widely used benchmarks and their forks using static checkers across the corpora. summary.tldr: An audit of Lean benchmarks shows that specification defects and evaluation failures can distort scores despite machine-checked proofs.

title: Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking: Dataset Defects and Evaluation Failures in Lean Theorem Proving

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-running settings where improving through experience at test time becomes important. A common approach is to update an explicit memory after each interaction to guide future decisions. However, most existing methods rely on hand-designed prompting rules, making it difficult to align memory updates with downstream objectives over multi-step horizons consistently. We propose MemoPilot, a plug-in memory copilot that explicitly trains the memory update process to improve a frozen LLM’s performance across sequential interactions. We formulate memory updating as a multi-turn decision problem and optimize it end-to-end with multi-turn GRPO. Our training recipe introduces (i) a turn-wise reward signal and (ii) a context-independent, turn-level advantage estimation across rollouts, enabling finer-grained credit assignment and more stable training in multi-turn settings. We evaluate MemoPilot on two testbeds: multi-round Rock-Paper-Scissors (RPS) and Limit Texas Hold’em (LHE). Across both environments, MemoPilot substantially improves test-time learning of a frozen player over strong baselines, ranking first in Elo ratings on both games (1762 on LHE and 1590 on RPS) and outperforming all baseline memory methods and proprietary models, including Deepseek-V3.2. Our code is publicly available.

paragraphs: An agent that acts repeatedly can use explicit memory to improve future decisions without changing its underlying language model. However, hand-written rules for updating memory may not consistently preserve information that helps over several interactions. MemoPilot addresses this by training a separate memory copilot around a frozen language-model player.

The authors formulate memory updating as a multi-turn decision problem and optimize it with multi-turn GRPO. Their training procedure combines rewards at individual turns with context-independent, turn-level advantage estimates across rollouts. These mechanisms provide finer-grained credit assignment, helping training distinguish which memory-update decisions contribute to downstream performance and making optimization more stable across multiple turns.

The reported comparisons include baseline memory methods and proprietary models. These results demonstrate that training the memory-update process can improve sequential adaptation even when the player’s own model remains frozen.
summary.tldr: MemoPilot trains memory updates with reinforcement learning, improving a frozen language-model player’s adaptation across two sequential game environments.

title: From Player to Master: Enhancing Test-Time Learning of LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning over Memory

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have intensified the need for low-precision formats for efficient inference. The Open Compute Project Microscaling (MX) standard is attractive due to its favorable hardware efficiency, but its 4-bit variant (MXFP4) lags behind NVIDIA’s NVFP4 in accuracy, limiting adoption. We introduce two software-only techniques, Overflow-Aware Scaling (OAS) and Macro Block Scaling (MBS), that improve MXFP4 quantization fidelity without requiring hardware changes. OAS reduces overall errors by increasing effective dynamic range under power-of-two block scaling, while MBS allocates higher-precision scaling at a coarser granularity to better preserve outliers. Across multiple LLMs and standard downstream benchmarks, OAS and MBS reduce the end-to-end accuracy gap between MXFP4 and NVFP4 from about 10% to below 1% on average, while incurring modest GEMM overhead (6.2% on average). These results re-establish MXFP4 as a practical alternative to NVFP4, enabling near-NVFP4 accuracy while retaining MX’s hardware-efficiency advantages (e.g., 12% relative area savings in tensor cores).

paragraphs: MXFP4 offers hardware-efficient low-precision computation, but its accuracy gap relative to NVFP4 has limited its usefulness for language-model inference. This paper introduces two software-only scaling techniques to improve MXFP4 quantization without changing hardware. Both target how numerical range is represented when model values are compressed into the format.

Overflow-Aware Scaling increases the effective dynamic range available under power-of-two block scaling, reducing overall error. Macro Block Scaling assigns higher-precision scaling at a coarser granularity to preserve outliers more effectively. The methods address different parts of the same issue: how scaling choices influence the information retained by low-precision values.

Across multiple language models and standard downstream benchmarks, the techniques reduce the average end-to-end accuracy gap from about 10% to below 1%. They incur an average 6.2% GEMM overhead while retaining MX’s hardware-efficiency advantages, including the cited 12% relative tensor-core area savings. These results support MXFP4 as a practical alternative approaching NVFP4 accuracy in the evaluated settings, with a measured computational cost.
summary.tldr: Two software-only scaling methods narrow MXFP4’s reported accuracy gap with NVFP4 to below 1% on average with modest GEMM overhead.

title: Unveiling the Potential of Quantization with MXFP4: Strategies for Quantization Error Reduction

abstract: Real-world data is frequently noisy and ambiguous. In crowdsourcing, for example, human annotators may assign conflicting class labels to the same instances. Partial-label learning (PLL) addresses this challenge by training classifiers when each instance is associated with a set of candidate labels, only one of which is correct. While early PLL methods approximate the true label posterior, they are often computationally intensive. Recent deep learning approaches improve scalability but rely on surrogate losses and heuristic label refinement. We introduce a novel probabilistic framework that directly approximates the posterior distribution over true labels using amortized variational inference. Our method employs neural networks to predict variational parameters from input data, enabling efficient inference. This approach combines the expressiveness of deep learning with the rigor of probabilistic modeling, while remaining architecture-agnostic. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and efficiency.
originalAbstract: Real-world data is frequently noisy and ambiguous. In crowdsourcing, for example, human annotators may assign conflicting class labels to the same instances. Partial-label learning (PLL) addresses this challenge by training classifiers when each instance is associated with a set of candidate labels, only one of which is correct. While early PLL methods approximate the true label posterior, they are often computationally intensive. Recent deep learning approaches improve scalability but rely on surrogate losses and heuristic label refinement. We introduce a novel probabilistic framework that directly approximates the posterior distribution over true labels using amortized variational inference. Our method employs neural networks to predict variational parameters from input data, enabling efficient inference. This approach combines the expressiveness of deep learning with the rigor of probabilistic modeling, while remaining architecture-agnostic. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Partial-label learning trains a classifier from examples that each have several possible labels, with exactly one assumed to be correct. The central problem is deciding which candidate to trust while learning from the same ambiguous data. Earlier probabilistic approaches can require substantial computation, while newer deep learning methods often use substitute objectives and heuristic updates to resolve labels.

This paper proposes learning a probability distribution over the true label directly through amortized variational inference. A neural network predicts the parameters of an approximate label posterior from the input. Sharing this inference procedure across examples makes probabilistic label disambiguation efficient, rather than requiring a separate intensive inference process for every instance.

The framework accommodates different neural network architectures, connecting scalable prediction with an explicit treatment of label uncertainty. The authors report theoretical support and state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on synthetic and real-world datasets. These results support probabilistic inference as a practical approach to ambiguous supervision under the setting’s one-correct-candidate assumption.
summary.tldr: A neural variational inference framework efficiently resolves ambiguous candidate labels while achieving reported state-of-the-art classification accuracy.

title: Amortized Variational Inference for Partial-Label Learning: A Probabilistic Approach to Label Disambiguation

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to decompose neural network activations into human-interpretable features. Typically, features learned by a single SAE are used for downstream applications. However, it has recently been shown that a single SAE captures only a limited subset of features that can be extracted from the activation space. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce and formalize SAE ensembles. Furthermore, we propose to ensemble multiple SAEs through naive bagging and boosting. In naive bagging, SAEs trained with different weight initializations are ensembled, whereas in boosting SAEs sequentially trained to minimize the residual error are ensembled. Theoretically, naive bagging and boosting are justified as approaches to reduce reconstruction error. Empirically, we evaluate our ensemble approaches with three settings of language models and SAE architectures. Our empirical results demonstrate that, compared to an expanded SAE that matches the number of features in the ensemble, ensembling SAEs improves the reconstruction of language model activations along with SAE stability. Additionally, on downstream tasks such as concept detection and spurious correlation removal, SAE ensembles achieve better performance, showing improved practical utility.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders decompose a neural network’s activations into features intended to be understandable to people. A single autoencoder, however, captures only part of the feature structure available in those activations. This paper studies whether combining several sparse autoencoders can provide a more useful representation.

The authors formalize ensembles and develop two approaches. Naive bagging combines autoencoders trained from different random initializations. Boosting trains them sequentially so that later models focus on reconstruction errors left by earlier ones. Theoretical analysis justifies both approaches as ways to reduce reconstruction error, connecting the ensemble design to a concrete representational objective.

Experiments span three combinations of language models and autoencoder architectures. Against a single expanded autoencoder with the same total number of features, ensembles improve activation reconstruction and stability. They also perform better on concept detection and removal of spurious correlations. These comparisons indicate that organizing features across multiple autoencoders can offer practical benefits beyond simply increasing the feature count of one model.
summary.tldr: Combining sparse autoencoders improves reconstruction, stability, and downstream utility compared with a single autoencoder containing the same number of features.

title: Ensembling Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) enable parallel token generation, and their block-wise variants have attracted significant attention. However, existing dLLMs usually exhibit an accuracy–parallelism trade-off, where raising tokens per forward (TPF) via aggressive parallel decoding often degrades task accuracy. To address this, we suggest developing a post-training approach to directly optimize the speed–quality frontier of pre-trained dLLMs. Conceptually, we do not require the model to decode aggressively along all sampling trajectories, but rather to find several highly parallelizable ones that can yield correct results. To this end, we resort to a reinforcement learning paradigm, i.e., LightningRL, to optimize rewards regarding both the final accuracy and inference parallelism. LightningRL follows the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework, with further improvements for dLLMs: 1) stabilized training via per-reward decoupled normalization, 2) token-level negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss on correct trajectories for regularization, and 3) improved training efficiency through dynamic sampling with TPF-aware filtering. Across maths and code tasks, LightningRL consistently advances the Pareto frontier, maintaining competitive accuracy while increasing parallelism to an average TPF of 7.3 (up to 11.10 on MBPP).

paragraphs: Block-wise diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but pushing parallelism too aggressively often reduces accuracy. LightningRL treats the balance between correct answers and tokens generated per forward pass as a post-training objective. Its premise is that a model can learn useful, highly parallel generation trajectories without making every trajectory equally aggressive.

The method builds on Group Relative Policy Optimization with rewards for both final accuracy and inference parallelism. It normalizes these rewards separately to stabilize training, adds a token-level likelihood loss on correct trajectories, and uses dynamic sampling with filtering informed by tokens per forward pass. These components jointly encourage efficient generation while reinforcing successful reasoning paths.

Across mathematics and coding tasks, the reported results improve the frontier of achievable accuracy and parallelism. LightningRL maintains competitive accuracy while reaching an average of 7.3 tokens per forward pass, with up to 11.10 on MBPP. These are parallelism measurements, so the contribution is specifically a better demonstrated quality–parallelism balance through reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: LightningRL rewards correctness and parallel generation together, improving the accuracy–parallelism frontier of block-wise diffusion language models.

title: LightningRL: Breaking the Accuracy–Parallelism Trade-off of Block-wise dLLMs via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have demonstrated both effectiveness and efficiency in reasoning via a block-based semi-autoregressive generation paradigm. Despite their progress, the fixed-size block generations remain a critical bottleneck for effective and coherent reasoning. (I) From a global perspective, different reasoning tasks would correspond to different optimal decoding block sizes, which makes a "one-size-fits-all" assumption ineffective. (II) Even within a single reasoning task, the rigid block partitioning would break the logical flow and reduce reasoning coherence. Through empirical observations, we reveal that, for block-wise entropy, incorrect reasoning exhibits a fluctuating and unsteady trend between blocks, while the correctly generated tasks follow a consistent descending paradigm. Therefore, this paper proposes b1, a novel post-training framework that learns dynamic-size reasoning blocks via a Monotonic Entropy Descent objective with reinforcement learning to enhance reasoning coherence. b1 integrates seamlessly as a plug-and-play module with existing dLLM’s post-training algorithms. Extensive experiments across various reasoning benchmarks showcase b1’s consistent improvement over fixed-size block baselines. Our code has been released at https://github.com/YanJiangJerry/Block-R1.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate reasoning through a sequence of blocks, but fixed block sizes impose a rigid structure on that process. The paper identifies two problems: different tasks can favor different block sizes, and a fixed boundary can interrupt the logical flow even within one task.

The authors observe that block-level entropy behaves differently in successful and unsuccessful reasoning. Incorrect traces show an uneven, fluctuating pattern, while correct examples exhibit a consistent downward trend. Their b1 framework uses this observation to guide reinforcement learning, training dynamic block sizes with an objective that encourages entropy to decrease monotonically as reasoning proceeds.

b1 is a post-training component designed to integrate with existing diffusion-language-model training algorithms. Across the evaluated reasoning benchmarks, it consistently improves on fixed-size block baselines. The finding supports adapting generation boundaries to the reasoning process rather than choosing one size for every task. The entropy pattern provides an empirical training signal for coherence; the abstract does not present it as a universal guarantee of correctness.
summary.tldr: b1 trains diffusion language models to use dynamic reasoning-block sizes, improving benchmark performance through an objective that encourages steadily decreasing entropy.

title: Break the Block: Dynamic-size Reasoning Blocks for Diffusion Large Language Models via Monotonic Entropy Descent with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce OPO-CMDP, the first policy optimization algorithm for stochastic Contextual Markov Decision Process (CMDPs) under general offline function approximation. Our approach achieves a high probability regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(H^4\sqrt{T|S||A|\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{P}|)}),$ where $S$ and $A$ denote the state and action spaces, $H$ the horizon length, $T$ the number of episodes, and $\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{P}$ the finite function classes used to approximate the losses and dynamics, respectively. This is the first regret bound with optimal dependence on $|S|$ and $|A|$, directly improving the current state-of-the-art (Qian, Hu, and Simchi-Levi, 2024). These results demonstrate that optimistic policy optimization provides a natural, computationally superior and theoretically near-optimal path for solving CMDPs.

Our approach achieves a high probability regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(H^4\sqrt{T|S||A|\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{P}|)}),$ where $S$ and $A$ denote the state and action spaces, $H$ the horizon length, $T$ the number of episodes, and $\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{P}$ the finite function classes used to approximate the losses and dynamics, respectively. paragraphs: This paper introduces OPO-CMDP for stochastic contextual Markov decision processes, where learning concerns sequences of decisions in context-dependent environments. The algorithm uses optimistic policy optimization with general offline function approximation. Its analysis allows finite function classes to represent both losses and environment dynamics, bringing those two modeling tasks into the guarantee.

The authors establish a high-probability regret bound proportional to the fourth power of the horizon times the square root of the number of episodes, states, actions, and the logarithm of the product of the two function-class sizes, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a benchmark policy, so the bound describes learning performance across repeated episodes.

The central theoretical improvement is optimal dependence on the numbers of states and actions, which improves the cited state of the art. The authors also characterize optimistic policy optimization as computationally superior and theoretically near-optimal for this setting. The optimality claim specifically concerns state and action dependence; the overall bound still includes its stated horizon and approximation-class factors.
summary.tldr: OPO-CMDP provides a high-probability regret bound with optimal state and action dependence for contextual sequential decision problems.

title: Near-Optimal Regret for Policy Optimization in Contextual MDPs with General Offline Function Approximation

abstract: Continual Model Merging (CMM) enables rapid customization of foundation models by sequentially incorporating task-adapted models without repeated retraining. However, existing merging rules usually update the deployed model through fixed algebraic or projection-based operations, providing limited control over how much previously accumulated knowledge should be retained relative to the incoming task model. This limitation leads to unstable retention and performance degradation in long task streams, and becomes more pronounced when tasks have heterogeneous utilities. We propose ODE-driven Merging (ODE-M), a controllable framework that formulates each continual merge as a trajectory in parameter space rather than a one-step endpoint update. Motivated by mode connectivity, ODE-M constructs a barrier-aware trajectory using a rectified time-dependent velocity field, where lightweight first-order feedback from a small calibration set suppresses loss-increasing motion while preserving progress toward the incoming model. The next merged model is then obtained by selecting an operating point along this trajectory through a utility-aware time schedule, providing an explicit mechanism for balancing retained historical knowledge and incoming task expertise. Extensive experiments on standard CMM benchmarks show that ODE-M consistently improves over strong continual merging baselines across CLIP ViT backbones, stream lengths, and heterogeneous task-utility settings.
