paragraphs: Continual model merging incorporates successive task-adapted models into a deployed model without repeatedly retraining it. Fixed merging rules offer limited control over the balance between accumulated knowledge and incoming expertise. This can destabilize retention over long task streams, especially when some tasks matter more than others.

ODE-M treats each merge as a trajectory through parameter space. A time-dependent velocity field defines the motion, while lightweight first-order feedback from a small calibration set suppresses moves that increase loss and maintains progress toward the incoming model. A utility-aware time schedule then selects a point along this trajectory as the next deployed model.

The path and the stopping point provide explicit control over how far a merge moves toward new expertise. Experiments on standard continual-merging benchmarks report consistent improvements over strong baselines across CLIP ViT backbones, stream lengths, and unequal task-utility settings. These findings support trajectory-based merging as a practical way to regulate the retention-and-adaptation balance throughout repeated model updates.
summary.tldr: ODE-M turns continual model merging into a guided trajectory with a utility-aware stopping point to balance retained knowledge and incoming expertise.

title: Unlocking the Potential of Continual Model Merging: An ODE Perspective

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is often tuned by selecting checkpoints with high preference margins. We show that this selection rule can fail. Across dense $\beta$ sweeps in three 7B open-weight families under controlled DPO recipes, the DPO preference margin can strongly anticorrelate with capability probes, with the strongest observed case in Llama logic probes (Pearson $r=-0.91$, $n=13$). In Mistral, matched-duration controls show that transient exposure to higher $\beta$ produces persistent arithmetic ($d_z = 3.73$, $p = 0.002$) and format ($d_z = 3.38$, $p = 0.003$) degradation relative to a duration-matched constant-$\beta$ run, while logic and sycophancy show no significant effect. An expanded 14-probe logic suite further shows that aggregate capability scores can hide stable opposition between probe clusters: direct-inference probes are consistently negative while fallacy-detection probes are consistently positive, with 13 of 14 probes sign-stable across 3 seeds and 3 $\beta$ values. Sensitivity profiles differ across architectures: Mistral shows elevated seed variance near $\beta \approx 10^{-2}$, Llama shows capability-specific rigidity, and Qwen trades off smoothly. These findings motivate probe-resolved $\beta$ sweeps rather than margin-based checkpoint selection.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization is often monitored using a preference margin, with higher-margin checkpoints treated as better choices. This study shows that the rule can select models with weaker capabilities. Across controlled sweeps of the beta parameter in three open-weight 7B model families, preference margins can move strongly in the opposite direction from capability measurements.

The strongest reported anticorrelation appears in Llama logic probes. In Mistral, matched-duration experiments also find that temporary exposure to higher beta leaves persistent arithmetic and formatting degradation compared with a constant-beta run. Because sensitivity also differs across architectures, the authors recommend examining individual probes throughout beta sweeps instead of relying on preference margins alone.
summary.tldr: Higher DPO preference margins can accompany capability losses, motivating checkpoint selection based on individual capability probes.

title: Capability Traps in DPO

abstract: State-of-the-art model-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches either use gradient-free, population-based methods for planning, learned policy networks, or a combination of policy networks and planning. Hybrid approaches that combine Model Predictive Control (MPC) with a learned model and a policy prior to leverage the advantages of both paradigms have shown promising results. However, these approaches typically rely on gradient-free optimization methods, which can be computationally expensive for high-dimensional control tasks. While gradient-based methods are a promising alternative, recent works have empirically shown that gradient-based methods often perform worse than their gradient-free counterparts. We propose Dream-MPC, a novel approach that generates few candidate trajectories from a rolled-out policy and optimizes each trajectory by gradient ascent using a learned world model, uncertainty regularization and amortization of optimization iterations over time by reusing previously optimized actions. Our results on 24 continuous control tasks show that Dream-MPC can significantly improve the performance of the underlying policy and can outperform gradient-free MPC and state-of-the-art baselines. Code and videos are available at https://dream-mpc.github.io.

paragraphs: Planning with a learned world model can improve a reinforcement-learning policy, but searching over candidate actions can be expensive in high-dimensional control. Gradient-based optimization is a possible alternative to population-based search, although prior empirical work has often found it less effective. Dream-MPC investigates how to make gradient-based planning work better in this setting.

The method begins with a small number of candidate trajectories generated by rolling out a learned policy. It then improves each candidate through gradient ascent using the learned world model. Uncertainty regularization is part of this optimization, and previously optimized actions are reused over time. Reuse spreads the benefit of optimization iterations across successive planning steps.

Across 24 continuous-control tasks, the results show that Dream-MPC can substantially improve the underlying policy and can outperform gradient-free model predictive control and state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a particular combination of policy-generated candidates, model-based gradients, uncertainty regularization, and action reuse. The findings establish that this combination can make gradient-based planning effective, without claiming that gradients always outperform gradient-free search.
summary.tldr: Dream-MPC improves policy-generated action trajectories with world-model gradients, uncertainty regularization, and action reuse, showing gains across continuous-control tasks.

title: Dream-MPC: Gradient-Based Model Predictive Control with Latent Imagination

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pretrained on corpora containing trillions of tokens and, therefore, inevitably memorize sensitive information. Locate-then-edit methods, as a mainstream paradigm of model editing, offer a promising solution by modifying model parameters without retraining. However, in this work, we reveal a critical vulnerability of this paradigm: the parameter updates inadvertently serve as a side channel, enabling attackers to recover the edited data. We propose a two-stage reverse-engineering attack named KSTER (KeySpaceReconsTruction-then-EntropyReduction) that leverages the low-rank structure of these updates. First, we theoretically show that the row space of the update matrix encodes a "fingerprint" of the edited subjects, enabling accurate subject recovery via spectral analysis. Second, we introduce an entropy-based prompt recovery attack that reconstructs the semantic context of the edit. Extensive experiments on multiple LLMs demonstrate that our attacks can recover edited data with high success rates. Furthermore, we propose subspace camouflage, a defense strategy that obfuscates the update fingerprint with semantic decoys. This approach effectively mitigates reconstruction risks without compromising editing utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/reanatom/EditingAttack.

paragraphs: Model editing changes a language model’s stored information without retraining the entire model. This paper examines a privacy vulnerability in locate-then-edit methods: the parameter changes can themselves reveal information about the edited data. The concern is a side channel in the update, separate from what the edited model says in ordinary responses.

The proposed KSTER attack has two stages and exploits the low-rank structure of parameter updates. The authors theoretically show that an update matrix’s row space contains a fingerprint of the edited subjects, which supports subject recovery through spectral analysis. An entropy-based prompt recovery stage then reconstructs the semantic context associated with the edit.

Experiments across multiple language models report high success rates in recovering edited data. The authors also propose subspace camouflage, which obscures the fingerprint using semantic decoys. They report that this defense reduces reconstruction risk without compromising editing utility. The work shows why evaluating an editing method’s privacy requires considering information exposed by its parameter updates as well as its resulting behavior.
summary.tldr: KSTER recovers edited information from model-update structure, while a proposed camouflage defense reduces this leakage without harming editing utility.

title: Reverse-Engineering Model Editing on Language Models

abstract: We consider the computational problem of compacting Tsetlin Machine classifiers by reducing the number of propositional clauses while preserving predictive accuracy. TMs trained with limited clause capacity often perform poorly because stochastic optimization cannot reliably find the few precise clauses needed in a vast configuration space. High-quality compact subsets also exist in the case of larger Tsetlin Machines. The difficulty here lies in extracting them. Local pruning heuristics can fail badly on TMs because clauses interact through Boolean logic: a clause may appear unimportant in isolation yet becomes critical when others are removed. We formalize compression as the Minimum Discriminating Clause Set (MDCS) problem, which asks to find a smallest subset of clauses that preserves the trained model’s discrimination of training samples. We show that MDCS is NP-hard. We solve MDCS using weighted partial Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT). A partition-and-merge strategy allows us to scale to 100,000 samples. Across 13 datasets, the compressed model preserves the 200-clause teacher’s accuracy within a few percentage points while using a median of only 16 clauses, and outperforms a matched-capacity TM trained from scratch on every dataset where direct training has room to improve, by up to 45 percentage points.

paragraphs: Tsetlin Machines classify using propositional clauses, but obtaining a small accurate collection is difficult. Training with few clauses can struggle to find the necessary precise rules. Pruning a larger trained model also presents a problem: clauses interact logically, so a clause that appears dispensable alone may become essential after other clauses are removed.

The authors formalize compression as finding the smallest clause subset that preserves the trained model’s discrimination of training samples. They prove this Minimum Discriminating Clause Set problem is NP-hard and formulate its solution using weighted partial Maximum Satisfiability. They outperform directly trained models of matching capacity on every dataset where direct training has room to improve, with gains reaching 45 percentage points. These results support selecting logically compatible subsets from larger models as an effective route to compact classifiers.
summary.tldr: MaxSAT-based clause selection compresses trained Tsetlin Machines substantially while retaining accuracy close to their larger teachers.

title: MaxSAT-Based Compression for Tsetlin Machines

abstract:
We study gradient testing and gradient estimation of smooth functions using only a comparison oracle that, given two points, indicates which one has the larger function value. For any smooth $f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R$, $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\varepsilon>0$, we design a gradient testing algorithm that determines whether the normalized gradient $
abla f(\mathbf{x})/\lVert
abla f(\mathbf{x})Vert$ is $\varepsilon$-close or $2\varepsilon$-far from a given unit vector $\mathbf{v}$ using $O(1)$ queries, as well as a gradient estimation algorithm that outputs an $\varepsilon$-estimate of $
abla f(\mathbf{x})/\lVert
abla f(\mathbf{x})Vert$ using $O(n\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries which we prove to be optimal. Furthermore, we study gradient estimation in the quantum comparison oracle model where queries can be made in superpositions, and develop a quantum algorithm using $O(\log (n/\varepsilon))$ queries.

abla f(\mathbf{x})/\lVert
abla f(\mathbf{x})Vert$ is $\varepsilon$-close or $2\varepsilon$-far from a given unit vector $\mathbf{v}$ using $O(1)$ queries, as well as a gradient estimation algorithm that outputs an $\varepsilon$-estimate of $

paragraphs: This paper studies how much can be learned about a smooth function's gradient when the only available feedback compares two points. The oracle says which point has the larger function value, without revealing either value. The target is the normalized gradient, meaning its direction rather than its magnitude.

Estimating the direction to epsilon accuracy requires O(n log(1/epsilon)) queries in n dimensions, and the authors prove this query complexity is optimal.

title: Gradient Testing and Estimation by Comparisons

abstract: Sampling useful three-dimensional molecular structures along with their most favorable conformations is a key challenge in drug discovery. Current state-of-the-art 3D de-novo molecular design generative models are limited to generating a single conformation. However, the conformational landscape of a molecule determines its observable properties and how tightly it is able to bind to a given protein target. By generating a representative set of low-energy conformers, we can more directly assess these properties and potentially improve the ability to generate molecules with desired thermodynamic observables. Towards this aim, we propose FlexiFlow, a novel architecture that extends flow-matching models, allowing for the joint sampling of molecules along with multiple conformations while preserving both equivariance and permutation invariance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the QM9 and GEOM Drugs datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in 3D molecular generation producing valid, unique, and novel molecules with high fidelity to the training data distribution. Moreover, we show that our model can generate unstrained conformational ensembles capturing the conformational diversity and providing similar coverage to state-of-the-art physics-based methods at a fraction of the inference time. Finally, FlexiFlow can be successfully transferred to the protein-conditioned ligand generation task, even when the dataset contains only static pockets without accompanying conformations.

paragraphs: A molecule can adopt multiple three-dimensional shapes, and that range influences its observable properties and binding to proteins. FlexiFlow extends flow-matching generation to jointly produce molecules and sets of conformations, aiming to represent their flexibility through low-energy structures.

By producing an ensemble alongside molecular identity, the approach provides a basis for assessing conformational diversity and could help generate molecules with desired thermodynamic properties.

summary.tldr: FlexiFlow jointly generates molecules and diverse conformations, achieving strong molecular-generation results with fast ensemble sampling.

title: FlexiFlow: decomposable flow matching for generation of flexible molecular ensemble

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used for real-world tasks involving multi-step reasoning and long-form generation, where reliability requires grounding model outputs in heterogeneous input sources and verifying individual factual claims. However, existing multimodal grounding benchmarks and evaluation methods focus on simplified, observation-based scenarios or limited modalities and fail to assess attribution in complex multimodal reasoning. We introduce MuRGAt (Multimodal Reasoning with Grounded Attribution), a benchmark for evaluating fact-level multimodal attribution in settings that require reasoning beyond direct observation. Given inputs spanning video, audio, and other modalities, MuRGAt requires models to generate answers with explicit reasoning and precise citations, where each citation specifies both modality and temporal segments. To enable reliable assessment, we introduce an automatic evaluation framework that strongly correlates with human judgments. Benchmarking with human and automated scores reveals that even strong MLLMs frequently hallucinate citations despite correct reasoning. Moreover, we observe a key trade-off: increasing reasoning depth or enforcing structured grounding often degrades accuracy, highlighting a significant gap between internal reasoning and verifiable attribution.

paragraphs: A multimodal model can give a correct explanation while citing evidence that does not support it. MuRGAt evaluates this distinction in tasks involving reasoning across video, audio, and other input modalities. It moves beyond grounding directly observable details to examine whether individual factual claims remain traceable during more complex reasoning.

Models must produce answers with explicit reasoning and precise citations. Each citation identifies both the source modality and the relevant time segment, making the claimed evidence specific enough to assess. The authors also introduce an automatic evaluation framework whose scores strongly correlate with human judgments, supporting systematic assessment of attribution alongside answer and reasoning quality.

Human and automated evaluations reveal frequent citation hallucinations even among strong models whose reasoning is correct. The benchmark also exposes a trade-off: deeper reasoning or more structured grounding often reduces accuracy. These findings show that successful internal reasoning does not automatically produce verifiable evidence references. MuRGAt makes that gap measurable by testing both the reasoning and the factual support attached to it.
summary.tldr: MuRGAt tests whether multimodal reasoning includes valid fact-level citations and finds frequent attribution failures despite correct reasoning.

title: Multimodal Fact-Level Attribution for Verifiable Reasoning

abstract: Despite remarkable performance on complex tasks, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often generate excessively long Chain-of-Thoughts (CoT), inflating computational costs even for simple queries. Existing efforts to mitigate this inefficiency typically rely on discrete reasoning modes or fixed budget tiers, lacking a principled criterion of when reasoning is sufficient. In this work, we introduce Minimal Sufficient CoT (MSC), defined as the shortest prefix of a CoT trajectory which is adequate for producing the correct answer. We empirically show that MSC not only reduces reasoning tokens, but also improves accuracy across difficulty levels. Building on MSC, we propose Sufficiency-guided Continuous Adaptive Reasoning (SuCo), a two-stage training framework for autonomous reasoning control along a continuous spectrum. In stage 1, MSC-Aligned Fine-Tuning (MFT) constructs MSC data using problem-adaptive sufficiency thresholds that naturally scale with question difficulty, then fine-tunes the model to internalize concise yet sufficient reasoning patterns. In stage 2, Sufficiency-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) further optimizes the model through reinforcement learning with dynamic complexity tracking and sufficiency-aware rewards that penalize both over- and under-thinking. Extensive experiments across mathematics, code, and science benchmarks show that SuCo consistently achieves improvements in both accuracy and reasoning efficiency.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend unnecessary computation producing long chains of thought, even for simple questions. Experiments across mathematics, programming, and science benchmarks show consistent gains in accuracy and reasoning efficiency. The approach makes sufficiency the organizing criterion for reasoning effort, extending beyond fixed budgets or a few discrete reasoning modes. Its findings support learning when enough reasoning has been done, while avoiding the assumption that simply shortening every reasoning trace will improve the answer.
summary.tldr: SuCo trains reasoning models to adapt their effort around sufficient reasoning, improving both accuracy and token efficiency in the evaluated tasks.

title: SuCo: Sufficiency-guided Continuous Adaptive Reasoning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a cornerstone technique for post-training large language models. While most existing approaches rely on the reverse KL-regularization, recent empirical studies have begun exploring alternative divergences (e.g., forward KL, chi-squared) as regularizers in RLHF. However, a unified theoretical understanding of general $f$-divergence regularization remains under-explored. To fill this gap, this work develops a comprehensive theoretical framework for online RLHF with an $f$-divergence regularized objective. Rather than treating each divergence in isolation, we adopt a holistic perspective across the entire class and propose two algorithms based on distinct sampling principles. The first extends the classical optimism principle with a carefully designed exploration bonus, while the second introduces a new method that exploits the sensitivity of the optimal policy to reward perturbations under $f$-divergence regularization. Theoretical analysis shows that $O(\log T)$ regret and $O(1/T)$ sub-optimality gap are achievable, establishing provable efficiency of both algorithms and, to the best of our knowledge, the first performance bounds for online RLHF under general $f$-divergence regularization.

This paper develops a common theoretical treatment for online RLHF objectives regularized by the wider family of f-divergences.

The authors propose two algorithms with different approaches to sampling. One extends optimism-based exploration by adding a carefully constructed exploration bonus. The other uses how the optimal policy responds to perturbations in the reward under f-divergence regularization. These approaches connect data collection to the structure of the regularized objective in two distinct ways.

These rates describe how accumulated decision loss and distance from the optimum behave as the online process continues. The contribution is a set of provable efficiency results across a general regularization class, extending theoretical coverage beyond the reverse-KL formulation commonly used in RLHF.
summary.tldr: Two sampling algorithms provide provable online RLHF efficiency across general f-divergence regularizers.

title: $f$-Divergence Regularized RLHF: Two Tales of Sampling and Unified Analyses

abstract: Lagrangian-based methodologies are one of the fundamental paradigms of safe reinforcement learning (RL) for constrained Markov decision processes, particularly when dealing with multi-constraint cases. While the specific details of the methodologies may differ, with some using a single estimator for the overall mixed penalty term of the constraints and others using separate estimators for the constraints, the fundamental question of the theoretical validity of the methodologies has remained largely unexplored. The present paper performs the first theoretical analysis of the methodologies and proves that the use of the mixed critic structure leads to the presence of a bias due to the target drift of the Lagrange multipliers. On the other hand, the use of the dedicated critic structure, where separate critics are used for the reward function and the constraint functions, does not suffer from this bias. The theoretical analysis is supported with experiments on a realistic power system environment with multiple constraints, where the dedicated critic structure succeeds in satisfying the constraints, whereas the mixed critic structure fails.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with multiple constraints often uses Lagrange multipliers to balance rewards against penalties. Some methods estimate a combined penalty through one critic, while others maintain separate estimates. This paper studies whether that architectural choice changes the validity of the learned estimates as the multipliers evolve during training.

The theoretical analysis shows that a mixed critic develops bias from target drift: changing multipliers change the combined quantity it is trying to estimate. Dedicated critics separately estimate the reward and each constraint function, avoiding this particular source of bias. The distinction isolates estimation from the changing weights used to combine its outputs.

Experiments in a realistic power-system environment with multiple constraints support the analysis. The dedicated-critic approach satisfies the constraints in the reported setting, whereas the mixed-critic approach fails. The finding connects a specific estimation problem to a practical constraint-satisfaction outcome. Avoiding multiplier-induced target drift is the established advantage; it should not be read as a universal guarantee that separate critics solve every difficulty in constrained reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Separate reward and constraint critics avoid bias caused by changing Lagrange multipliers, with supporting constraint-satisfaction results in a power-system experiment.

title: Why Dedicated Critics: Eliminating Target Drift in Multi-Constraint RL

abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) provides a principled framework for optimizing multiple expensive black-box functions. However, existing MOBO methods often struggle with coverage, scalability, and handling constraints and preferences. In this work we propose STAGE-BO, Sequential Targeting Adaptive Gap-Filling $\varepsilon$-Constraint Bayesian Optimization: by analyzing the coverage of the surrogate Pareto front, our method identifies the Pareto front point with the largest uncovered gap, and uses its coordinates to define adaptive constraints in $\varepsilon$-constraint method, which transforms the problem into a sequence of inequality-constrained subproblems, efficiently solved via constrained expected improvement acquisition. Our approach provides uniform Pareto coverage without hypervolume computation and naturally handles constraints and preferences. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate superior coverage and competitive hypervolume performance against state-of-the-art baselines. Our code implementation can be found at https://github.com/YangYaohong1/STAGE-BO.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate superior coverage and competitive hypervolume performance against state-of-the-art baselines. paragraphs: Optimizing several expensive objectives involves finding a useful range of trade-offs. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization uses surrogate models to guide evaluations, but covering the trade-off frontier evenly can be difficult. STAGE-BO focuses its search on gaps in the currently modeled Pareto front, the set of solutions representing competing objective trade-offs.

The method identifies the frontier point associated with the largest uncovered gap and uses its coordinates to set adaptive epsilon constraints. These convert the search into a sequence of subproblems with inequality constraints. Constrained expected improvement then guides evaluation within each subproblem. This construction targets coverage directly without requiring hypervolume computation and accommodates constraints and preferences.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report better coverage and competitive hypervolume performance against state-of-the-art baselines. These outcomes capture complementary qualities: how evenly the trade-offs are represented and how well the resulting solutions perform collectively. The approach offers a structured way to direct expensive evaluations toward underexplored trade-offs while retaining flexibility about which regions or constraints matter.
summary.tldr: STAGE-BO adaptively targets gaps in the Pareto front, improving trade-off coverage without computing hypervolume during optimization.

title: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization via Adaptive $\varepsilon$-Constraints Decomposition

abstract: World models are essential for autonomous robotic planning. However, the substantial computational overhead of existing dense Transformer-based models significantly hinders real-time deployment. To address this efficiency-performance bottleneck, we introduce DDP-WM, a novel world model centered on the principle of Disentangled Dynamics Prediction (DDP). We hypothesize that latent state evolution in observed scenes is heterogeneous and can be decomposed into sparse primary dynamics driven by physical interactions and secondary context-driven background updates. DDP-WM realizes this decomposition through an architecture that integrates efficient historical processing with dynamic localization to isolate primary dynamics. By employing a cross-attention mechanism for background updates, the framework optimizes resource allocation and provides a smooth optimization landscape for planners. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DDP-WM achieves superior efficiency and performance across diverse tasks, including navigation, precise tabletop manipulation, and complex deformable or multi-body interactions. Specifically, on the challenging Push-T task, DDP-WM achieves an approximately 9 times inference speedup and improves the MPC success rate from 90% to 98% compared to state-of-the-art dense models.

paragraphs: Robotic planning benefits from world models that predict how a scene will change, but dense Transformer models can be expensive to run. DDP-WM starts from the hypothesis that different parts of a scene need different kinds of prediction. Physical interactions drive sparse primary changes, while surrounding context requires secondary background updates.

The architecture separates these two kinds of dynamics. It processes historical information efficiently and localizes the primary changes, then uses cross-attention to update the background. This division allocates computation according to the proposed structure of scene evolution. The framework also provides a smooth optimization landscape for planners, connecting prediction efficiency with the process of choosing actions.

Experiments cover navigation, precise tabletop manipulation, and deformable or multi-body interactions, with reported improvements in both efficiency and performance. On Push-T, DDP-WM runs inference approximately nine times faster than the compared state-of-the-art dense models and increases model predictive control success from 90% to 98%. These results support the proposed decomposition across the evaluated tasks without establishing that every scene follows it.
summary.tldr: DDP-WM separates primary physical dynamics from background updates to make robotic world models faster and more effective.

title: DDP-WM: Disentangled Dynamics Prediction for Efficient World Models

abstract: Modeling complex dynamics from observational data is fundamental to scientific discovery and artificial intelligence. However, existing approaches are often plagued by the entanglement of static state representations and instantaneous motion, leading to accumulated errors and off-manifold hallucinations where predicted trajectories violate intrinsic geometric constraints. To address this, we propose Geometric Flow Grounding, a unified framework that enforces dynamic evolution strictly along the tangent bundle of the learned data manifold via a differentiable Neural Tangent Projection Layer. By geometrically decoupling state representation from tangential dynamics, our method generalizes across diverse data regimes. In scientific discovery, GFG reduces numerical aliasing and improves long-horizon stability in sparse dynamical systems, while recovering interpretable gene regulatory motifs from single-cell data. For trustworthy AI, the projection residual provides a zero-shot metric for deepfake video detection by revealing inconsistencies with the implicit flow of pre-trained world models. Our results establish manifold-constrained projection as a universal operator for both discovering natural laws and verifying synthetic content. Code will be available at https://github.com/yuchang97/GFG-public

paragraphs: Geometric Flow Grounding addresses a problem in learning dynamics from observations: a model can mix up what a state represents with how it is moving. Over time, its predicted trajectory may leave the geometric structure learned from the data. The framework separates state representation from motion to constrain that evolution.

Its differentiable Neural Tangent Projection Layer restricts dynamics to tangent directions of the learned data manifold. These are directions compatible with the local geometry of that representation. The same projection also produces a residual measuring the component inconsistent with the allowed motion, giving the framework a signal for verification as well as prediction.

The reported applications include reduced numerical aliasing and better long-horizon stability in sparse dynamical systems, plus recovery of interpretable gene regulatory motifs from single-cell data. For deepfake detection, the projection residual serves as a zero-shot measure of inconsistency with pretrained world-model flows. Together, these applications demonstrate how one geometric operation can support both discovering dynamics and checking synthetic content.
summary.tldr: Geometric Flow Grounding constrains learned motion to manifold-compatible directions, supporting dynamics discovery and zero-shot deepfake detection.

title: Geometric Flow Grounding: A Unified Manifold Decoupling Framework for Dynamics Discovery and Verification

abstract: Adversarial images pose a severe security threat to multimodal large language models through prompt injection. Existing defenses largely lack a principled understanding of the underlying mechanisms and struggle to balance efficiency and fidelity. In this work, we show that successful adversarial attacks do not rely on the entire image uniformly but instead depend on a small subset of critical image tokens. Based on this insight, we propose a defense that first localizes these critical tokens via gradient analysis and then neutralizes them through masking. We show that attribution based on output probabilities fails when adversarial attacks preserve the predicted token. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Hidden-State Gradient Norm score for adversarial behavior attribution and prove that its ranking is consistent with that of the full adversarial loss gradient, providing a theoretical guarantee for accurate localization. GTM requires only a single forward–backward pass to identify and zero out a small number of high-scoring tokens, effectively disrupting the adversarial attack path. Extensive experiments on prompt injection and multimodal jailbreak attacks demonstrate that our approach reduces attack success rates (ASR) to near zero while preserving model utility with negligible computational overhead. The code is available at: https://github.com/fish883/GTM-Defense.

paragraphs: Visual prompt injection can redirect a multimodal model through an adversarial image. This paper finds that successful attacks depend on a small set of critical image tokens rather than drawing equally on the whole image. That observation motivates a targeted defense: locate those tokens and mask them to interrupt the attack.

The authors identify a weakness in attribution methods based on output probabilities: they fail when an attack preserves the predicted token. Their alternative, the Hidden-State Gradient Norm score, measures attribution through internal states. They prove that its token ranking agrees with the ranking from the full adversarial-loss gradient, supplying theoretical support for the localization method.

The resulting defense, GTM, needs one forward–backward pass to score tokens and zero out a small number of high-scoring ones. Experiments on visual prompt injection and multimodal jailbreak attacks reduce attack success rates to near zero while preserving utility with negligible reported computational overhead. These results support selective suppression as an efficient defense in the evaluated attacks, with localization central to balancing protection and useful image information.
summary.tldr: GTM identifies and masks a few influential image tokens, reducing tested visual attacks to near-zero success while preserving model utility.

abstract: The goal of feature induction is to automatically create nonlinearcombinations of existing features as additional input features to improveclassification accuracy. Typically, nonlinear features are introduced into asupport vector machine (SVM) through a nonlinear kernel function. Onedisadvantage of such an approach is that the feature space induced by a kernelfunction is usually of high dimension and therefore will substantiallyincrease the chance of over-fitting the training data. Another disadvantage isthat nonlinear features are induced implicitly and therefore are difficult forpeople to understand which induced features are critical to the classificationperformance. In this paper, we propose a boosting-style algorithm that canexplicitly induces important nonlinear features for SVMs. We present empiricalstudies with discussion to show that this approach is effective in improvingclassification accuracy for SVMs. The comparison with an SVM model usingnonlinear kernels also indicates that this approach is effective and robust,particularly when the number of training data is small.

paragraphs: Feature induction creates nonlinear combinations of existing inputs and adds them as features for classification. This paper examines how to do that explicitly for support vector machines. The authors identify two concerns with nonlinear kernels: their induced feature spaces are usually high-dimensional, increasing the chance of overfitting, and their implicit features make important combinations difficult to understand.

The proposed boosting-style algorithm explicitly induces important nonlinear features for an SVM. This makes the created combinations part of the model's input representation. The approach addresses the authors' concern about identifying which induced features matter while pursuing the original goal of improving classification accuracy.

Empirical studies show that the method improves SVM classification accuracy. Comparisons with SVMs using nonlinear kernels also indicate effectiveness and robustness, particularly when training data are scarce. These findings support explicit feature induction as a useful approach in the evaluated settings, with the reported small-sample behavior especially relevant to the paper's concern about overfitting.
summary.tldr: A boosting-style algorithm explicitly creates nonlinear SVM features and shows effective, robust performance, especially with small training sets.

title: Robust feature induction for support vector machines
Qualitative reinforcement learning

abstract: Graph clustering has become ubiquitous in the study of relational data sets. We examine two simple algorithms: a new graphical adaptation of the k -medoids algorithm and the Girvan-Newman method based on edge betweenness centrality. We show that they can be effective at discovering the latent groups or communities that are defined by the link structure of a graph. However, both approaches rely on prohibitively expensive computations, given the size of modern relational data sets. Network structure indices (NSIs) are a proven technique for indexing network structure and efficiently finding short paths. We show how incorporating NSIs into these graph clustering algorithms can overcome these complexity limitations. We also present promising quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the modified algorithms on synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: Graph clustering seeks groups whose relationships are expressed through links in a network. This paper examines two approaches: a new graph adaptation of k-medoids and the Girvan-Newman method, which uses edge betweenness centrality. The authors show that both can uncover latent communities defined by graph connectivity, making them useful for relational data.

Their obstacle is computational cost. The operations needed by these approaches can become prohibitively expensive for large relational datasets. The paper brings in network structure indices, an existing technique for indexing network structure and finding short paths efficiently. Incorporating these indices into the clustering algorithms targets the expensive graph computations that restrict their practical use.

The authors show how this incorporation can overcome the identified complexity limitations and evaluate the modified methods on synthetic and real datasets. They describe the quantitative and qualitative results as promising. The contribution is thus an efficiency-oriented adaptation of useful clustering ideas, supported by evidence about both measured behavior and the communities produced, rather than a claim that every network will yield equally strong results.
summary.tldr: Network structure indices reduce expensive graph computations in two community-detection methods, with promising evaluations on synthetic and real data.

title: Graph clustering with network structure indices

abstract: The kernel stick-breaking process (KSBP) is employed to segment general imagery, imposing the condition that patches (small blocks of pixels) that are spatially proximate are more likely to be associated with the same cluster (segment). The number of clusters is not set a priori and is inferred from the hierarchical Bayesian model. Further, KSBP is integrated with a shared Dirichlet process prior to simultaneously model multiple images, inferring their inter-relationships. This latter application may be useful for sorting and learning relationships between multiple images. The Bayesian inference algorithm is based on a hybrid of variational Bayesian analysis and local sampling. In addition to providing details on the model and associated inference framework, example results are presented for several image-analysis problems.

paragraphs: Image segmentation groups parts of an image into regions. This paper applies a kernel stick-breaking process to small pixel patches, making nearby patches more likely to share a segment. Spatial proximity therefore influences the grouping probabilistically. The hierarchical Bayesian model also infers the number of segments, so that number does not have to be fixed beforehand.

The authors extend the approach to multiple images by combining the kernel stick-breaking process with a shared Dirichlet process prior. This allows the images to be modeled together while their interrelationships are inferred. The shared model connects segmentation with a broader image-analysis goal: learning how different images relate to one another.

Inference combines variational Bayesian analysis with local sampling. The paper describes this computational framework and presents example results for several image-analysis problems. The authors suggest that the multiple-image formulation may be useful for sorting images and learning their relationships. That proposed usefulness follows from the model's ability to share information across images, while remaining a qualified application claim.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model infers image segments and their number, while a shared prior enables joint modeling of relationships across images.

title: Hierarchical kernel stick-breaking process for multi-task image analysis

abstract: We consider the general, widely applicable problem of selecting from n real-valued random variables a subset of size m of those with the highest means, based on as few samples as possible. This problem,which we denote Explore-m, is a core aspect in several stochastic optimization algorithms, and applications of simulation and industrial engineering. The theoretical basis for our work is an extension of a previous formulation using multi-armed bandits that is devoted to identifying just the one best of n random variables(Explore-1). In addition to providing PAC bounds for the general case, we tailor our theoretically grounded approach to work efficiently in practice. Empirical comparisons of the resulting sampling algorithm against state-of-the-art subset selection strategies demonstrate significant gains in sample efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select a group of promising options when each option produces random numerical outcomes. Given n such options, the objective is to identify m with the highest mean outcomes while taking as few samples as possible. The authors call this problem Explore-m and connect it to stochastic optimization, simulation, and industrial engineering.

Their theoretical starting point is a multi-armed bandit formulation for identifying a single best option. They extend that formulation to selecting several options and establish probably approximately correct bounds for the general case. These bounds provide a formal account of selection reliability and accuracy within that framework.

The authors also adapt their theoretically grounded approach for practical sampling efficiency. Empirical comparisons with state-of-the-art subset-selection strategies show significant reductions in the samples required. The contribution therefore addresses both the broader selection problem and how to solve it effectively in practice. Its focus is learning which options belong in a good subset from limited observations.
summary.tldr: An algorithm for selecting multiple high-mean bandit arms combines PAC guarantees with demonstrated gains in sample efficiency.

title: Efficient Selection of Multiple Bandit Arms: Theory and Practice

abstract: Discrete mixed membership modeling and continuous latent factor modeling (also known as matrix factorization) are two popular, complementary approaches to dyadic data analysis. In this work, we develop a fully Bayesian framework for integrating the two approaches into unified Mixed Membership Matrix Factorization (M3F) models. We introduce two M3F models, derive Gibbs sampling inference procedures, and validate our methods on the Each Movie, Movie Lens, and Netflix Prize collaborative filtering datasets. We find that, even when fitting fewer parameters, the M3F models outperform state-of-the-art latent factor approaches on all benchmarks, yielding the greatest gains in accuracy on sparsely-rated, high-variance items.

paragraphs: Data describing interactions between two kinds of entities, such as users and movies, can be modeled through discrete memberships or continuous latent factors. These approaches capture complementary forms of structure. This paper combines them in a fully Bayesian framework called Mixed Membership Matrix Factorization, abbreviated M3F.

The authors introduce two models and derive Gibbs-sampling procedures for inference. The shared framework incorporates both mixed membership and matrix factorization into the explanation of the observed interactions. This gives a unified modeling approach in which discrete and continuous latent descriptions can contribute to the same prediction task.

Evaluation uses the Each Movie, Movie Lens, and Netflix Prize collaborative-filtering datasets. The authors report that M3F outperforms the compared state-of-the-art latent-factor approaches on every benchmark, even while fitting fewer parameters. The largest accuracy gains occur for items with sparse ratings and high rating variance. Those findings support combining the two modeling approaches, especially for the difficult item groups highlighted in the experiments.
summary.tldr: M3F combines discrete mixed memberships with continuous factors and improves collaborative-filtering accuracy on all reported benchmarks.

title: Mixed Membership Matrix Factorization

abstract: Time plays an essential role in the diffusion of information, influence and disease over networks. In many cases we only observe when a node copies information, makes a decision or becomes infected -- but the connectivity, transmission rates between nodes and transmission sources are unknown. Inferring the underlying dynamics is of outstanding interest since it enables forecasting, influencing and retarding infections, broadly construed. To this end, we model diffusion processes as discrete networks of continuous temporal processes occurring at different rates. Given cascade data -- observed infection times of nodes -- we infer the edges of the global diffusion network and estimate the transmission rates of each edge that best explain the observed data. The optimization problem is convex. The model naturally (without heuristics) imposes sparse solutions and requires no parameter tuning. The problem decouples into a collection of independent smaller problems, thus scaling easily to networks on the order of hundreds of thousands of nodes. Experiments on real and synthetic data show that our algorithm both recovers the edges of diffusion networks and accurately estimates their transmission rates from cascade data.

paragraphs: Diffusion data often reveal when nodes adopt information or become infected without revealing who transmitted to whom. This paper uses those observed times to infer both the network's edges and the transmission rate associated with each edge. It therefore seeks to recover connectivity and the timing dynamics of spread together.

The model represents a discrete network with continuous-time transmission processes operating at different rates. It selects edges and rates that best explain the observed cascades through a convex optimization problem. The formulation naturally produces sparse solutions and, as stated in the abstract, requires no parameter tuning. Sparsity follows from the model rather than an added heuristic.

The optimization separates into independent smaller problems, supporting networks with hundreds of thousands of nodes. Experiments on real and synthetic data show recovery of network edges and accurate estimates of their transmission rates. These findings support using cascade timing to reconstruct otherwise hidden diffusion dynamics. Such reconstruction provides information relevant to forecasting and influencing spread, which motivates the problem.
summary.tldr: A scalable convex model infers diffusion-network edges and transmission rates from observed cascade times.

title: Uncovering the Temporal Dynamics of Diffusion Networks
